turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, sir. Did you just have a birthday? I don't have my chart with me right now, the nurse is bringing it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good afternoon, sir. Yes, I just turned fifty five.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You identify as African American, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When was your last visit, sir?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it was on July twenty ninth two thousand eight.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I see. Did we go over your M R I results?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I was having those new seizures, remember?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I do. Well, the M R I demonstrated right contrast temporal mass.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What exactly does that mean, doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, given this mass, and your new seizures, I am concerned that this could be a high grade glioma, we'll need to do more tests.

reference_section: The patient is a 55-year-old African-American male that was last seen in clinic on 07/29/2008 with diagnosis of new onset seizures and an MRI scan, which demonstrated right contrast-enhancing temporal mass.  Given the characteristics of this mass and his new onset seizures, it is significantly concerning for a high-grade glioma.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: How old is the patient?

turns.text: She was sedated with Ativan, correct?

turns.text: Did they find anything?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The report showed what we believe to be free air under her right diaphragm.

reference_section: The patient is a 77-year-old female who is unable to give any information.  She has been sedated with Ativan and came into the emergency room obtunded and unable to give any history.  On a chest x-ray for what appeared to be shortness of breath she was found to have what was thought to be free air under the right diaphragm.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is your family medical history?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My parents do not have any health conditions. I have two half brothers that are in good health as well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are your brothers?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Twenty six and twenty eight. My grandmother on my mom's side had D V T in her leg. I think she was in her forty's.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any family history of diabetes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think my aunt from my dad's side of the family and my cousins on my mom's side of the family are diabetic? Oh. My great grandfather had bone cancer.  He was in his eighties. My mom's brother was recently diagnosed with leukemia. He is around fifty years old. Then my dad's dad had colon cancer at seventy three. He had it since he was sixty eight, though. I think that is it.

reference_section: Two half-brothers, ages 26 and 28, both in good health.  Parents are in good health.  A maternal great-grandmother had a deep venous thrombosis (DVT) of leg in her 40s.  A maternal great-uncle developed leukemia around age 50.  A maternal great-grandfather had bone cancer around age 80.  His paternal grandfather died of colon cancer at age 73, which he had had since age 68.  Adult-onset diabetes is present in distant relatives on both sides.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Nice to see you again, miss. I see your last visit was back on August tenth two thousand and four. How are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi, doctor. Nice to see you again as well. I've been doing fine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How is your husband doing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: He's doing fine. Just working a lot.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great! I hope the work isn't getting him too stressed out. Also, I need to fill out the ethnicity section in your paperwork; it seems to be missing. What ethnicity do you identify as?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, yes. I am white.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thanks! Are you still working too?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I am. My secretary position has been super stressful lately.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I understand. How is your acne doing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think it's been getting better, but I've had this rash for the last two months on my chest, stomach, neck, and back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Let me take a look at this rash. I see you have these small folliculitis lesions that are pus filled bumps centered on your hair.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, no. Is that bad?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's treatable. It seems like it's happening because your acne is flaring up.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, really. Is it because I stopped my medication for the last three days?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I forgot what I prescribed you. Let me take a look at my notes. Oh, I see. I prescribed you five hundred milligrams of Amoxicillin to take twice a day and a point one Tazorac cream. Have those been working?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, they have. I noticed my face started to get better.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Continue to take those and try not to stop it. Have you been trying anything else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I actually started going to Healing Waters to get photofacials.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Has that been helpful?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, it has, but I want a faster treatment. I'm only forty nine and want to look younger. Are there any procedures or skin care products that can be used to help my face look better?

reference_section: The patient is a 49-year-old white female, established patient to Dermatology, last seen in the office on 08/10/2004.  She comes in today for reevaluation of her acne plus she has had what she calls a rash for the past two months now on her chest, stomach, neck, and back.  On examination, this is a flaring of her acne with small folliculitis lesions.  The patient has been taking amoxicillin 500 mg b.i.d. and using Tazorac cream 0.1, and her face is doing well, but she has been out of her medicine now for three days also.  She has also been getting photofacials at Healing Waters and was wondering about what we could offer as far as cosmetic procedures and skin care products, etc.  The patient is married.  She is a secretary.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello! How are you doing today?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long have your legs been swollen like this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They swell up like this from time to time but it has been happening for a long time. I also can't feel my toes.

turns.text: How long has the numbness of your toes been going on?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: A long time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you able to get up and move around?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I can't walk because of my weight. It is too much for me. When I try to get up, I get short of breath. I have C O P D. I can't do much but sit here. I am in a lot of pain all the time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When you get up and try to walk around, do you experience any chest pain or visual problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I just feel out of breath.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you take anything for your pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I take OxyContin for my back pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you ever experience any constipation, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I have these sore on my legs, that ooze.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Let me look.

reference_section: He says he has had numbness of toes for a long time.  He denies any visual problems.  His legs have been swelling up from time to time for a long time.  He also has history of COPD and gets short of breath with minimal activity.  He is also not able to walk due to his weight.  He has had ulcers on his legs, which he gets discharge from.  He has chronic back pain and takes OxyContin.  He denies any constipation, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting.  There is no chest pain.  He does get short of breath on walking.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, sir. Welcome back. Looks like we are going to revaluate your heart issues. You have a history of ischemic cardiac disease, correct? Can you also state your age?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sixty eight. Yes. I saw doctor X Y Z in February two thousand four and he made me walk on a treadmill for eight minutes. Do you have the results from that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I do. The scan showed some wall scarring but also that the amount of blood leaving your heart per contraction was normal. Do you experience any chest pain, palpitations, difficulty sleeping at night, leg or arm swelling, or shortness of breath while lying flat?

turns.text: Have you had any other pain any where else in your body?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is the back pain been mild, moderate, or severe?

turns.text: I would say mild. I have also been having cramping in both calves.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long has that been going on?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: For the past year but it stopped about two months ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any weakness in the left leg?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I don't think so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any pain around right leg and the area of numbness and tingling?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Everything that is going on with my right leg has pretty much been the same since it started six months ago. I have not gotten worse or better.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any bowel or bladder incontinence? Any radicular pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did you first see a doctor for the issue? I remember that you told me you saw a different provider prior to coming to see me.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I saw the other doctor in October. That was a couple of months before I came to see you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see in your chart that we did a CT scan that shows degenerative changes, but nothing obviously abnormal. Remind me why we did not do a MRI of your spine?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I cannot have an MRI because of my ear implant.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is unfortunate. It looks like we were able to do an EMG and nerve conduction studies. What medications are you taking currently?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had an elevated CK before I started taking stat medications.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What medications are those?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am not taking Lipitor anymore. I think I took it for about fifteen months.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know what your levels of your CK were before you started taking medication?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I thought that my CK was in the five hundred or six hundreds prior to starting it. Once I started it, my levels increased to about eight hundred and then came down to about five hundred again when it was stopped. I recently stopped taking Lipitor because my levels were up to the thousand's and then my CK apparently has returned to about the five hundreds or six hundreds.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I don't see any labs in your chart. Did your primary do labs for your CK levels?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, he did.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Have you started any other medications?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I just started Zetia.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you experienced any weakness or pain after starting Zetia?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you remind me how old you are?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am fifty-five.

reference_section: The patient is a 55-year-old gentleman who presents for further evaluation of right leg weakness.  He has difficulty recollecting the exact details and chronology of his problem.  To the best of his recollection, he thinks that about six months ago he developed weakness of his right leg.  He describes that he is reaching to get something from a cabinet and he noticed that he was unable to stand on his right toe.  Since that time, he has had difficulty pushing off when he walks.  He has mild tingling and numbness in his toes, but this has been a chronic problem and nothing new since he has developed the weakness.  He has chronic mild back pain, but this has been persistent for many years and has not changed.  He has experienced cramps in both calves for the past year.  This dissipated about two months ago.  He does not think that his left leg is weak.  He does not have any bowel or bladder incontinence.  There is no radicular pain.  He does not think that the problem is progressive, meaning that the weakness that he perceives in his right leg is no different than when it was six months ago. He first sought medical attention for this problem in October.  He then saw you a couple of months later.  He has undergone an EMG and nerve conduction studies.  Unfortunately, he cannot undergo an MRI of his spine because he has an ear implant.  He has had a CT scan that shows degenerative changes, but nothing obviously abnormal. In addition, the patient has hyperCKemia.  He tells me that he has had an elevated CK prior to starting taking stat medications, although this is not entirely clear to me.  He thinks that he is not taking Lipitor for about 15 months and thought that his CK was in the 500 or 600s prior to starting it.  Once it was started, it increased to about 800 and then came down to about 500 when it was stopped.  He then had a recent bump again up to the 1000 and since Lipitor has been stopped, his CK apparently has returned to about the 500 or 600s.  I do no have any laboratory data to support these statements by the patient, but he seems to be up to speed on this.  More recently, he has been started taking Zetia. He does not have any proximal weakness.  He denies any myalgias.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Well, I went back to Doctor X Y Z, and then he thought that the symptoms I was having were coming from my right hip.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did he do any imaging on this hip?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I had some done when I saw him on, um, August fourth two thousand four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, the x rays we took today show marked degenerative changes, and a progression since the x rays taken back in August when you saw Doctor X Y Z.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh no. Oh, he also did the injections into my right hip.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When was that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it was on April seventh two thousand five, and the last time I saw him was April fifteenth.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is that when you had the last injections?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has anyone talked to you about doing a hip replacement?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, but right now I'm not sure if I want to do it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you still having pain in that right hip today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it still hurts.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What makes the pain worse?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, anything that puts weight on this hip hurts really bad.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, if it hurts that bad you should be using a cane. Did you ever get one?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I used one to come in here today, in fact.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good. Do you have any other appointments scheduled?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I made an appointment with an orthopedist in Newton. It's closer to my house.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's fine. What medicines are you taking?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I take the generic for Ultracet. Sometimes I take as many as four times a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does this help the pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I'm still in pretty significant pain, doctor.

reference_section: The patient comes back to see me today.  She is a pleasant 77-year-old Caucasian female who had seen Dr. XYZ with right leg pain.  She has a history of prior laminectomy for spinal stenosis.  She has seen Dr. XYZ with low back pain and lumbar scoliosis post laminectomy syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, and clinical right L2 radiculopathy, which is symptomatic.  Dr. XYZ had performed two right L2-L3 transforaminal epidural injections, last one in March 2005.  She was subsequently seen and Dr. XYZ found most of her remaining symptoms are probably coming from her right hip.  An x-ray of the hip showed marked degenerative changes with significant progression of disease compared to 08/04/2004 study.  Dr. XYZ had performed right intraarticular hip injection on 04/07/2005.  She was last seen on 04/15/2005.  At that time, she had the hip injection that helped her briefly with her pain.  She is not sure whether or not she wants to proceed with hip replacement.  We recommend she start using a cane and had continued her on some pain medicines. The patient comes back to see me today.  She continues to complain of significant pain in her right hip, especially with weightbearing or with movement.  She said she had made an appointment to see an orthopedic surgeon in Newton as it is closer and more convenient for her.  She is taking Ultracet or other the generic it sounds like, up to four times daily.  She states she can take this much more frequently as she still has significant pain symptoms.  She is using a cane to help her ambulate.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient has a previous history of a left traumatic wrist injury, which has left him with a chronic scapholunate problem and possibly other problems in his wrist.  However, he was doing relatively fine and tolerating the wrist soreness that he had, which is day to day, but it has not gotten much worse until this injury.  Once he lifted the object out of the back of his car and it started to hurt, then he was significantly more affected than he was before, and now pain is more on the ulnar side of his wrist than on the radial side of his wrist.  He is here now for evaluation.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello there, how are you doing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm doing good. Thank you. How about you?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, same old, same old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, looks like we're here to discuss your diet. Is that right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yep. That's right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let me look through your chart. It looks like you have high lipid levels, high blood pressure and a possibility for a metabolic syndrome.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That looks like my chart. I'm kind of struggling here and I need your help.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, tell me did you follow the meal plan that we gave to you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I tried for many weeks to follow that meal plan that you gave me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, did it help?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't know. I felt like I was still gaining weight instead of losing it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you follow it exactly as you are, as you were asked to do?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I tried my best. But I feel like I am not doing it correctly or something.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, tell me what kind of activities are you doing? How much physical activity are you doing on a regular basis?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I try to walk around one and a half to two miles like every other day, but I'm spending more time in my garden and doing the yard work by myself.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's good. Gardening gets-- can get hard and it helps you keep active.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh yes, picking up all those pots from here to there and knowing that backyard of mine, it's a hard job.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Tell me what brings you here today? Like how can I help you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: So, I think the meal plan that you gave was not working for me and there was definitely some weight gain, so I went back to my old South Beach Diet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. What were the results with your South Beach Diet then? Was it effective?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was able to get some pounds off. I felt pretty good about it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's good. Then what's the issue?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, you see, deep in my heart I know this South Beach Diet is not a healthy diet for me and that's why I'm back to you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I appreciate your honesty. You don't know how happy you made me by saying that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. You know, I'm here. So, tell me what to do to lose all this extra weight and how to enforce a low fat diet? What are your recommendations for that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's set a plan for you.

reference_section: This is a followup dietary consultation for hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and possible metabolic syndrome.  The patient reports that she has worked hard for a number of weeks following the meal plan prescribed, but felt like she was gaining weight and not losing weight on it.  She is not sure that she was following it accurately.  She is trying to walk 1-1/2 to 2 miles every other day, but is increasing her time in the garden and doing other yard work as well.  Once she started experiencing some weight gain, she went back to her old South Beach Diet and felt like she was able to take some of that weight off.  However she realizes that the South Beach Diet is not a healthy diet for her and so is coming back for better instruction on safe weight loss and low-fat eating.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: You have hypothyroidism, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any fever, chills, or night sweats?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.text: No.

turns.text: Any hearing changes or ear problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any shortness of breath, cough, coughing up excessive mucus or blood, or breathing problems?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, how about any kind of chest pain or discomfort, trouble breathing at night or when lying down, palpitations or heart attacks?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.text: Any urinary problems, anything with your kidneys?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, I know you have had some anemia in the past, any new problems with that? Any blackouts, convulsions, seizures, paralysis, strokes, or headaches?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I have not had anemic labs in a while. And, no to any of those things you just listed as well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Alright, good. That is it for all of my symtom questions. Thank you for bearing with me for that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No problem, I am just glad to not be experiencing a lot of those.

reference_section: General:  No fever, chills, or night sweats.  Weight stable. HEENT:  No sudden blindness, diplopia, loss of vision, i.e., in one eye or other visual changes.  No hearing changes or ear problems.  No swallowing problems or mouth lesions. Endocrine:  Hypothyroidism but no polyuria or polydipsia.  She watches her blood sugars.  They have been doing quite well. Respiratory:  No shortness of breath, cough, sputum production, hemoptysis or breathing problems. Cardiovascular:  No chest pain or chest discomfort.  No paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, palpitations, or heart attacks. GI:  As mentioned, has had diarrhea though thought to be possibly due to Clostridium difficile colitis that now has gotten better.  She has had some irritable bowel syndrome and bowel abnormalities for years. GU:  No urinary problems, dysuria, polyuria or polydipsia, kidney stones, or recent infections.  No vaginal bleeding or discharge. Musculoskeletal:  As above. Hematological:  She has had some anemia in the past. Neurological:  No blackouts, convulsions, seizures, paralysis, strokes, or headaches.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient is a 56-year-old right-handed female with longstanding intermittent right low back pain, who was involved in a motor vehicle accident in September of 2005.  At that time, she did not notice any specific injury.  Five days later, she started getting abnormal right low back pain.  At this time, it radiates into the buttocks down the posterior aspect of her thigh and into the right lateral aspect of her calf.  Symptoms are worse when sitting for any length of time, such as driving a motor vehicle.  Mild symptoms when walking for long periods of time.  Relieved by standing and lying down.  She denies any left leg symptoms or right leg weakness.  No change in bowel or bladder function.  Symptoms have slowly progressed.  She has had Medrol Dosepak and analgesics, which have not been very effective.  She underwent a spinal epidural injection, which was effective for the first few hours, but she had recurrence of the pain by the next day.  This was done four and a half weeks ago. On examination, lower extremities strength is full and symmetric.  Straight leg raising is normal.

turns.text: Hm, what kind of pain is it? Like sharp pain or dull?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, did you try any medicines?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let's try something stronger, I will write you a prescription for it. You can take it for a week and if your pain does not improve, we will take some x rays.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you again eighty-five?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Overall, you do look better today and these medicines should take care of the pain.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Take care.

reference_section: This is a return visit to the renal clinic for this patient.  She is an 85-year-old woman with history as noted above.  Her last visit was approximately four months ago.  Since that time, the patient has been considerably more compliant with her antihypertensive medications and actually had a better blood pressure reading today than she had had for many visits previously.  She is not reporting any untoward side effect.  She is not having weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, abdominal pain, chest pain, shortness of breath or difficulty breathing.  She has no orthopnea.  Her exercise capacity is about the same.  The only problem she has is musculoskeletal and that pain in the right buttock, she thinks originating from her spine.  No history of extremity pain.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient is a previously healthy 2-month-old female, who has had a cough and congestion for the past week.  The mother has also reported irregular breathing, which she describes as being rapid breathing associated with retractions.  The mother states that the cough is at times paroxysmal and associated with posttussive emesis.  The patient has had short respiratory pauses following the coughing events.  The patient's temperature has ranged between 102 and 104.  She has had a decreased oral intake and decreased wet diapers.  The brother is also sick with URI symptoms, and the patient has had no diarrhea.  The mother reports that she has begun to regurgitate after her feedings.  She did not do this previously.

reference_section: The patient had several episodes where she felt like her face was going to twitch, which she could suppress it with grimacing movements of her mouth and face.  She reports she is still having right posterior head pressure like sensations approximately one time per week.  These still are characterized by a tingling, pressure like sensation that often has a feeling as though water is running down on her hair.  This has also decreased in frequency occurring approximately one time per week and seems to respond to over-the-counter analgesics such as Aleve.  Lastly during conversation today, she brought again the problem of daydreaming at work and noted that she occasionally falls asleep when sitting in non-stimulating environments or in front of the television.  She states that she feels fatigued all the time and does not get good sleep.  She describes it as insomnia, but upon questioning she works from 4 till mid night and then gets home and cannot go to sleep for approximately two hours and wakes up reliably by 9.00 a.m. each morning and sleeps no more than five to six hours ever, but usually five hours.  Her sleep is relatively uninterrupted except for the need to get up and go to the bathroom.  She thinks she may snore, but she is not sure.  She does not recall any events of awakening and gasping for breath.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient is a 2-1/2-year-old female with a history of known febrile seizures, who was placed on Keppra oral solution at 150 mg b.i.d. to help prevent febrile seizures.  Although this has been a very successful treatment in terms of her febrile seizure control, she is now having occasional brief periods of pauses and staring, where she becomes unresponsive, but does not lose her postural tone.  The typical spell according to dad last anywhere from 10 to 15 seconds, mom says 3 to 4 minutes, which likely means probably somewhere in the 30- to 40-second period of time.  Mom did note that an episode had happened outside of a store recently, was associated with some perioral cyanosis, but there has never been a convulsive activity noted.  There have been no recent changes in her Keppra dosing and she is currently only at 20 mg/kg per day, which is overall a low dose for her.

reference_section: This patient presents to the office today because of some problems with her right hand.  It has been going tingling and getting numb periodically over several weeks.  She just recently moved her keyboard down at work.  She is hoping that will help.  She is worried about carpal tunnel.  She does a lot of repetitive type activities.  It is worse at night.  If she sleeps on it a certain way, she will wake up and it will be tingling then she can usually shake out the tingling, but nonetheless it is very bothersome for her.  It involves mostly the middle finger, although, she says it also involves the first and second digits on the right hand.  She has some pain in her thumb as well.  She thinks that could be arthritis.

turns.text: I just had few questions. Can you tell me about my diagnosis?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Sure. It's called Serotonin syndrome, ma'am. After careful evaluation of your labs, we found out that your white count and C P K was high, and those abnormalities lined up with serotonin syndrome. What are you experiencing right now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have been very restless and easily agitated, I have diarrhea. But no fever or shakiness.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: These can match serotonin syndrome as well. You deny any fever, tremor or hypperflexia so we will give you some IV fluids and I will check on you in an hour or so.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Looks like your C P K counts improved with I V fluids and after discontinuing Prozac.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: How are the counts now? Are they normal? Because I feel normal.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, your C P K and white blood cell counts have come back down. Almost normal now.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My husband left me two weeks ago. My panic attacks are increasing day by day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, I see that you have a history of panic attacks and you do have depression and anxiety, is that correct? Last Friday, I talked to psychiatrist about your issues, and he recommended Cymbalta as an alternative to Prozac.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I stopped taking Prozac, and I am going to see him on Monday or Tuesday. I have a counselor too.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I do think it will be difficult to go home alone but my daughter is coming to visit me in two weeks.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh wow.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's nice. Do you have someone who can drop you home and help you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I have a friend who does that, I am staying with her for next three days.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay that sounds good. Just continue with your medications for high blood pressure and diabetes as well. So, we treated your imbalance issues and gave you IV fluids, you do not have any more diarrhea, right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's right.

reference_section: 1.  Serotonin syndrome.  After reevaluation of the patient including evaluation of the lab abnormalities it was felt that she likely had serotonin syndrome with obvious restlessness, increased bowel activity, agitation, and elevated white count and CPK.  She did not have fever, tremor or hyperreflexia.  Her CPK improved with IV fluids.  She dramatically improved with this discontinuation of her Prozac.  Her white count came back down towards normal.  At time of discharge, she was really feeling back to normal. 2.  Depression and anxiety with history of panic attacks exacerbated by her husband leaving her 2 weeks ago.  We discussed this.  Also, discussed the situation with a psychiatrist who is available on Friday and I discussed the situation with the patient.  In regards to her medications, we are discontinuing the Prozac and she is being reevaluated by Dr. X on Monday or Tuesday.  Cymbalta has been recommended as a good alternative medication for her.  The patient does have a counselor.  It is going to be difficult for her to go home alone.  I discussed the resources with her.  She has a daughter who will be coming to town in a couple of weeks, but she does have a friend that she can call and stay the next few days with. 3.  Hypertension.  She will continue on her usual medications. 4.  Diabetes mellitus.  She will continue on her usual medications. 5.  Diarrhea resolved.  Her electrolyte abnormalities resolved.  She had received fluid rehydration.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That treatment management we are focusing on-

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: This is a 78-year-old male who has prostate cancer with metastatic disease to his bladder and in several locations throughout the skeletal system including the spine and shoulder.  The patient has had problems with hematuria in the past, but the patient noted that this episode began yesterday, and today he has been passing principally blood with very little urine.  The patient states that there is no change in his chronic lower back pain and denies any incontinence of urine or stool.  The patient has not had any fever.  There is no abdominal pain and the patient is still able to pass urine.  The patient has not had any melena or hematochezia.  There is no nausea or vomiting.  The patient has already completed chemotherapy and is beyond treatment for his cancer at this time.  The patient is receiving radiation therapy, but it is targeted to the bones and intended to give symptomatic relief of his skeletal pain and not intended to treat and cure the cancer.  The patient is not enlisted in hospice, but the principle around the patient's current treatment management is focusing on comfort care measures.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Yes, I can see that your liver function test were normal at eighteen and hepatitis C and H I V, both were negative. We took these labs on February seventh. You do not have any local signs of infection, right?  Except acute intestinal problem?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nothing local, but I do have intestinal squeakiness and vomiting.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let me look at your exam.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Abdomen is fine, no fever and no swellings. That's great.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: The patient presents for evaluation after a contaminated needlestick to the index finger. The source patient was tested and found to be negative for HIV. However, he did test positive for hepatitis C. He was described as a carrier without active disease. The patient has been followed with periodic evaluation including blood testing. He has completed a 3 shot series for hepatitis B and had titers drawn that showed protected antibodies. He also was up-to-date on his immunization including tetanus. The patient has been well during this time except for the onset of a intestinal illness being investigated with some squeakiness and vomiting. He had no other symptoms that were suggestive of acute hepatitis. His abdominal exam was normal. He had no generalized lymphadenopathy and no fever. Blood tests were drawn on 02/07/2005. The results of which were reviewed with the patient. His liver function test was normal at 18. His hepatitis C and HIV, both of which were negative. He had no local signs of infection, and otherwise has been doing well except for his acute intestinal illness as described above.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Anything else?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Were your family members young when they were diagnosed, or did they develop it later in life?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I believe they all were adults when they were diagnosed with diabetes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ah, yes. They had adult onset diabetes mellitus.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good morning, young man. Is this your mother?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, nice to mee you. Can you tell me more about your son, please?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Good morning to you too, doctor. Well, he's about five and a half now, and he broke both the bones in his forearm in September of two thousand seven.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did the fracture heal? Generally, children heal very well.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, yes, until he also rebroke it about a month ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I see now, there's an ulnar nail pretty prominently visible under the skin, did he have surgery for this?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, about a month ago now. Should we remove the nail?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We'll have to, even though its early.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What will we do after the nail is removed?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: After that, we'll put him back in a cast for about another three weeks. We'll evaluate him and see how he's doing.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay. What are the risks of infection for this surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The risk of infection is overall very low, honestly its less than one percent. We use antibiotics to control for infection the entire time. Other risks include bleeding, changes in sensation in most of the extremity, or need for longer casting. I would not worry too much about these risks. I have not seen anything bad happen before. Guest_family_1: Will he be asleep for the surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, he won't feel a thing.

reference_section: The patient is a 5-year, 5-month-old male who sustained a both-bone forearm fracture in September 2007.  The fracture healed uneventfully, but then the patient subsequently suffered a refracture one month ago.  The patient had shortening in arms, noted in both bones.  The parents opted for surgical stabilization with nailing.  This was performed one month ago on return visit.  His ulnar nail was quite prominent underneath the skin.  It was decided to remove the ulnar nail early and place the patient in another cast for 3 weeks. Risks and benefits of the surgery were discussed with the mother.  Risk of surgery incudes risks of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation in most of the extremity, need for longer casting.  All questions were answered and mother agreed to above plan.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: Mother died of a stroke at age 58. Father had CAD and HTN. The patient quit smoking in 1991, but was a heavy smoker (2-3ppd) for many years. He had been a feed salesman all of his adult life.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: My baby is sick.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Don't worry, I will help you.

turns.text: He has had a fever for five days.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old is he?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Just eighteen months. He is a Swedish American.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You gave him medication?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, he finished Amoxil several days ago for sinus infection.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: He takes Zyrtec as well right?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes. For allergies.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Is the fever constant throughout the day or it fluctuates?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: It is higher at night.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you checked it?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, it was one o two point six for two days. I have not checked it since then. But isn't it strange just when I thought to bring him to the doctor, he is better.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ha, that tends to happen?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: His tooth is coming out.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No wonder! Maybe that's why he is fussy and drooling so much.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah. How about any diarrhea or vomiting?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, he doesn't have that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Cough?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No coughing.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you seen any change in the color of his mucous that is coming out of his nose?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, his snots are discolored in the morning but not so much in the day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is he eating well? He seems hungry?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, yeah.

reference_section: This is an 18-month-old white male here with his mother for complaint of intermittent fever for the past five days.  Mother states he just completed Amoxil several days ago for a sinus infection.  Patient does have a past history compatible with allergic rhinitis and he has been taking Zyrtec serum.  Mother states that his temperature usually elevates at night.  Two days his temperature was 102.6.  Mother has not taken it since, and in fact she states today he seems much better.  He is cutting an eye tooth that causes him to be drooling and sometimes fussy.  He has had no vomiting or diarrhea.  There has been no coughing.  Nose secretions are usually discolored in the morning, but clear throughout the rest of the day.  Appetite is fine.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Good morning, Miss XYZ.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, I hear from my nurses you have F C R tendinitis. Have you seen another doctor for this?

turns.text: Okay, thank you for explaining that for me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You're very welcome, my dear. So, you don't have his reports, but do you remember how this has been treated in the past?

turns.text: I see. So, what do you do for fun? Do you have any hobbies?

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: XYZ was seen by Dr. ABC for an FCR tendinitis.  We do not have his reports, but by history she has had two cortisone shots.  She plays musical instruments, and it does bother her from time to time.  She was considering surgery, but she takes ibuprofen and it seems to be well-controlled.  She is here now for consultation.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, ma'am, I see you're a new patient with us.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yep, this is my first time in.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, welcome. Before we get started, how old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm only thirty eight.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you, what seems to be the problem today.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have pain in my hips, but my right hurts more than my left.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long have you been dealing with this pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's been about two years now on the right, and it just started in the left recently.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is the pain getting worse?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, it's been getting worse since it started.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you show me where the pain is?

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: The patient is a 38-year-old woman presenting to our clinic for the first time for evaluation of hip pain, right greater than left, of greater than 2 years duration.  The patient states that she began with right hip pain getting steadily worse over the last 2 years and has now developed some pain in the left hip.  The pain is located laterally as well as anteriorly into the groin.  She states that the pain is present during activities such as walking, and she does get some painful popping and clicking in the right hip.  She is here for evaluation for the first time.  She sought no previous medical attention for this.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We have a fifty eight year old female who was allegedly in her typical healthy state until four o'clock P M on January eighth, nineteen ninety three when she suddenly became blind.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Did she experience any slurred speech or other neurological symptoms?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: She complained of tongue numbness and slurred speech in conjunction with vision loss. She explained that her vision improved slightly on her way to the local E R. She noticed severe blurring right before arrival, but the vision problems worsened shortly after.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Is this the first time she had experienced any of these symptoms?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes. While being evaluated, she became unresponsive. She wasn't responding to deep noxious stimuli.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Did they transfer her?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes. She was transferred to U I H C. Her symptoms improved markedly upon her arrival.

reference_section: This 58 y/o RHF was in her usual healthy state, until 4:00PM, 1/8/93, when she suddenly became blind. Tongue numbness and slurred speech occurred simultaneously with the loss of vision. The vision transiently improved to "severe blurring" enroute to a local ER, but worsened again once there. While being evaluated she became unresponsive, even to deep noxious stimuli. She was transferred to UIHC for further evaluation. Upon arrival at UIHC her signs and symptoms were present but markedly improved.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What complications did you have?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Since stopping the medicine, have these symptoms gone away?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, since I stopped taking the medicine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any pain with urination or blood in your urine?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, nothing to report there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about fever or chills?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, nothing there either.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, it's about every two or three hours, and then maybe once at night.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you controlling your urine well?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I'm having no problems there. It's getting better under stress too, with the pelvic exercises and rehab.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you familiar with the results of this renal ultrasound from August fifth two thousand eight?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It was normal, right?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Basically, yes. There's nohydronephrosis, masses, or stones.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's good to hear.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I hear that you've had E coli few times, once in November of two thousand seven, and then in May and July of two thousand eight.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that sounds familiar.

reference_section: The patient presents today for followup, recently noted for E. coli urinary tract infection.  She was treated with Macrobid for 7 days, and only took one nighttime prophylaxis.  She discontinued this medication to due to skin rash as well as hives.  Since then, this had resolved.  Does not have any dysuria, gross hematuria, fever, chills.  Daytime frequency every two to three hours, nocturia times one, no incontinence, improving stress urinary incontinence after Prometheus pelvic rehabilitation. Renal ultrasound, August 5, 2008, reviewed, no evidence of hydronephrosis, bladder mass or stone.  Discussed. Previous urine cultures have shown E. coli, November 2007, May 7, 2008 and July 7, 2008.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello nurse, who do we have here today?

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: This is a thirty-seven-year-old, left-handed male. He visited us one month ago for headaches, nausea, and vomiting. His exams from that time showed no evidence of bowel obstruction and he was released home.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Was there any improvement after your discharge, sir?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I had the same symptoms on and off after that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What problems are you facing now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am seeing things blurred and having difficulty concentrating. My headaches are worse when sitting up. I notice them first thing in the morning.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How would you describe your headaches?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They're dull, constant, and it feels like as if my head is wrapped in a tight band.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your headache starts from which part of your head?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It normally starts on the forehead and then it kind of goes to the back. It happens like six times a day. Lying down or putting my head down between my knees helps.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What else do you feel along with your headaches?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Like I told the Nurse here before, I get blurry eyesight, nausea and there is vomiting. Any kind of bright light hurts. I'm just afraid of loud sounds.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: I discussed with him about any blind spots, positive visual phenomena, weakness, numbness, tingling or double vision or any speech disorder, but he denies everything.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about your weight?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It has been going up and down like for over past three months. I was one hundred and sixty three and then I know it was one hundred and forty eight at a point.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Today his weight is one hundred and fifty four pounds.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you eating habits in the last, let's say, one month?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It has been bad. I don't feel like eating anymore. Looks like I have lost my appetite.

reference_section: This 37y/o LHM was seen one month prior to this presentation for HA, nausea and vomiting. Gastrointestinal evaluation at that time showed no evidence of bowel obstruction and he was released home. These symptoms had been recurrent since onset. At presentation he complained of mild blurred vision (OU), difficulty concentrating and HA which worsened upon sitting up. The headaches were especially noticeable in the early morning. He described them as non-throbbing headaches. They begin in the bifrontal region and radiate posteriorly. They occurred up to 6 times/day. The HA improved with lying down or dropping the head down between the knees towards the floor. The headaches were associated with blurred vision, nausea,vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. He denied any scotomata or positive visual phenomena. He denies any weakness, numbness, tingling, dysarthria or diplopia. His weight has fluctuated from 163# to 148# over the past 3 months and at present he weighs 154#. His appetite has been especially poor in the past month.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. What do you do for a living?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Right now, I work full time as a project manager.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What does this entail?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have to walk a lot for long periods of time throughout the day.

reference_section: The patient states she lives in a single-level home with her husband, who is in good health and is able to assist with any tasks or activities the patient is having difficulty with.  The patient rates her general health as excellent and denies any smoking and reports very occasional alcohol consumption.  The patient does state that she has completed exercises on a daily basis of one to one and a half hours a day.  However, has not been able to complete these exercise routine since approximately June 2008, secondary to back pain.  The patient is working full-time as a project manager, and is required to do extensive walking at various periods during a workday.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Good afternoon, and who is this with you today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: This is my power of attorney, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any major medical conditions that I should know about, ma'am?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I'm fifty five, and I've had a stroke.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, thank you. So, what brings you in for a visit today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have the urge to use the bathroom all the time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you ever pee on yourself because of this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has this problem been getting worse?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it has been recently.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What medications have you taken for this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've had VESIcare, but it hasn't improved yet. I'm taking Enablex right now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any improvement with that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not yet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has the nursing home done a voiding diary?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, they haven't done that either.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you having any blood in the urine, or pain with urination?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, thankfully I'm not.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about fever or chills?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, none of that either?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about bowel issues?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, but I go through several pairs of Depends a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, and I'm looking at the results of your urodynamics from April of two thousand eight, which we did in the office.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What does that show, doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, it shows significant detrusor instability with involuntary urinary incontinence and low bladder volumes, and the cystoscopy was unremarkable, which is good.

reference_section: This is a 55-year-old female with a history of stroke, who presents today for followup of frequency and urgency with urge incontinence.  This has been progressively worsening, and previously on VESIcare with no improvement.  She continues to take Enablex 50 mg and has not noted any improvement of her symptoms.  The nursing home did not do a voiding diary.  She is accompanied by her power of attorney.  No dysuria, gross hematuria, fever or chills.  No bowel issues and does use several Depends a day. Recent urodynamics in April 2008, here in the office, revealed significant detrusor instability with involuntary urinary incontinence and low bladder volumes, and cystoscopy was unremarkable.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Have you had any medical complications recently?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What was that for?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How is the abscess today?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, what about your medical history?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, thank you. What about newly diagnosed conditions?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I got diagnosed with diabetes too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What symptoms have you been experiencing with your diabetes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I've been peeing a lot, and I've been really thirsty, too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have you been treated for this to date?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I saw the endocrinologists while I was in the hospital, and they gave me insulin.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you still taking the insulin?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I can't afford to pay for it. So, they gave me Glucophage and, um, glyburide.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been taking these?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, exactly as instructed.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, and how do you feel today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Overall, I'd say I'm feeling better.

reference_section: The patient is a 41-year-old white male with a history of HIV disease.  His last CD4 count was 425, viral load was less than 50 in 08/07.  He was recently hospitalized for left gluteal abscess, for which he underwent I&D and he has newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus.  He also has a history of hypertension and hypertriglyceridemia.  He had been having increased urination and thirst.  He was seen in the hospital by the endocrinology staff and treated with insulin while hospitalized and getting treatment for his perirectal abscess.  The endocrine team apparently felt that insulin might be best for this patient, but because of financial issues, elected to place him on Glucophage and glyburide.  The patient reports that he has been taking the medication.  He is in general feeling better.  He says that his gluteal abscess is improving and he will be following up with Surgery today.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: My husband, he is trying to find parking outside.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Remind me, please, when was your last appointment, miss?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it was about three months ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have your diabetes and kidney disease progressed since?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I've had a lot of variability in my glucose control too largely, and recent upper and lower respiratory illnesses.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Who treated you for these?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I didn't see anyone, the symptoms just kind of improved on their own.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see, are you still having difficulties with blood sugar management?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, my two week average is one hundred ninety one, and it was high this morning.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you think caused this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I had problems with my infusion set.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's try a correction bolus. Okay, now your blood sugar is quite low. Let's try to get some glucose and crackers into you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I feel a little better now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, your blood sugar is back up to over one hundred, which is good.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I should be able to manage this on my own.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, Are you having any other medical problems that have interfered with glucose control?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not that I know of.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any diet changes recently?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: A little bit, I've been away traveling and visiting my family for some time.

reference_section: This is a return visit to the renal clinic for the patient where she is followed up for diabetes and kidney disease management.  Her last visit to this clinic was approximately three months ago.  Since that time, the patient states that she has had some variability in her glucose control too largely to recent upper and lower respiratory illnesses.  She did not seek attention for these, and the symptoms have begun to subside on their own and in the meantime, she continues to have some difficulties with blood sugar management.  Her 14-day average is 191.  She had a high blood sugar this morning, which she attributed to a problem with her infusion set; however, in the clinic after an appropriate correction bolus, she subsequently became quite low.  She was treated appropriately with glucose and crackers, and her blood sugar came back up to over 100.  She was able to manage this completely on her own.  In the meantime, she is not having any other medical problems that have interfered with glucose control.  Her diet has been a little bit different in that she had been away visiting with her family for some period of time as well.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, they told me I might have C Diff? They did a CT of my abdomen and that is when they thought I got the infection.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: After all this I still see your white blood cells high. Are you still nauseous?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Anything else any other symptoms?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Actually no. Everything's well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah.

reference_section: Briefly, the patient is a very pleasant 72-year-old female with previous history of hypertension and also recent diagnosis of C. diff for which she was admitted here in 5/2009, who presents to the hospital on 6/18/2009 with abdominal pain, cramping, and persistent diarrhea.  After admission, she had a CT of the abdomen done, which showed evidence of diffuse colitis and she was started on IV Flagyl and also on IV Levaquin.  She was also placed on IV Reglan because of nausea and vomiting.  In spite of the above, her white count still continues to be elevated today.  On questioning the patient, she states the nausea and vomiting has resolved, but the diarrhea still present, but otherwise denies any other specific complaints except for some weakness.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, sir. My chart here says that you are a fifty one year old white male, is that correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good afternoon, doctor. Yes, all of that is correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, thank you. Please, walk me through the history of your symptoms, when did everything begin.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I was diagnosed with P T L D towards the end of two thousand seven.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What symptoms were you experiencing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had swollen lymph nodes, stomach pain, I was losing a lot of weight, and I wasn't really eating.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have you been treated for this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I didn't go to the doctor right away, but eventually I went to the hospital, and they did a biopsy of my groin lymph nodes, and they found large scale lymphoma.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Who's care were you under in the hospital?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it was the renal transplant services. Oh yeah, they talked about my case at the hematopathology conference.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's interesting. After you were diagnosed, what treatments were you given?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I started chemo with, um, I have it written down, cyclophosphamide, daunorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you have any complications with chemo?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, yeah, I had sepsis during my first cycle, they said that I had it even with growth factor support. I was also disoriented.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How many cycles of chemo have you completed?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've done five to date.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you have your P E T Scan after your first three cycles?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I wasn't feeling well at all, so I didn't go.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has your chemotherapy been interrupted for any other reason?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I had an infection related to the skin cancer, and a chest infection, sir.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you have surgery for the skin cancer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I did.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, and you're here for your sixth round of chemo, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you feeling today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Overall, I feel pretty well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you having any cold or flu like symptoms today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any shortness of breath, or chest pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Finally, your E C O G score is one according to the nurse, is that correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, doctor. That's correct.

reference_section: A 51-year-old white male diagnosed with PTLD in latter half of 2007.  He presented with symptoms of increasing adenopathy, abdominal pain, weight loss, and anorexia.  He did not seek medical attention immediately.  He was finally hospitalized by the renal transplant service and underwent a lymph node biopsy in the groin, which showed diagnosis of large cell lymphoma.  He was discussed at the hematopathology conference.  Chemotherapy with rituximab plus cyclophosphamide, daunorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone was started.  First cycle of chemotherapy was complicated by sepsis despite growth factor support.  He also appeared to have become disoriented either secondary to sepsis or steroid therapy. The patient has received 5 cycles of chemotherapy to date.  He did not keep his appointment for a PET scan after 3 cycles because he was not feeling well.  His therapy has been interrupted for infection related to squamous cell cancer, skin surgery as well as complaints of chest infection. The patient is here for the sixth and final cycle of chemotherapy.  He states he feels well.  He denies any nausea, vomiting, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain or fatigue.  He denies any tingling or numbness in his fingers.  Review of systems is otherwise entirely negative. Performance status on the ECOG scale is 1.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: I think they are just scared for me to be alone, but I am doing just fine. I have had a bunch of other family members that have recently passed away. I think that made them nervus.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you still working?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I am. I just returned to full time again, but they put me on light duty until I am fully healed.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is it that you do for work?

turns.text: Did you have difficulties in school?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I primarily got B's and C's in school.  I received some tutoring for algebra in middle school, but I was never held back a grade failing any classes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.text: Yes. I still do all that and more.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been able to continue the other activities that you enjoy?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes! I am in the choir at church.  I am back to my knitting and cooking too. At the end of October I am going on a cruise to the Bahamas with a group of ladies from my church.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Excellent!

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: So many of my family members have passed away that I have realized I need to live my life to the fullest.

reference_section: Ms. A completed high school degree.  She reported that she primarily obtained B's and C's in school.  She received some tutoring for algebra in middle school, but denied ever having been held back a grade failing any classes or having any problems with attention or hyperactivity. She currently works for the Social Security Administration in data processing.  she has returned to full-time work, but continues to perform only light duties due to her physical condition.  She is now living on her own.  She has never driven.  She reported that she continues to perform ADLs independently such as cooking and cleaning.  She lost her husband in 2005 and has three adult daughters.  She previously reported some concerns that her children wanted her to move into assisted living, but she did not discuss that during this current evaluation.  She also reported number of other family members who had recently passed away.  She has returned to activities she enjoys such as quire, knitting, and cooking and plans to go on a cruise to the Bahamas at the end of October.

reference_section: Pulmonary function studies reportedly show a mild restrictive ventilatory defect without obstruction.  Diffusing capacity is well preserved. An overnight sleep study was performed on this patient at the end of 02/07.  At that time, she reported that her sleep was better in the laboratories compared to home.  She slept for a total sleep time of 398 minutes out of 432 minutes in bed (sleep proficiency 92 percent).  She fell asleep in the middle of latency of less than 1 minute.  She woke up after sleep onset of 34 minutes.  She had stage I sleep that was some elevated at 28 percent of total sleep time, and stage I sleep is predominantly evident in the lateral portion of the night.  The remainders were stage II at 69 percent, stage III and IV at 3 percent of total sleep time. The patient had no REM sleep. The patient had no periodic limb movements during sleep. The patient had no significant sleep-disordered breathing during non-REM sleep with less than one episode per hour.  Oxyhemoglobin saturation remained in the low to mid 90s throughout the night. Intermittent inspiratory flow limitation compatible with snoring was observed during non-REM sleep.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She speaks in full sentences, maybe just a little shy now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No problem, how old is she?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She is two years old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. So, what is going on with her?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, she is having some congestion and stuffiness and she also has a runny nose.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, are you giving her any medicine?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I gave her over the counter antiallergic.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know the name?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, its Zyrtec. I use it often.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Is anybody else sick in the house?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Actually, I am having some allergies myself right now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Do you have any other concerns?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Not really, but I wanted to talk about her growth.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, as per the growth chart she is doing fantastic. Her growth curve for both height and weight is at eighty percen-

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Percentage?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Eighty percentile. And her head percentile is still at ninety five.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is she potty trained or did you start training her?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I tried couple of times, but she is showing no interest.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Give it time. Does she identify shapes and colors?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She knows some shapes, but still struggles with colors.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Any other concerns other than the congestion?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, no other concerns.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Alright then nice meeting you, bye Emma.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Bye.

reference_section: The patient is a 2-year-old little girl who comes in with concerns about stuffiness, congestion and nasal drainage.  She does take Zyrtec on a fairly regular basis.  Mom is having some allergy trouble herself right now.  She does not know her colors.  She knows some of her shapes.  She speaks in sentences.  She is not showing much interest in the potty.  She is in the 80th percentile for height and weight, and still over 95th percentile for head circumference.  Mom has no other concerns.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Let me go ahead and place these orders for you and we'll hopefully get you feeling better soon.

turns.speaker: patient
