turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, young man. Is this your mother with you today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's my mommy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you tell me more about your son, ma'am?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, he's three now, and he's become a really picky eater.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is he eating in general?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, no, not really. My real concern today is that he vomits sometimes after eating particular foods.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which foods?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, after eating raw carrots, like five to ten minutes after, he'll complain his stomach hurts and then vomit.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I assume you've stopped giving him carrots, then?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, but last week after he ate celery the same thing happened.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are there any other foods?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, not that he's tried yet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, there's no pain or vomiting with other foods that you can notice?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is he going to the bathroom regularly?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, no problems there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does he have any other major conditions?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Um, reactive airway disease, it happens sometimes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does he have asthma?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, he does not.

reference_section: This 3-year-old male is brought by his mother with concerns about his eating.  He has become a very particular eater, and not eating very much in general.  However, her primary concern was he was vomiting sometimes after particular foods.  They had noted that when he would eat raw carrots, within 5 to 10 minutes he would complain that his stomach hurt and then vomit.  After this occurred several times, they stopped giving him carrots.  Last week, he ate some celery and the same thing happened.  They had not given him any of that since.  He eats other foods without any apparent pain or vomiting.  Bowel movements are normal.  He does have a history of reactive airway disease, intermittently.  He is not diagnosed with intrinsic asthma at this time and takes no medication regularly.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, how are you doing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hanging in there. Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, you just celebrated your birthday. How was it? How is it feeling to be close to forties?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I just turned thirty nine. I would say older the wiser.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's true. Okay, so you are here for your follow up. Let's see, you have type one diabetes mellitus, right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that's right. Last time I was here almost four months ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you doing since last visit?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have been good. My sugar has been under the range. Unfortunately, my pump was having some issues for the last two weeks.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh no. What happened?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't know. I tried to get it fixed but nothing worked out, so I had to buy a new one and then being old kind of hit me. You know, I was not able to set it up. I was stuck on the pump settings and was having a lot of difficulties. With all this going on, I was not able to control my sugar over past two weeks and there might have been like some ups and downs in my levels which I could not notice or register.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: During this, did you notice anything like, did you lose your consciousness? Did you faint?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about sweating, tired, or lightheadedness and or change in vision? Or any kind of confusion in mind?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope, nothing like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's good, so there hasn't been any hypoglycemic event. I mean, your sugar didn't drop down.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh yeah, I didn't think so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let's see how about hyperglycemia? Did you think your sugar levels went high?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think, there was some difficulties with both the fasting and after meals, but I'm not sure.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you urinating more than normal?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you eating more than normal or drinking more than normal? Are you feeling thirsty or not?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not that I noticed.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you exercising?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, I tried but didn't work out so not exercising at this point, but I follow a fixed diet. But you know, being a mother is in itself full of physical activities. I mean, I have twins and also a young baby who keep me busy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you working?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I'm working as a medical coder. It is a full time job and you just keep busy. Sometimes I don't even realize that I missed my meal, but I do keep some snacks with me I'm just eating while completing my work. It might not be the best case scenario, but I don't get any time for any kind of physical activities.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you visiting your physician regularly?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Of course. I'm very regular. I keep a track of my annual visits. My annual examinations. I take my dental visits after every six months, and I recently had my eye examination done. All was good.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: This reminded me that we did a lab last time I came. How did it go?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh yes, thank you for reminding me. Let's see how your numbers are. Your cholesterol is still high. Your L D L recorded one hundred and forty four.

reference_section: The patient is a 39-year-old woman returns for followup management of type 1 diabetes mellitus.  Her last visit was approximately 4 months ago.  Since that time, the patient states her health had been good and her glycemic control had been good, however, within the past 2 weeks she had a pump malfunction, had to get a new pump and was not certain of her pump settings and has been having some difficulty with glycemic control over the past 2 weeks.  She is not reporting any severe hypoglycemic events, but is having some difficulty with hyperglycemia both fasting and postprandial.  She is not reporting polyuria, polydipsia or polyphagia.  She is not exercising at this point and has a diet that is rather typical of woman with twins and a young single child as well.  She is working on a full-time basis and so eats on the run a lot, probably eats more than she should and not making the best choices, little time for physical activity.  She is keeping up with all her other appointments and has recently had a good eye examination.  She had lab work done at her previous visit and this revealed persistent hyperlipidemic state with a LDL of 144.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi there, so tell me what is going on with you?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi there! How are you today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hello! I am hanging in there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you remember me from our last visit?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes! You are the doctor that comes to see me here. It is nice of you to come and see me here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How do you like it here at the Nursing Home?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I wish I didn't have to be here, but they are all very nice to me here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is good to hear. The nurses have been a bit concerned about you and have noticed some changes that they would like me to address.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I fell. I lost my balance.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you remember when that was?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: When what was?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The fall.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Not long ago.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: It was about a month ago that she fell.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The nurses tell me that you have had a trouble walking. Can you tell me what you have noticed?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: When I try to get up and walk around my legs are weak. I have never had problems with walking before.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has the weakness in your legs been something that has been getting worse over time?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. It just was like that when I woke up one morning.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your nurse tells me that you had and accident trying to get to the bathroom in time the other day. Does this happen to you often?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I don't remember having any accidents.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The nurse said you went number two in the sink.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh dear. I did that? I am so sorry dear. I don't remember that.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: It's okay ma'am. We are just concurred about you. She has never had any bathroom issues in the past.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been eating well?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I eat three times a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How much is left on your plate after each meal?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I eat about half of what they give me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's not bad.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: She has lost a little weight.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have?

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Just a few pounds.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you experienced any diarrhea or loose stool?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How has your energy level been? Do you join in on any of the activities that they have going on here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I don't ever feel like doing things. I don't have any energy anymore. I wonder if I could try those drinks. What are they called?

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Ensure?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes!

reference_section: The patient was seen today by me at Nursing Home for her multiple medical problems.  The nurses report that she has been confused at times, having incontinent stool in the sink one time but generally she does not do that poorly.  She does have trouble walking which she attributes to weak legs.  She fell a couple of months ago.  Her eating has been fair.  She has been losing weight a little bit.  She denies diarrhea.  She does complain of feeling listless and unambitious and would like to try some Ensure.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did the nurse give you the handout for a cardiac diet?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It is important for you stick to the cardiac diet. The cardiac diet emphasizes low fat foods such as vegetables, whole grains, and fish. I would like for you limit processed foods that are high in sugar and sodium, as these increase the risk of heart disease.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: Low-fat, low-salt, cardiac diet.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any changes to your family history since your last visit?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, no changes.

reference_section: As previously documented.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello! I would like to get some background on what brings you in today. What symptoms have you been having?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am exhausted. I get lightheaded when I stand up. My family noticed that my skin and eyes are yellow. I have not been feeling well. I had a fever about a week ago. There has been a few nights where I woke up all sweaty with chills.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any trouble drinking or eating?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. I have not been able to eat normally for that last three to four weeks. I lost twenty six pounds.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you experienced any nausea or vomiting?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have been nauseous, but I have not vomited.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any pain anywhere in the abdomen or low back area?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, there has been some pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you tell me or show me where the pain is coming from?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It comes and goes. It hurts all around my stomach. Oh, my pee has been a vary dark color for about a week now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have a history of liver disease?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No but I did have a cholecystectomy a long time ago.

reference_section: 40 year old Hispanic male presented to the emergency room complaining of generalized weakness, fatigue and dark urine for one week. In addition, he stated that his family had noticed yellowing of his skin and eyes, though he himself had not noticed. He did complain of subjective fever and chills along with occasional night sweats during the prior week or so and he noted anorexia for 3-4 weeks leading to 26 pound weight loss (213 lbs. to 187 lbs.). He was nauseated but denied vomiting. He did admit to intermittent abdominal discomfort which he could not localize. In addition, he denied any history of liver disease, but had undergone cholecystectomy many years previous.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient is employed in the finance department.  He is a nonsmoker.  He does consume alcohol on the weekend as much as 3 to 4 alcoholic beverages per day on the weekends.  He denies any IV drug use or abuse.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Calm down sir and stop moving your hands, you might get hurt.

turns.text: Oh, what happened?

turns.speaker: guest_clinician

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Sir, you need to tell us, or we will call an ambulance for you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am going to ask nurse to call an ambulance.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello there, how are you?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I am little scared.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I understand, so how old is she?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She is ten days old today.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And just wanted to confirm the ethnicity is Caucasian, right?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, so tell me what's going on with her?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I was feeding her and then I suddenly noticed this unusual jerky movement in both her arms and legs.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: It lasted about a minute.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did you first notice it?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: The first day when I was feeding her. She was barely a day old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, and how many times till now?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: About six times.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you notice any interrupted breathing or bluish color around her mouth?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: While the episode occurs do you notice any color changes in the baby?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you happened to notice any arching of the back or eyes rolling back?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, it usually happens while she is sleeping, so I didn't notice her eye movements. But I am able to wake her up and stop the hand and leg movements.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Otherwise, is she feeding well and is active?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, absolutely! Although she falls asleep a lot during breast feeding but other than that everything is fine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And how often are you feeding her and for how long?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I breast feed her every two to three hours for about fifteen to twenty minutes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, and how many dirty diapers?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, her pee diapers have increased up to eight and I would say about six to seven poopy diapers a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And did you notice the color of her poop?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, it's like dirty yellowish color.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: Negative fever, negative fussiness, tracks with her eyes, some sneezing and hiccups.  This patient has developed some upper airway congestion in the past day.  She has not had any vomiting or diarrhea.  Per mom, she does not spit up, and mom is also unable to notice any relationship between these movements and feeds.  This patient has not had any rashes.  Mom was notified by the nurses at birth that her temperature may be low of approximately 97.5 degrees Fahrenheit.  Otherwise, the above history of present illness and other review of systems negative.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'd like you to give her four ounces of formula every two to three hours.

turns.text: And what if she doesn't take the bottle?

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, sir. How are you doing today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I need help. My neck is killing me. I can't sleep at night.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Has it hurt before?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: A long time ago. I don't know how it came back. I gave my report to the nurse.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Hello, Doctor. Here is his report. It documents any previous medical findings.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you, Nurse. Let me take a look.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hurry. My neck is hurting so much. I can't take it anymore.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It looks like you had cervical spondylosis. You were evaluated fifteen years ago for it, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Cervical what? Can you dumb it down for me? I remember getting checked for something fifteen years ago, but I forgot what it was.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's like a degenerative disease that softens the tissue between the vertebras in your neck.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Is that why my neck is hurting? Can you fix it?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'll see what I can do. We'll have to do some tests first.

reference_section: He has had documented cervical spondylosis, apparently with an evaluation over 15 years ago.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: So, how long has your stomach been hurting?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any nausea or vomiting?

turns.text: No.

turns.text: No, I am fine.

turns.text: Hm, everything else looks fine. No problem there with your eyes, nose, throat, and other systems.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's just my tummy which is hurting.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Don't worry we will take care of it.

reference_section: Positive for diarrhea and abdominal pain, otherwise main other complaints are weakness.  She denies any cough, sputum production, or dysuria at this time.  Otherwise, a 10-system review is essentially negative.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Yes, doctor, that's right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your surgery was eight days ago, right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I'm recovering now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you aware of the details behind your surgery?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Honestly, all the details are pretty foggy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, well you had acute cholecystitis, so we tried a laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Did everything go well, doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, we had to do an open procedure due to some difficult anatomy. You were a tough case. How are you doing today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm improving, I guess.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How is your strength?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's getting better.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you eating well?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I'm back to having my regular diet now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you going to the bathroom regularly? What medicines are you taking for this prolonged ileus?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I wasn't, but it's gotten with the tetracycline and Reglan.

reference_section: She is a 79-year-old female who came in with acute cholecystitis and underwent attempted laparoscopic cholecystectomy 8 days ago.  The patient has required conversion to an open procedure due to difficult anatomy.  Her postoperative course has been lengthened due to a prolonged ileus, which resolved with tetracycline and Reglan.  The patient is starting to improve, gain more strength.  She is tolerating her regular diet.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, ma'am, how are you today, my dear?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's good to see you too, doctor. I'm in some pain today.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Before we begin, refresh my memory, how old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Doctor, I'm fifty eight years young.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, what seems to be the problem today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, about two years ago I had a fall, and then I had blood clots in my left knee.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How were you treated for this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I went to the hospital, and then to a nursing home. I had to live there for a year.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you have any problems before your fall?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope, not at all, I was mostly doing everything by myself. I used a pickup walker around the house, but that's it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been to P T for this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, they referred me to P T because of the arthritis in this knee.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Since the injury, have you been able to walk?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not really, I spend most of my time laying down or seated. My knee is in so much pain, I just want to be able to walk around my house again.

reference_section: The patient is a 58-year-old female, referred to therapy due to left knee osteoarthritis.  The patient states that approximately 2 years ago, she fell to the ground and thereafter had blood clots in the knee area.  The patient was transferred from the hospital to a nursing home and lived there for 1 year.  Prior to this incident, the patient was ambulating independently with a pickup walker throughout her home.  Since that time, the patient has only been performing transverse and has been unable to ambulate.  The patient states that her primary concern is her left knee pain and they desire to walk short distances again in her home.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am Doctor Frank. It is nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi Doctor Frank. It is nice to meet you as well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I would like to start with a little background information.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you working currently?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am retired.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of work did you used to do?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was an engine mechanic. I worked in the same shop, little shop, for many years. I was the oldest guy there before I retired.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How was the ventilation in shop that you worked in?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not great. I always had the doors open to try to get some air flow in there, but it didn't help very much.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you married?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I am. We have thirteen children together.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh wow.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah! That is most people's reaction to how many children we have.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It used to be very normal to have that many children. Now people only have two or three children at most.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Right!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you currently or have you had a history of drinking alcohol?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I don't drink.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any use of recreational drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you or have you ever used any tobacco products.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Great. What is your family medical history?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, my brother had a brain aneurysm and he died.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am so sorry. Was he older than you or younger?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: He was my older brother. My father had a stroke. He was left with tremors after his stroke.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. That is very common for people to have tremors following a significant stroke.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. The doctors said that he was lucky to have had only tremors after the stroke that he experienced.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is fortunate. Do you have any family history of Huntington's disease?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Not that I can recall.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about depression or suicide in the family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

reference_section: Retired small engine mechanic who worked in a poorly ventilated shop. Married with 13 children. No history of ETOH, Tobacco or illicit drug use. Father had tremors following a stroke. Brother died of brain aneurysm. No history of depression, suicide, or Huntington's disease in family.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm seventy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did you get diagnosed with diabetes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It was last fall.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you keeping a tab of your sugar?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I'm checking with Accu Cheks. Mostly, once a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are your numbers coming?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They are ranging from eighties to as high as one hundred and thirty two.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you feeling overall?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's good. I go for a walk, almost daily.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How far do you go?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any other issues?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: For the last several days, I do have this feeling of congestion. Looks like everything is congested and sometimes it's like something is coming out.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Where did you have your last mammogram?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had it in the Baylis Building. It was, it was last month, I think.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Who is the gynecologist?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I go to Doctor Cheng.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any pain in your tummy, nausea, or vomiting, diarrhea or constipation? Any changes with the bowel movements?

reference_section: A 70-year-old female who was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus last fall.  She has been checking her Accu-Cheks generally once a day, and they range from 82 to a high of 132.  She feels well.  She walks 1-2 miles most days.  If the weather is bad, they go to a local mall.  Otherwise they walk outside.  She does complain of some sinus congestion and drainage for the last several days.  She is up-to-date on her mammogram that she had at the Baylis Building.  She sees Dr. Cheng for her gynecological care.  She is a nonsmoker.  Denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, blood in her urine, blood in her stools.  She has nocturia x 1.  Denies swelling in her ankles.  She checks her feet regularly.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Have you had any other symptoms associated with this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have been having some balancing problems. It has been getting worse. I don't know if this is related but I have been having trouble breathing while eating. I feel like I am choking on my food, but I am not, and I gasp for air. It is scary.

reference_section: 28 y/o male presented with a 3 month history of progressive right sided numbness; now anesthetic to pain. In addition, he experienced worsening balance, and episodes of aspiration while eating.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How has she been doing since her last admission?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Not great. She still can't seem to hold her urine or bowels. For this reason, we've been using a diaper and changing it at least three times a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How does she communicate her needs to you?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She'll usually point to things or wave her hands when she needs something.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Does she have a visiting nurse or anyone who checks her vitals weekly?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: We have a nurse who comes in three times a week to help take care of her.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did she first become wheelchair bound?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: About two years ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How often does she get turned over in bed to prevent bed sores?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: We try to adjust her once every hour or so. It's harder on the days where we don't have an extra set of hands.

reference_section: Because of the patient's inability to communicate, is not obtainable, but apparently, she has urine incontinence and also stool incontinence, and is wheelchair bound.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When we did the surgery there were no complications with the patient.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: How did her skin look?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, ma'am. Before we begin, I just need a few pieces of information.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure, no problem, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: First, how old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm fifty six, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, did the nurses talk to you about the weight they took today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, they did not.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, ma'am, you're obese. That's posing a serious danger to your health.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I know. I've been trying to lose weight.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, so, what seems to be troubling you today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I have a history of degenerative arthritis in my hips, so my other doctors have said.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have you been treated for this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had a right hip replacement with Doctor X in two thousand.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did this help the pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, on the right, but over the last three years or so the pain on the left hip has been getting worse.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has it gotten worse faster recently?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, over the last few months it's gotten really bad.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of medications are you taking for this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Honestly, it's gotten so bad, its uncontrollable pain at this point. I'm taking narcotics now because it's so bad.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you able to do any activities?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, the pain is messing with my daily living, activities are out of the question.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I think we should do another hip replacement on the left, ma'am.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Me too, can you remind me the risk of infection from this surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, historically it's less than one percent. We use antibiotics to control for infection.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good, and will I be asleep for this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, the whole time. You won't feel a thing.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good, yes, I want to do this procedure.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The other risks include scar, dislocation, need for further surgery, deep vein thrombosis, and implant failure. I would not worry about any of these things since you have had a replacement before with no issues.

reference_section: This is a 56-year-old obese female with a history of bilateral degenerative hip arthritis.  She underwent a right total hip arthroplasty by Dr. X in the year of 2000, and over the past three years, the symptoms in her left hip had increased tremendously especially in the past few months. Because of the increased amount of pain as well as severe effect on her activities of daily living and uncontrollable pain with narcotic medication, the patient has elected to undergo the  procedure.  All risks as well complications were discussed with the patient including but not limited to infection, scar, dislocation, need for further surgery, risk of anesthesia, deep vein thrombosis, and implant failure.  The patient understood all these risks and was willing to continue further on with the procedure.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And what about surgeries? Have you had any in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, a part of my intestine was removed due to some obstruction.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ah, I see. Big or small?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Small intestine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay anything else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, my appendix was removed and--and then I had a vasectomy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's it, I think.

reference_section: 1.  Small bowel resections. 2.  Appendectomy. 3.  A vasectomy.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old was your dad when he passed away from a heart attack?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sixty seven.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did he have a history of any medical problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, he had C O P D and smoked a ton.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And how about your mom? How is she doing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: She's not bad. Turned eighty eight last week. She's recovering from lung cancer. Two years ago, she had a piece of her lung taken out.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm glad to hear that she's in recovery and staying healthy. Do you have any siblings?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have two brothers that are both younger than me. I also had a sister, but she passed away from pneumonia at only twenty months old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm so sorry to hear that.

reference_section: Father died of an MI at age 67 with COPD and was a heavy smoker.  His mother is 88, living and well, status post lung cancer resection.  Two brothers, living and well.  One sister died at age 20 months of pneumonia.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any medical concerns or issues in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: With ten being the worst pain ever, out of ten, how would you rate your knee pain at rest?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: At rest, um, I'd have to say there's no pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, what about when you move the left knee? We call this active motion, how would you rate it then?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: When I move it, um, the front of the knee hurts. I'd say its about a five out of ten.

reference_section: The patient reports that when seated and at rest, her knee pain is 0/10.  The patient states that with active motion of the left knee, the pain in the anterior portion increases to 5/10.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How's your family? Are they in good health?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My mom just turned sixty one and my brother is thirty nine. I'd say they're both doing good for their age.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Always great to hear. Do you know of any medical problems that run in the family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My dad died of colon cancer at the age of forty eight. I think he may have also had pancreatic cancer, but we're not sure.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm so sorry for your loss. Cancer is a horrible disease.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's okay. It's been several years now since we lost him. My uncle on my dad's side also had bile duct cancer and colon cancer.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is he still with us today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, sadly. He passed away at thirty two years of age. Another one of my uncles on my dad's side had colon cancer in his forties. It seems to run deep in our family.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh my. Is there anyone else in your family who has battled cancer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'd say about thirty some people on my dad's side had cancer. A lot of them had colon cancer and two girls had breast cancer. Oh and I remember learning from one of our cousins that we have some weird genetic syndrome that runs in the family, but I couldn't give you the name. I don't think any of us have been able to figure out the name. Sucks that we have so many problems.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's definitely difficult to process, however, it's good that you and your family are aware so that you're able to seek preventative measures and get tested early for these particular cancers. If you recall the name of the genetic syndrome, please feel free to call me back so that I can update your records.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure thing.

reference_section: Mother is 61 years old and brother is 39 years old, both alive and well. Father died at 48 of colon cancer and questionable pancreatic cancer. One paternal uncle died at 32 of colon cancer and bile duct cancer. One paternal uncle had colon cancer in his 40s. Thirty cancers are noted on the fathers side of the family, many are colon; two women had breast cancer. The family was told that there is a genetic syndrome in the family, but no one remembers the name of the syndrome.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, ma'am, I just need some information before we get started today.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Absolutely, good afternoon, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: My chart says here that you're fifty nine years old, is that correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I also see that you have a history of breast cancer, is that correct as well?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's also correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When were you diagnosed initially?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I was diagnosed in June of nineteen ninety four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How has this been managed in the past, ma'am?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I've taken Zometa, Faslodex, and Aromasin.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How has the cancer progressed since you were diagnosed?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The doctors said I had rising tumor markers.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What imaging have you done to evaluate the cancer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've had a P E T C T Scan done.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What did that scan show?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It showed that the cancer was metastatic.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see here that you were involved in a clinical trial for your breast cancer, can you tell me more about that, please?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was in the C T S U C four zero five zero two trial, and I was randomized into the ixabepilone plus Avastin group.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did you respond to this treatment?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I had something called dose limiting toxicity with the fourth cycle. I skipped the Ixempra on the first and eighth days.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did they respond once this happened?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They just reduced the dose I was given.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did you handle this reduced dose?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Honestly, I've been tolerating the treatment pretty well. I only have some neuropathy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any other concerns of note?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I thought that I had a perforated septum earlier this month, and I went to my E N T right away, but everything was okay. There was no perforation.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, so, you're here for your eighth day of Ixempra, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, doctor, that's correct.

reference_section: She is a very pleasant 59-year-old nurse with a history of breast cancer.  She was initially diagnosed in June 1994.  Her previous treatments included Zometa, Faslodex, and Aromasin.  She was found to have disease progression first noted by rising tumor markers.  PET/CT scan revealed metastatic disease and she was enrolled in clinical trial of CTSU/C40502.  She was randomized to the ixabepilone plus Avastin.  She experienced dose-limiting toxicity with the fourth cycle.  The Ixempra was skipped on day 1 and day 8.  She then had a dose reduction and has been tolerating treatment well with the exception of progressive neuropathy.  Early in the month she had concerned about possible perforated septum.  She was seen by ENT urgently.  She was found to have nasal septum intact.  She comes into clinic today for day eight Ixempra.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I have to check for any swollen lymph nodes. I will go through different areas like in your neck, in your armpit, and in your groin.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that's okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your neck looks clear. I cannot find any kind of swelling or abnormality there.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's good, right?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, it's true. Other parts also look clear.

reference_section: LYMPH: No lymphadenopathy was appreciated in the neck, axillae or groin.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I will check your skin for anything abnormal, okay?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm okay with that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hm, I don't see any rashes or any red spots.

reference_section: SKIN: Inspection of the skin reveals no rashes, ulcerations or petechiae.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any allergies to medications?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

reference_section: No known medicine allergies.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any allergies?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not that I know.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, miss. What brings you into our clinic today? Also, before we start, it looks like you forgot to fill out your ethnicity on the new patient paperwork. Do you mind telling me what you identify as?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hello, doctor. I am white and I am a young sixty two years old. I have a list of issues I would like to talk about.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's begin. I know that you have been dealing with hypertension and lipometabolism disorder. Doctor X Y Z and I follow you on the hypertension. What else do we have going on?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: First off I have a history of diabetes in my family. My father had it and my brother has it currently. I am afraid because I know I have gained some weight. My knee also has been hurting for a long time. The left knee.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you locate where the pain is?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think it is everywhere in the knee. It hurts to kneel. I had imaging done on it a while ago. Can you check to see the results?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ah, yes. We have on file that you had an X Ray done in nineteen ninety nine. I see that a joint is narrowing. We can talk about possible surgery.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Can I have it x rayed again? I don't want any surgery, but I want to know what is going on. I am afraid of surgery.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's see what else I can do. Any other issues?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. I am very concerned because my poop is baby yellow and I have some rectal bleeding occasionally. It is always bright red and drips into the toilet. My last colonoscopy was in nineteen ninety nine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any history of colon cancer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I do not, but I think my mother did. She is gone now, so I cannot check. Do you think my poop is baby yellow because of my stomach pain? I have some stomach pain and have been laying off the fast food and soda, but it doesn't seem to work. Sometimes my poop is hard or runny. It is always random.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you bleed when the stool is hard?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not really. Oh, and lastly, I had cold symptoms. Like a sore throat and I was sneezing a lot. I think it was a cold or flu because Claritin did not work. I think the body aches were also from this illness. I feel okay today, but I wanted to bring this up just in case it had to do with my stool being discolored. During this sick period I also am wondering if I have sleep apnea because I wake up in the middle of the night randomly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you snore? That is a sign of sleep apnea. Smoking also can contribute to restlessness.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No I do not snore and I do not smoke.

reference_section: The patient is a 62-year-old white female with multiple chronic problems including hypertension and a lipometabolism disorder.  She follows with Dr. XYZ on her hypertension, as well as myself.  She continues to gain weight.  Diabetes is therefore a major concern.  In fact, her dad had diabetes and she has a brother who has diabetes.  The patient also has several additional concerns she brings up today.  One is that her left knee continues to bother her and it hurts.  She cannot really isolate where the pain is, it just seems to hurt through her knee.  She has had this for some time now and in fact as we reviewed her records, her left knee has been x-rayed in 1999.  There was some minimal narrowing of the weightbearing joint with some minor hypertrophic spurring medially.  She would like to have this x-rayed again today.  She is certainly not interested in any surgery.  She has noted that it particularly hurts to kneel.  In addition, she complains of her stools being a baby-yellow.  She has rectal bleeding off and on.  It is bright red.  She had a colonoscopy done in 1999.  She does have a family history of colon cancer questionable in her mother, who is deceased.  She complains of some diffuse abdominal pain off and on.  She has given up fast foods and her pop and this has not seemed to help.  She does admit however, that she is not eating right.  Sometimes her stools are hard.  Sometimes they are runny.  The blood does not really seem to be related to necessarily a hard stool.  It is always bright red and will sometimes drip into the toilet.  Over the last couple of days, she had also been sneezing and has had an itchy throat.  She tried some Claritin and this did not help.  She has had some body aches.  She is finally feeling better today with this.  She also is questioning whether she has some sleep apnea.  She will awaken suddenly in the middle of the night.  She was told that she does snore.  She does not smoke.  As stated, she has gained significant weight.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did anyone in your family have any medical issues?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, you see, my father died of a brain tumor. Doctors tried their best, but no surgery was possible for him.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about your mother?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good morning, young man, and can I assume that you're his mother?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, doctor, good morning, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, tell me a little more about your son, please.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, he's seven years old now, and he's been healthy all his life. But he recently started having pain in his fingers, elbows, and neck.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What race does your family identify with?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: We're white, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, how long has he had this pain?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: It's been, um, about two months now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has the pain improved any since it began?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, it's a little better now.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, he says it's almost gone now, but he was at a point where he was in so much pain that he would cry.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is this behavior unusual for him?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, he's not really a complaining kid.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Was he playing and everything before this pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I like playing sports with my friends.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has he had any illnesses, or stomach issues in the past?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, nothing major, he just has some allergies.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of allergies?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: He just deals with seasonal allergies.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, does he just take a Claritin for this?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there any swelling?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Not really, the other doctor said he saw some though.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are there any other major medical conditions that you're aware of, anything at all?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, there's absolutely nothing to report.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has he ever had a rash on the painful area?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any diarrhea, fevers, weigh loss, or mouth ulcers?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No. Just canker sores, but no to everything else.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is he going to the bathroom fine? What about visual issues?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. His lymph nodes look fine.

reference_section: We had the pleasure of seeing the patient today in our Pediatric Rheumatology Clinic.  He was sent here with a chief complaint of joint pain in several joints for few months.  This is a 7-year-old white male who has no history of systemic disease, who until 2 months ago, was doing well and 2 months ago, he started to complain of pain in his fingers, elbows, and neck.  At this moment, this is better and is almost gone, but for several months, he was having pain to the point that he would cry at some point.  He is not a complainer according to his mom and he is a very active kid.  There is no history of previous illness to this or had gastrointestinal problems.  He has problems with allergies, especially seasonal allergies and he takes Claritin for it.  Other than that, he has not had any other problem.  Denies any swelling except for that doctor mentioned swelling on his elbow.  There is no history of rash, no stomach pain, no diarrhea, no fevers, no weight loss, no ulcers in his mouth except for canker sores.  No lymphadenopathy, no eye problems, and no urinary problems.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What do you think, doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, I can't really explain why your glucose have not climbed despite the decrease in insulin.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's strange, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: My staff tells me that your appetite is good, and you're eating as well as ever, is that correct?

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: I am asked to see the patient today with ongoing issues around her diabetic control.  We have been fairly aggressively, downwardly adjusting her insulins, both the Lantus insulin, which we had been giving at night as well as her sliding scale Humalog insulin prior to meals.  Despite frequent decreases in her insulin regimen, she continues to have somewhat low blood glucoses, most notably in the morning when the glucoses have been in the 70s despite decreasing her Lantus insulin from around 84 units down to 60 units, which is a considerable change.  What I cannot explain is why her glucoses have not really climbed at all despite the decrease in insulin.  The staff reports to me that her appetite is good and that she is eating as well as ever.  I talked to Anna today.  She feels a little fatigued.  Otherwise, she is doing well.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: This is a 77-year-old African-American female with multiple medical problems including CHF (O2 dependent), atrial fibrillation, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, possible stroke, multiple joint disease including gout, arthritis, both rheumatoid and DJD, who presents with a complaint of one month of dizziness.  She reports a rotational sensation upon arising from the bed or chair that lasts for several minutes and requires her to sit back down and stay in one place.  She gets similar symptoms when she rolls over in bed.  She is not able to describe what direction she feels like she is spinning.  At times, she also feels as though she is going to pass out.  These sensations stop if she just sits in one place or lies down for several minutes.  She does note that it is worse when she turns to the right and when she turns to the left.  She also complains that she gets similar sensations when she looks up.  She denies any recent fever, chills, earache, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, other change in vision, or recent new headaches.  She also notes occasional tinnitus to her right ear.

reference_section: The patient is a 63-year-old left-handed gentleman who presents for further evaluation of multiple neurological symptoms.  I asked him to discuss each symptom individually as he had a very hard time describing the nature of his problems.  He first mentioned that he has neck pain.  He states that he has had this for at least 15 years.  It is worse with movement.  It has progressed very slowly over the course of 15 years.  It is localized to the base of his neck and is sharp in quality.  He also endorses a history of gait instability.  This has been present for a few years and has been slightly progressively worsening.  He describes that he feels unsteady on his feet and "walks like a duck."  He has fallen about three or four times over the past year and a half. He also describes that he has numbness in his feet.  When I asked him to describe this in more detail, the numbness is actually restricted to his toes.  Left is slightly more affected than the right.  He denies any tingling or paresthesias.  He also described that he is slowly losing control of his hands.  He thinks that he is dropping objects due to weakness or incoordination in his hands.  This has also been occurring for the past one to two years.  He has noticed that buttoning his clothes is more difficult for him.  He also does not have any numbness or tingling in the hands.  He does have a history of chronic low back pain. At the end of the visit, when I asked him which symptom was most bothersome to him, he actually stated that his fatigue was most troublesome.  He did not even mention this on the initial part of my history taking.  When I asked him to describe this further, he states that he experiences a general exhaustion.  He basically lays in bed all day everyday.  I asked him if he was depressed, he states that he is treated for depression.  He is unsure if this is optimally treated.  As I just mentioned, he stays in bed almost all day long and does not engage in any social activities.  He does not think that he is necessarily sad.  His appetite is good.  He has never undergone any psychotherapy for depression. When I took his history, I noticed that he is very slow in responding to my questions and also had a lot of difficulty recalling details of his history as well as names of physicians who he had seen in the past.  I asked if he had ever been evaluated for cognitive difficulties and he states that he did undergo testing at Johns Hopkins a couple of years ago.  He states that the results were normal and that specifically he did not have any dementia. When I asked him when he was first evaluated for his current symptoms, he states that he saw Dr. X several years ago.  He believes that he was told that he had neuropathy but that it was unclear if it was due to his diabetes.  He told me that more recently he was evaluated by you after Dr. Y referred him for this evaluation.  He also saw Dr. Z for neurosurgical consultation a couple of weeks ago.  He reports that she did not think there was any surgical indication in his neck or back at this point in time.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Have you seen another doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let me write down the medicines you are taking and attach it to the chart.

reference_section: Patient is a 50-year-old white male complaining of continued lower back pain.  Patient has a history of chronic back pain, dating back to an accident that he states he suffered two years ago.  He states he helped a friend unload a motorcycle from a vehicle two-and-a-half days ago, after which he "felt it" in his lower back.  The following day (two days ago), he states he rode to Massachusetts and Maine to pick up clients.  He feels that this aggravated his chronic back pain as well.  He also claims to have a screw in his right hip from a previous surgery to repair a pelvic fracture.  He is being prescribed Ultram, Celebrex, gabapentin, and amitriptyline by his PCP for his chronic back pain.  He states that his PCP has informed him that he does not prescribe opiate medications for chronic back pain. The patient did self-refer to another physician, who suggested that he follow up at a pain clinic for his chronic back pain to discuss other alternatives, particularly the medications that the patient feels that he needs.  Patient states he did not do this because he was feeling well at that time. The patient did present to our emergency room last night, at which time he saw Dr. X.  He was given a prescription for 12 Vicodin as well as some to take home last night.  The patient has not picked up his prescription as of yet and informed the triage nurse that he was concerned that he would not have enough to last through the weekend.  Patient states he also has methadone and Darvocet at home from previous prescription and is wondering if he should restart these medicines.  He is on several medications, the list of which is attached to the chart.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: Mr. XYZ is 41 years of age, who works for Chevron and lives in Angola.  He was playing basketball in Angola back last Wednesday, Month DD, YYYY, when he was driving toward the basket and felt a pop in his posterior leg.  He was seen locally and diagnosed with an Achilles tendon rupture.  He has been on crutches and has been nonweightbearing since that time. He had no pain prior to his injury.  He has had some swelling that is mild.  He has just been on aspirin a day due to his traveling time.  Pain currently is minimal.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, thank you. So, this is an African American gentleman who has stage four C K D secondary to P K D. He's had a high creatinine level over the last six months, so we've been following him closely.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's all correct, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been going to the end stage kidney disease classes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I haven't been able to get in yet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We've talked about how important it is for you to take your blood pressure medication, have you been doing that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, and look at the reading from today.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, this is much better. Good job! Have you gone to the transplant orientation classes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not yet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about dialysis education classes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I haven't been to those either.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Sir, we've talked about this, it's important for you to get into these classes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I know, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, well, we need to follow up his P S A today, it's been about two years since the last time.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Why do you need that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, we'll most likely need cardiac clearance if we're ever able to see if you can get a transplant.

reference_section: This is a followup for this 69-year-old African American gentleman with stage IV chronic kidney disease secondary to polycystic kidney disease.  His creatinine has ranged between 4 and 4.5 over the past 6 months, since I have been following him.  I have been trying to get him educated about end-stage kidney disease and we have been unsuccessful in getting him into classes.  On his last visit, I really stressed the importance of him taking his medications adequately and not missing some of the doses, and he returns today with much better blood pressure control.  He has also brought a machine at home, and states his blood pressure readings have been better.  He has not gone to the transplant orientation class yet and has not been to dialysis education yet, and both of these I have discussed with him in the past.  He also needs followup for his elevated PSA in the past, which has not been done for over 2 years and will likely need cardiac clearance if we ever are able to evaluate him for transplant.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Did you have any other imagine done?

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I remember that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you seen another doctor for this pain?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you want to go forward with the surgery?

turns.text: No, not really. I'm pretty reluctant to do any kind of surgery.

reference_section: The patient is a 45-year-old African-American female whose symptoms first started some one and a half years ago with pain in the left shoulder and some neck pain.  This has subsequently resolved.  She started vigorous workouts in November 2005.  In March of this year, she suddenly could not feel her right foot on the bathroom floor and subsequently went to her primary care physician.  By her report, she had a nerve conduction study and a diagnosis of radiculopathy was made.  She had an MRI of lumbosacral spine, which was within normal limits.  She then developed a tingling sensation in the right middle toe.  Symptoms progressed to sensory symptoms of her knees, elbows, and left middle toe.  She then started getting sensory sensations in the left hand and arm.  She states that she feels a little bit wobbly at the knees and that she is slightly dragging her left leg.  Symptoms have been mildly progressive.  She is unaware of any trigger other than the vigorous workouts as mentioned above.  She has no associated bowel or bladder symptoms.  No particular position relieves her symptoms. Workup has included two MRIs of the C-spine, which were personally reviewed and are discussed.  She saw you for consultation and the possibility of surgical decompression was raised.  At this time, she is somewhat reluctant to go through any surgical procedure.

reference_section: Significant for mesothelioma, which was diagnosed seemingly more than 20 to 25 years ago.  The patient was not sure of exactly when it was diagnosed.  This has been treated surgically by debulking operations for which she states that she has undergone about 10 operations.  The mesothelioma is in her abdomen.  She does not know of any history of having lung mesothelioma.  She states that she has never gotten chemotherapy or radiation for her mesothelioma.  Furthermore, she states that her last surgical debulking was more than 10 years ago and her disease has been fairly stable.  She does have a history of three car accidents that she says were all rear-enders where she was hit while essentially in a stopped position.  These have all occurred over the past five years.  She also has a diagnosis of dementing illness, possibly Alzheimer disease from her previous neurology consultation.  This diagnosis was given in March 2006.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What will the surgery do?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: This will help take some stress off of the knee joint. It should help you feel a lot better.

turns.text: What are the risks of infection from the surgery, doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, you'll be relieved to know that it's less than one percent. We use prophylactic antibiotics the entire time.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Will I be asleep for this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, you won't feel a thing.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, yes. I agree, we should do the surgery.

reference_section: This is a 36-year-old Caucasian female with a long-standing history of right knee pain.  She has been diagnosed in the past with chondromalacia patella.  She has failed conservative therapy.  It was discussed with her the possibility of a arthroscopy lateral release and a tubercle transfer (anterior medialization of the tibial tubercle) to release stress from her femoral patellofemoral joint.  She elected to proceed with the surgical intervention.  All risks and benefits of the surgery were discussed with her.  She was in agreement with the treatment plan.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: This is a 62-year-old right-handed now left-handed white female with tremor since 5th grade.  She remembers that the tremors started in her right hand around that time subsequently later on in early 20s she was put on propranolol for the tremor and more recently within the last 10 years she has been put on primidone and clonazepam.  She thinks that her clonazepam is helping her a lot especially with anxiety and stress, and this makes the tremor better.  She has a lot of trouble with her writing because of tremor but does not report as much problem with other activities of daily living like drinking from a cup and doing her day-to-day activity.  Since around 6 to 7 years, she has had a head tremor, which is mainly "no- no" and occasional voice tremor also.  Additionally, the patient has been diagnosed with migraine headaches without aura, which are far and few apart.  She also has some stress incontinence.  Last MRI brain was done in 2001 reportedly normal.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient is a 25-year-old right-handed Caucasian female who presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of headache occurring at approximately 11 a.m. on the morning of the July 31, 2008. reference_section: The patient is an 89-year-old lady.  She actually turns 90 later this month, seen today for a short-term followup.  Actually, the main reasons we are seeing her back so soon which are elevated blood pressure and her right arm symptoms are basically resolved.  Blood pressure is better even though she is not currently on the higher dose Mavik likely recommended.  She apparently did not feel well with the higher dose, so she just went back to her previous dose of 1 mg daily.  She thinks, she also has an element of office hypertension.  Also, since she is on Mavik plus verapamil, she could switch over to the combined drug Tarka.  However, when we gave her samples of that she thought they were too big for her to swallow.  Basically, she is just back on her previous blood pressure regimen.  However, her blood pressure seems to be better today.  Her daughter says that they do check it periodically and it is similar to today's reading.  Her right arm symptoms are basically resolved and she attributed that to her muscle problem back in the right shoulder blade.  We did do a C-spine and right shoulder x-ray and those just mainly showed some degenerative changes and possibly some rotator cuff injury with the humeral head quite high up in the glenoid in the right shoulder, but this does not seem to cause her any problems.  She has some vague 'stomach problems', although apparently it is improved when she stopped Aleve and she does not have any more aches or pains off Aleve.  She takes Tylenol p.r.n., which seems to be enough for her.  She does not think she has any acid reflux symptoms or heartburn.  She does take Tums t.i.d. and also Mylanta at night.  She has had dentures for many, many years and just recently I guess in the last few months, although she was somewhat vague on this, she has had some sores in her mouth.  They do heal up, but then she will get another one.  She also thinks since she has been on the Lexapro, she has somewhat of a tremor of her basically whole body at least upper body including the torso and arms and had all of the daughters who I not noticed to speak of and it is certainly difficult to tell her today that she has much tremor.  They do think the Lexapro has helped to some extent.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

She denied any recent colds/flu-like illness or history of multiple sclerosis. She denied symptoms of Lhermitte's or Uhthoff's phenomena.

reference_section: This is the initial clinic visit for a 29-year-old man who is seen for new onset of right shoulder pain.  He states that this began approximately one week ago when he was lifting stacks of cardboard.  The motion that he describes is essentially picking up a stack of cardboard at his waist level, twisting to the right and delivering it at approximately waist level.  Sometimes he has to throw the stacks a little bit as well.  He states he felt a popping sensation on 06/30/04.  Since that time, he has had persistent shoulder pain with lifting activities.  He localizes the pain to the posterior and to a lesser extent the lateral aspect of the shoulder.  He has no upper extremity .

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello sir. Let me first start by asking your age. How old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm twenty four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, what brought you here? How can I help you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was out for fishing this weekend, I think I got into some poison ivy and I have these rashes all over my chest, legs, arms and also some are on my back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You seem so confident of it being poison ivy has it happened before?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh yes, it has happened several times before. It usually takes some time to get over. Last time I was here Doctor Blackman gave me a steroid injection.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let me check my records. It looks like he gave you eighty milligrams of depomedrol. How was it last time after the injection?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It worked fine. It did take us some time to get rid of it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you take any medicine or anything else this time?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I took over the counter Benadryl. Also, I'm applying cortisone cream on the rashes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did they help you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I saw a little bit of improvement. But this weekend it seemed to have been worst.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No worries, let's set you up for another injection.

reference_section: He is a 24-year-old male who said that he had gotten into some poison ivy this weekend while he was fishing.  He has had several cases of this in the past and he says that is usually takes quite awhile for him to get over it; he said that the last time he was here he got a steroid injection by Dr. Blackman; it looked like it was Depo-Medrol 80 mg.  He said that it worked fairly well, although it seemed to still take awhile to get rid of it.  He has been using over-the-counter Benadryl as well as cortisone cream on the areas of the rash and having a little bit of improvement, but this last weekend he must have gotten into some more poison ivy because he has got another outbreak along his chest, legs, arms and back.

turns.text: Have you noticed any blood while urinating? Any blood in your urine?

turns.text: Nope. I do leak, especially when I'm changing my positions like from sitting to standing so I do feel there is some involuntary urination. It's more like a urge. I'm loading data in like every one hour in the morning, especially when I take that Lasix.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does it taper off in the afternoon or night?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It tapers off in the afternoon. And by the night I don't do not feel anything.

turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The stream is good. It does feel like all is out in one go. I do not have any kind of bowel issues. I'm using my vaginal cream. Sometimes I feel difficulty in doing so because I feel that there is still something coming out from the vagina and I'm afraid that there might be a prolapse.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Don't worry, I will look into it.

reference_section: The patient presents today for followup.  No dysuria, gross hematuria, fever, chills.  She continues to have urinary incontinence, especially while changing from sitting to standing position, as well as urge incontinence.  She is voiding daytime every 1 hour in the morning especially after taking Lasix, which tapers off in the afternoon, nocturia time 0.  No incontinence.  No straining to urinate.  Good stream, emptying well.  No bowel issues, however, she also indicates that while using her vaginal cream, she has difficulty doing this as she feels protrusion in the vagina, and very concerned if she has a prolapse.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient is an 88-year-old gentleman followed by Dr. X, his primary care physician, Dr. Y for the indication of CLL and Dr. Z for his cardiovascular issues.  He presents to the Care Center earlier today with approximately a one-week history of increased progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea over the course of the past few nights, mild increase in peripheral edema, and active wheezing with dyspnea presenting this morning. He reports no clear-cut chest discomfort or difficulty with angina.  He has had no dizziness, lightheadedness, no near or true syncope, nothing supportive of CVA, TIA, nor peripheral vascular claudication.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, sir. How are you today? Can you confirm your age?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Fifty eight. I feel like my balance is off, and I've been feeling tired and weak.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long have you been experiencing this?

turns.text: I see. Did you feel any other symptoms?

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, wow. Do you know why your balance and coordination worsened?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I did fall recently, but I know for a fact my balance was off before my fall.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How high were you when you fell?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think I was three or five feet high when I fell.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you fall on your back?
