turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Funny. Did anything hurt after your fall?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not really, but I've been having some back pain in my lower and mid back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you always have that pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I haven't. It comes and goes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you done anything to treat it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I started to see a chiropractor like five days ago. He adjusts my neck and lower back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Did you start having problems with your balance after this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I was still having problems with that before I saw the chiropractor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. So, it wasn't the result of the adjustments. Is there anything else that may have caused it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was taking this other medicine for ten days, but I don't remember what it was for. Here is the name of the medication. I wrote it on another paper.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It looks like you took Cipro. This is usually used to treat a U T I. Were you aware you had a U T I?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, yeah. I forgot about that. I thought I had one, so I went to another doctor to get some medication.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. I have one more question. Do you have any trouble controlling your bowel movements or attempting to go to the bathroom?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope. I feel like I'm able to go to the bathroom whenever I want.

reference_section: This is a 58-year-old male who reports a six to eight-week history of balance problems with fatigue and weakness. He has had several falls recently. He apparently had pneumonia 10 days prior to the onset of the symptoms. He took a course of amoxicillin for this. He complained of increased symptoms with more and more difficulty with coordination. He fell at some point near the onset of the symptoms, but believes that his symptoms had occurred first. He fell from three to five feet and landed on his back. He began seeing a chiropractor approximately five days ago and had adjustments of the neck and lumbar spine, although he clearly had symptoms prior to this. He has had mid and low back pain intermittently. He took a 10-day course of Cipro believing that he had a UTI. He denies, however, any bowel or bladder problems. There is no incontinence and he does not feel that he is having any difficulty voiding.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient was initially evaluated at UIHC at 7 years of age. He had been well until 7 months prior to evaluation when he started having spells which were described as "dizzy spells" lasting from several seconds to one minute in duration. They occurred quite infrequently and he was able to resume activity immediately following the episodes. The spell became more frequent and prolonged, and by the time of initial evaluation were occurring 2-3 times per day and lasting 2-3 minutes in duration. In addition, in the 3 months prior to evaluation, the right upper extremity would become tonic and flexed during the episodes, and he began to experience post ictal fatigue.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

The patient lives with his wife and daughter in an apartment. He denied any smoking history. He used to drink alcohol rarely but stopped entirely with the onset of his symptoms. citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, how are you today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am good Doctor, thanks for asking.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: This is my colleague Doctor White, and she will be taking the notes. Is it okay if she joins us?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh sure, no problem.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Hello, I am Doctor White, nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nice to meet you too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, can you breathe in and out for me? Deep breaths please.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay breath sounds are clear. Lung function looks good. Symmetrical rise and fall in chest as patient breathes. I am going to palpate your chest, it's just a routine exam.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Doctor White can you make a note, no egophony or tactile fremitus.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Sure.

reference_section: RESPIRATORY: Good respiratory effort.  Clear to auscultation.  Clear to percussion.  Chest:  Symmetrical rise and fall.  Symmetrical expansion.  No egophony or tactile fremitus.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Where do you live?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I live in a board and care. It is a nice small care home with some very nice and supportive people. It is just next to the Safeway on Village Drive.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Nice. It looks like you love living there.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh yes. I feel very relaxed there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you consume alcohol in any way?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No Sir.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any tobacco consumption?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Never in my life.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you ever try any kind of illicit drugs? Any I V drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I have always kept myself away from all those things.

reference_section: The patient lives in a board and care.  No tobacco, alcohol or IV drug use.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any surgeries in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Actually, yes, I had my gallbladder removed in nineteen ninety two.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, any other surgeries? Think back a little further?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh yeah, I had my appendix out in nineteen eighty eight.

reference_section: Appendectomy 1988. Cholecystectomy. 1992
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are feeling now after the treatment?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am feeling pretty fair, improving slowly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: Fair, but improved.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Sir? Can you hear me? Are you Mister Smith's wife?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes. I am his wife.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old is he? Can you tell me a little bit of how your husband's condition has come to this point? His level of consciousness is concerning.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: He is eighty five. He took the entire M G of Xanax. He is only supposed to take point one twenty five M G of Xanax.  That is why he is like this.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It looks like your husband was admitted to the emergency room the night before.  How did these injuries to his face happen?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: He fell off his wheelchair.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The Adult Protective Services said they found your husband in the home barley conscious. How long had he been that way?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: All day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know what other medications your husband has taken other than the Xanax?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: He didn't take his regular medications for two days.

reference_section: The patient is an 85-year-old male who was brought in by EMS with a complaint of a decreased level of consciousness.  The patient apparently lives with his wife and was found to have a decreased status since the last one day.  The patient actually was seen in the emergency room the night before for injuries of the face and for possible elderly abuse.  When the Adult Protective Services actually went to the patient's house, he was found to be having decreased consciousness for a whole day by his wife.  Actually the night before, he fell off his wheelchair and had lacerations on the face.  As per his wife, she states that the patient was given an entire mg of Xanax rather than 0.125 mg of Xanax, and that is why he has had decreased mental status since then.  The patient's wife is not able to give a history.  The patient has not been getting Sinemet and his other home medications in the last 2 days.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have you been feeling? Is the Wellbutrin keeping your mood stabilized?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have been feeling good. The Wellbutrin is working well for me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It is important to not consume any alcohol or recreational drugs while taking Wellbutrin.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't drink or do drugs.

reference_section: The patient has a history of depression.  No history of substance abuse.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Tell me a little bit about your family history.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My dad and grandpa both had type two diabetes. My son is struggling with type one diabetes at the moment.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Does anyone in your family have heart problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about cancer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Two of my cousins had breast cancer.

reference_section: As far as heart disease there is none in the family.  As far as cancer two cousins had breast cancer.  As far as diabetes father and grandfather had type II diabetes.  Son has type I diabetes and is struggling with that at the moment.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Where do you work, miss?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, you see, I am a civil engineer. Right now, due to pandemic like everyone else I am working from home.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you working full time or is your disability affecting that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I can only work on half time. This disability does not let me work full time. I need to go to physical therapy quite frequently on and off and I also have a baby who consumes a lot of my time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke or drink?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I've never done any of them.

reference_section: The patient is a civil engineer, who currently works from home.  She is working approximately half time because of limitations imposed on her by her disability, need to attend frequent physical therapy, and also the needs of looking after her baby.  She does not smoke and does not drink and has never done either.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, no one in my family has anything like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great.

reference_section: Noncontributory.

turns.text: No.

turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello sir. How are you doing today? You still look a little uncomfortable. Is there still pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. Still a good amount of pain. I did not take my pain medication this morning though. Not sure if that will make a huge difference.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is possibly why you are still in pain. How is movement? Can you get out of the house and get around?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. I am quite happy that I can do my daily activities. I can get up with minimal assistance and do many activities out of the house. I think I am gaining muscle from moving around more too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How is the home exercise program going?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am loving pool therapy. I really feel like that is helping. I do the home exercises sometimes twice a day. I really want to get back to normal.

reference_section: The patient states pain still significant, primarily 1st seen in the morning.  The patient was evaluated 1st thing in the morning and did not take his pain medications, so objective findings may reflect that.  The patient states overall functionally he is improving where he is able to get out in the house and visit and do activities outside the house more.  The patient does feel like he is putting on more muscle girth as well.  The patient states he is doing well with his current home exercise program and feels like pool therapy is also helping as well.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: I blame my heart. It's caused me the most trouble. I had coronary artery bypass surgery in twenty ten along with an angioplasty.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, and I forgot to mention that I've had prostate biopsies in the past.

turns.text: When did you have the biopsies done?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Last year.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did they come back negative?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, fortunately. I guess my prostate isn't as troublesome as my heart.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I understand.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medical problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Let's see. I have diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and osteoporosis.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And any surgeries?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Several.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which ones?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had my tonsils taken out when I was a kid. I also had my uterus removed along with my ovaries and fallopian tubes. The list goes on. I had my appendix removed and two or three of my parathyroids taken out. Despite getting some of my parathyroids removed, I still have borderline high calcium levels according to my endocrinologist.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you experience any complications during or after surgery?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I forgot to mention that I had two carpel tunnel releases as well.

reference_section: She has also had a hysterectomy, salpingoophorectomy, appendectomy, tonsillectomy, two carpal tunnel releases.  She also has had a parathyroidectomy but still has had some borderline elevated calcium.  Also, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, as well as diabetes.  She also has osteoporosis.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: What is your family medical history?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am so sorry. Do you have siblings?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes! I have one sister. She is thirty eight. She has a lot of metal issues. She has attempted suicide two times.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you close with her?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Not really.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you married?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have children?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. We have two adopted kids.

citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is your dad being treated for lupus?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, so let's first check your neck area. It looks good. I don't feel any inflamed lymph node. Your armpits look good too and the last place to check is your groin area. It is all good. No sign of infection.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.text: Okay that helps.

turns.text: Please, tell me about your living situation.

turns.text: Well, right now, I live at home with my kids and my dad.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see here that you're not able to go up the stairs well, can you tell me more about that?

turns.text: Holding the rail makes navigating the stairs easier?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.text: I see. Do you smoke?

turns.text: As far as you know, are there any major health conditions that you know about?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What do you mean by that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Anything like cancer, or arthritis, do those sound familiar?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, um, no nothing like that.

reference_section: Otherwise, negative.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medical history that we should be aware of?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have type two diabetes. My numbers always come high.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, anything else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I also have high cholesterol.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: Diabetes type II, poorly controlled, high cholesterol.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello. How are you feeling today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Great. I'm just here for my yearly physical.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, good. I see your past medical history is missing. Do you, by chance, know if you've had any health related problems before?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Uhm. Let me check my notes on my phone. I knew this question would pop up, but I always forget. Oh, perfect. You can take a look at them.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you. I just want to verify the information with you. You had asthma, nasal inflammation, and some abnormal growth on you neck, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: If it's on there, then it's true. I usually don't remember these kinds of things. My wife is usually here with me. She knows all about my health.

reference_section: Significant for asthma, allergic rhinitis and cervical dysplasia.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How's the little one doing?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She is doing okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long was your pregnancy?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Thirty six weeks.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Was your delivery normal or C section?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: It was a C section.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How much did she weigh?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She was eight pounds and three ounces.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Tell me what's the issue?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, she has a history of seizures. It looks like she is having pain in her tummy and is throwing up.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What else did you notice?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: It looks like she is having some rashes on her skin. There is vomiting for sure. She also feels bloated. She also complains of pain in her tummy. Sometimes she does scratch her mouth. We also noticed some swelling around her lips, eyes and face.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It looks like she's having some food intolerance.

reference_section: Born at 36 weeks' gestation by C-section delivery at 8 pounds 3 ounces.  She does have a history of febrile seizures and what parents reported an abdominal migraine, but on further questioning, it appears to be more of a food intolerance issue.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What medications are you taking right now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am taking Advair and Allegra.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay is it helping you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't know, I am not sure the Allegra is helping. But I do take them regularly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: But is it like better than Claritin?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I think so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay that's good.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Shall I continue?

reference_section: Advair and Allegra.  He has been taking these regularly.  He is not sure the Allegra is working for him anymore.  He does think though better than Claritin.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Anybody sick in family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No one.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about any illnesses that run in your family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, everyone is healthy.

reference_section: Noncontributory.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi again! How has your acne been since you started the spironolactone?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It has been improving.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you experienced any increased thirst, mood changes or unusual fatigue?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

reference_section: The patient comes for a routine followup appointment.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, I don't think you need any restraints as you are doing fine. I do want to make sure you have a chair and bed monitor since you have a history of multiple falls. They can help detect fall.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't want that, I will manage.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you sure?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes!

reference_section: RESTRAINTS: None.  The patient has declined use of chair check and bed check.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Do you know when was the last time you got a tetanus shot?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No I don't remember.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: Not sure.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi there! How are you today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi! I am good.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Welcome in!

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Lets start with a little social history. Are you a tobacco or alcohol user?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you married? Do you have children?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am not married but I do have a two year old son.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you currently see a gynecologist?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. She is in Bartow.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great.

reference_section: She is followed by a gynecologist in Bartow.  She is not an alcohol or tobacco user.  She is not married.  She has a 2-year-old child.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Tell me about your family medical history.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My family is pretty healthy. I don't know of any health problems.

reference_section: Noncontributory.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Welcome in.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I don't. Smoking is gross.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I agree. Do you drink alcohol?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How much do you drink per day or week?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: When I get off work usually have a glass of wine. I don't ever have more then one glass.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: She does not smoke.  She takes one glass of wine per day.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The nurse applied antibiotic ointment and a bandage to your foot. Did she go over how to change the bandage at home?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

reference_section: The patient had antibiotic ointment and a bandage applied to his foot.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello. Before we begin, I need you to confirm some information for me.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What kind of information?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: About your family. Do you know if you have certain medical conditions that run in your family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope. My family is very healthy.

reference_section: Negative.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about any breathing issues or asthma?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Actually, I have a history of asthma.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh okay, and was it severe or mild?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, it was not severe but still remarkable.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hm, alright.  Anything else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I also struggled with a serious acne problem.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Got it.

reference_section: Significant for asthma and acne.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How's she doing?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She's had better days.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Aw and why's that?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She's been really congested recently. Snorting a lot more, too. She's onlt eleven and I think it is odd she snores so much. I took her to see the allergist and he said it's not her allergies so we stopped giving her Allegra.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does she happen to snore at night?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, not really.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hm.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: And while we're here, I also wanted you to check out her toe. The right big toe appears a bit red to me. The skin around it has been peeling for the last week and a half.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Lemme take a look. Have you applied anything to the area?

reference_section: This is an 11-year-old female who comes in for two different things.  1.  She was seen by the allergist.  No allergies present, so she stopped her Allegra, but she is still real congested and does a lot of snorting.  They do not notice a lot of snoring at night though, but she seems to be always like that.  2.  On her right great toe, she has got some redness and erythema.  Her skin is kind of peeling a little bit, but it has been like that for about a week and a half now.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Why are you holding your face?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Ah! Have pain in my tooth.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, how bad is it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, awfully bad.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am so sorry.

reference_section: Toothache.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had similar symptoms before?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No never like this.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any other complaints you have had in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Just some knee pain issues.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, so chronic knee pain.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

reference_section: Chronic knee pain.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you tell me about any cancers in your family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, my sister has ovarian cancer, and my father has liver cancer.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh I am so sorry.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That is okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any heart conditions?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My mom and dad both have heart disease. My dad has diabetes too.

reference_section: Consistent with a sister of his has ovarian cancer and his father had liver cancer.  Heart disease in the patient's mother and father, and father also has diabetes.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you tell me what problems you have had in the past. Or what medical issues are currently going on?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: You mean my heart problem and things?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, I have hypertension and kidney problems since many years.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I get frequent urinary infections.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your urine creatinine is normal.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay. I also have severe aortic stenosis.

reference_section: Significant for moderate to severe aortic stenosis, urinary tract infection, hypertension, chronic kidney disease (although her creatinine is near normal).
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does anyone else in your family have aneurysm problem?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, my grandmother had it. She actually passed away due to brain aneurysm.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, okay.

reference_section: Grandmother died of cerebral aneurysm.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is wrong with your back honey?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, it all started off with a little pimple on the buttock.  I was soaking it at home with hot water and stuff, but it did not improve. I hope this is not cancer. I am only twenty four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay what exactly are you experiencing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So you came to the hospital on the first and they did an I and D in E D?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes I was admitted to the hospitalist service with high blood sugars. My African American father was so scared.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay sugars high. Do you know the number? How high?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I do not know that but they found positive bacteria or some sort of thing in my blood culture.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So today we are evaluating you for surgery?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

reference_section: This patient is a 24-year-old African-American female who presented to the hospital with buttock pain.  She started off with a little pimple on the buttock.  She was soaking it at home without any improvement.  She came to the hospital on the first.  The patient underwent incision and drainage in the emergency department.  She was admitted to the hospitalist service with elevated blood sugars.  She has had positive blood cultures.  Surgery is consulted today for evaluation.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi there! I have the results from your ultrasound. You have kidney stones in the ureter close to the bladder.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh no.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: This explains the pain you have been having on your left side. Are you still experiencing nausea and vomiting?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I have been.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I would like to set you up with a consult with a consult with a surgeon.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: 1.  Left flank pain. 2.  Left ureteral stone. 3.  Nausea and vomiting.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any known drug allergies?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

reference_section: No known drug allergies.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your daughter had an exposure to the ant bait but we are not sure if she actually ingested any of it. Poison Control confirmed that even if she did ingest the small amount that she was found with, it is likely nontoxic. Do you have any questions?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No.

reference_section: Exposure to ant bait.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, sir. How are you today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am alright. I am here for a check up since I am feeling kind of dizzy lately.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is not good. How long has this been happening?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: A few months. This happened to my sister too. I think she is still dealing with it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there any other family medical history I should know about? Migraines or cancer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Not that I know of. The rest of my family seems pretty healthy.

reference_section: Sister is dizzy but no other acute illnesses.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know anyone in your family whose had cancer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No one that I know.

reference_section: Negative for cancer.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay so your blood report is back and the cardiac enzyme we were looking for are negative.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your blood urea nitrogen, also known as B U N, is within normal limits and hydrogen is stable. Creatinine is also within the normal range.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Great!

citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you on any medications?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not taking any medications.

reference_section: None.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi, how are you doing today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've been better. Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, you are here for your follow up right? Remind me how often are you coming here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's right. I'm coming around between a month or two.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, it's every four to eight weeks.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm not taking any medicine now. I just wanted to let you know.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, I can see it in your record. It says that you are off of all the immunosuppression. So, just let me check. It says here that you do have mild chronic G V H D. It is not that bad that I should be worried about any therapy or anything else. How long ago did you get that transplant?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think it was around four and a half years ago. I'm feeling much better after that. I do have complaints of blood in my stool. But after you sent me to that doctor, that gastro doctor, I feel good. I know they said that they removed something, but I'm not sure, but after that it has been improved a lot.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let me see in my chart. You had some rectal bleeding issues because of which I referred you to the gastroenterologist. A complete endoscopy was performed, which was both on the upper and the lower side. There was no evidence of ulcers or any other abnormality. That's  good news, right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I agree. That was a relief.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: They did find some polyps and they removed it. They turned out to be benign, so nothing to worry about there.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I remember this said they removed something, but I forgot the name.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there any other issue that I can help you with?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't know. I feel a lot of fatigue and like I'm not able to do things like I used to do before. I get tired very easily. I don't know if it is related to something or not, but things have been weird. I'm not able to do even the minor things like I lift two boxes and I'm done for the day. Is it something that I should be worried about?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It looks like you have a mild iron deficiency. I will work on that with you, don't worry.

reference_section: The patient comes to the clinic today for followup.  I am seeing him once every 4 to 8 weeks.  He is off of all immunosuppression.  He does have mild chronic GVHD but not enough to warrant any therapy and the disease has been under control and he is 4-1/2-years posttransplant. He has multiple complaints.  He has had hematochezia.  I referred him to gastroenterology.  They did an upper and lower endoscopy.  No evidence of ulcers or any abnormality was found.  Some polyps were removed.  They were benign.  He may have mild iron deficiency, but he is fatigued and has several complaints related to his level of activity.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you feeling any pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I feel great.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there any other medical issue that we should be worried about?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, it feels like I'm young again. I'm able to do all my activities.

reference_section: COMPLICATIONS: None.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you for coming in to see us at A B C D General Hospital today.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I wish I wasn't here right now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I understand, before we begin, how old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm seventy seven years young.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which race, and gender do you identify with?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm an African American woman.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What's seems to be causing you pain today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've had this bunion on my foot for as long as I can remember.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is the pain worsening?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it is so painful, I've tried to avoid surgery for so long, but I want this bunion gone.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have you managed this bunion in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've used antiinflammatories, rested, changed my activities, I've done everything, but this pain is getting worse and worse.  I need it gone.

reference_section: This 77-year-old African-American female presents to ABCD General Hospital.  The patient states she has had a bunion deformity for as long as she can remember that has progressively become worse and more painful.  The patient has attempted conservative treatment without long-term relief of symptoms and desires surgical treatment.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have diabetes or blood pressure problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I have hypertension but no diabetes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Alright.

reference_section: Hypertension.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you dealing with your pain now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh no, I have no issues with my pain. Today I'm here for a different cause. I'm having this weakness all around on my left side, especially in my arm. I feel like I cannot lift anything like even a glass of water. It's hard for me to lift it up. I'm not able to walk properly, let alone the balancing and everything else. It's just that my whole left side seems to be weak.

reference_section: The patient reports that the pain is not an issue at this time.  The patient states that her primary concern is her left-sided weakness as related to her balance and her walking and her left arm weakness.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you have any medical disorders previously, sir?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have diabetes. Also, I was quite overweight.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you taking any medications for that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I was still taking something called Zyprexa, but I stopped it after my last regular weight check. Also, I never took anything for diabetes. I also have chronic bronchitis for… I don't know… many years.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh yes, I am a smoker.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How many cigarettes do you take in a day?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe up to sixty a day.

turns.text: A minivan. The car in front of me stopped suddenly and I hit them right from behind. The front of my car is pretty wrecked.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Were you wearing a seatbelt? And did the airbag deploy?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes and yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any passengers in the car with you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, just me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you hit your head anywhere?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, but I do have some pain on the left side of my neck.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you think you lost consciousness at any point in time?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Actually, I do. Right after the crash.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any pain elsewhere?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um I'm having some pain in my lower stomach area. I think it could be due to slamming into the airbag or steering wheel.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How would you rate this pain, ten being the worst pain ever?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um I'd give it a five out of ten right now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any knee, ankle, or foot pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about pain in your shoulders, elbows, or wrists?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Uh no, but I guess I do have a little bit of pain in my pelvic area.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you remember walking before or after the ambulance arrived?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't think so. Someone told me that I was placed on the stretcher after they got me out of the car.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Just to confirm, no chest pain or difficulty breathing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you noticed any cuts on your skin?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any headache, nausea, or vomiting?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Fever or chills?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any chance of pregnancy?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I've been good at taking my birth control and I also have an I U D.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When was your last period?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um end of May I believe.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you taking anything besides birth control?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Accutane for my pimples.

reference_section: This is a 32-year-old Hispanic female who presents to the emergency department today via ambulance.  The patient was brought by ambulance following a motor vehicle collision approximately 45 minutes ago.  The patient states that she was driving her vehicle at approximately 40 miles per hour.  The patient was driving a minivan.  The patient states that the car in front of her stopped too quickly and she rear-ended the vehicle ahead of her.  The patient states that she was wearing her seatbelt.  She was driving.  There were no other passengers in the van.  The patient states that she was restrained by the seatbelt and that her airbag deployed.  The patient denies hitting her head.  She states that she does have some mild pain on the left aspect of her neck.  The patient states that she believes she may have passed out shortly after the accident.  The patient states that she also has some pain low in her abdomen that she believes is likely due to the steering wheel or deployment on the airbag.  The patient denies any pain in her knees, ankles, or feet.  She denies any pain in her shoulders, elbows, and wrists.  The patient does state that she is somewhat painful throughout the bones of her pelvis as well.  The patient did not walk after this accident.  She was removed from her car and placed on a backboard and immobilized.  The patient denies any chest pain or difficulty breathing.  She denies any open lacerations or abrasions.  The patient has not had any headache, nausea or vomiting.  She has not felt feverish or chilled.  The patient does states that there is significant deformity to the front of the vehicle that she was driving, which again was a minivan.  There were no oblique vectors or force placed on this accident.  The patient had straight rear-ending of the vehicle in front of her.  The pain in her abdomen is most significant pain currently and she ranks it at 5 out of 10.  The patient states that her last menstrual cycle was at the end of May.  She does not believe that she could be pregnant.  She is taking oral birth control medications and also has an intrauterine device to prevent pregnancy as the patient is on Accutane.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello sir, what brings you here today? Also, please confirm your age for the records.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am seventy years old. I am here for nothing particular but I just have discomfort on the right side.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We did electromyography study. This was to assess the health of muscles and the nerves in your body. When did you first notice this discomfort?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: About five years ago. After my stroke. I've been to a neurologist before.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, I can see that you have taken different kinds of medications, but nothing seems to help you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That sounds right. Nothing seems to help me to get rid of this discomfort.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How often do you check your sugar levels?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I do it at home. Mainly two to three times a day. I increase or decrease the amount of insulin that I take based on my numbers.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Don't you consult anyone before doing that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's been so many years now. I do it all by myself.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We did reevaluations of your symptoms. It turned out to be all negative. Do you smoke?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I used to chew tobacco a lot and then there were drinks. I used to drink at least half a bottle of single malt in one night. I quit everything five years ago after my stroke.

reference_section: This is a 70-year-old male who has no particular complaints other than he has just discomfort on his right side.  We have done EMG studies.  He has noticed it since his stroke about five years ago.  He has been to see a neurologist.  We have tried different medications and it just does not seem to help.  He checks his blood sugars at home two to three times a day.  He kind of adjusts his own insulin himself.  Re-evaluation of symptoms is essentially negative.  He has a past history of heavy tobacco and alcohol usage.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It is nice to see you again, miss.  We are following up on a few things today. How is your arm feeling?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My arm is all better. It is not in pain at all anymore.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How has your mood been? Are you feeling any relief from your symptoms since you have been on the Lexapro?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's helping a little bit.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How much Lexapro are you taking now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am taking ten M G.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long have you been taking the full dosage?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: About a week ago. I don't take it every day. I don't feel like I need it some days.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I want you to take the full dosage every day. This might be why you have not had much relief with your symptoms yet.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your hands are a little shaky. Is this a normal occurrence for you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I didn't even notice.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It is very subtle. We will keep an eye on it for now. Your blood pressure is a little better today. Have you experienced any worsening joint or bone pain?  I want to check on your osteoporosis and osteoarthritis.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

reference_section: 1.  Hypertension, better reading today. 2.  Right arm symptoms, resolved. 3.  Depression probably somewhat improved with Lexapro and she will just continue that.  She only got up to the full dose 10 mg pill about a week ago and apparently some days does not need to take it. 4.  Perhaps a very subtle tremor.  I will just watch that. 5.  Osteoporosis. 6.  Osteoarthritis.

reference_section: As mentioned before, this patient has been psychotic off and on for about 20 years now.  He has had years in which he did better on Clozaril and also his other medications. With typical anti-psychotics, he has done well at times, but he eventually gets another psychotic bout.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What happened to you? How did you get involved in this accident?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was just trying to adjust cable that my brother's dog was tied to. All of a sudden, he attacked me out of nowhere. The injury to my leg is V shaped and the V is pointing towards my foot.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of dog?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: German shepherd. But he is up to date on his shots, and he is completely healthy.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: He bit me on my foot, and it looks like his teeth went into my skin. I went to my P C P.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What did you do there?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They cleaned the wound and did some bandage along with it he gave me a tetanus shot.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And he sent you to us?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay let me examine your wound.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It looks like there is a flap injury developed after puncture wound. It seems like a centimeter long and viable. How old are you sir? And what ethnicity do you identify with?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: White male. I am fifty years old. Is my right leg going to be okay?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The skin looks viable. We can save the tissue.

reference_section: This 50-year-old white male earlier this afternoon was attempting to adjust a cable that a dog was tied to.  Dog was a German shepherd, it belonged to his brother, and the dog spontaneously attacked him.  He sustained a bite to his right lower leg.  Apparently, according to the patient, the dog is well known and is up-to-date on his shots and they wanted to confirm that.  The dog has given no prior history of any reason to believe he is not a healthy dog.  The patient himself developed a puncture wound with a flap injury.  The patient has a flap wound also below the puncture wound, a V-shaped flap, which is pointing towards the foot.  It appears to be viable.  The wound is open about may be roughly a centimeter in the inside of the flap.  He was seen by his medical primary care physician and was given a tetanus shot and the wound was cleaned and wrapped, and then he was referred to us for further assessment.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Can you tell me more about your daughter's injury?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, we came in in November, and she was diagnosed with an acute on chronic right slipped capital femoral epiphysis.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did she have surgery on this?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, let me look at my notes, I have it written down here, um, a situ pinning.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Remind me, how old are you, dear?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm thirteen now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, thank you. So, um, if you look her at the x rays, it appears that the screw is now going into the hip joint.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: They didn't see that before. What can we do about this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We'll need to do another operation in order to remove this screw and put a shorter one in. We need to do the surgery because this can cause further joint damage.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Are there any risks of infection from this surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Overall, the risk of infection is very low, honestly its less than one percent.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: That's good to hear, will she go to sleep during surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, we'll use anesthesia the entire time. She won't feel a thing.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What does recovery look like for this surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I expect her to heal up very well, but there's always a risk of some changes in sensation and motion, and she may be stiff for some time following everything. Other risks include bleeding, but I would not worry about these things.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, how does that sound, honey? Would you like to do this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I want to get back to playing sports with my friends.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I agree, Doctor, we'll do the surgery.

reference_section: The patient is a 13-year-old girl who presented in November with an acute on chronic right slipped capital femoral epiphysis.  She underwent in situ pinning.  The patient on followup; however, noted to have intraarticular protrusion of her screw.  This was not noted intraoperatively on previous fluoroscopic views.  Given this finding, I explained to the father and especially the mother that this can cause further joint damage and that the screw would need to be exchanged for a shorter one.  Risks and benefits of surgery were discussed.  Risks of surgery include risk of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremity, failure to remove the screw, possible continued joint stiffness or damage.  All questions were answered and parents agreed to above plan.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: This 76 y/o male complained of several months of generalized weakness and malaise, and a two week history of progressively worsening orthostatic dizziness. The dizziness worsened when moving into upright positions. In addition, he complained of intermittent throbbing holocranial headaches, which did not worsen with positional change, for the past several weeks. He had lost 40 pounds over the past year and denied any recent fever, SOB, cough, vomiting, diarrhea, hemoptysis, melena, hematochezia, bright red blood per rectum, polyuria, night sweats, visual changes, or syncopal episodes. He had a 100+ pack-year history of tobacco use and continued to smoke 1 to 2 packs per day. He has a history of sinusitis.

reference_section: This is a pleasant 49-year-old gentleman post lumbar disc replacement from January 2005.  Unfortunately, the surgery and interventional procedures have not been helpful in alleviating his pain.  He has also tried acupuncture, TENS unit, physical therapy, chiropractic treatment and multiple neuropathic medications including Elavil, Topamax, Cymbalta, Neurontin, and Lexapro, which he discontinued either due to side effects or lack of effectiveness in decreasing his pain.  Most recently, he has had piriformis injections, which did give him a brief period of relief; however, he reports that the Botox procedure that was done on March 8, 2006 has not given him any relief from his buttock pain.  He states that approximately 75% of his pain is in his buttock and leg and 25% in his back.  He has tried to increase in his activity with walking and does note increased spasm with greater activity in the low back.  He rated his pain today as 6/10, describing it is shooting, sharp and aching.  It is increased with lifting, prolonged standing or walking and squatting, decreased with ice, reclining and pain medication.  It is constant but variable in degree.  It continues to affect activities and sleep at night as well as mood at times.  He is currently not satisfied completely with his level of pain relief.

turns.text: Good morning, young lady. Is this your mother?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Good morning, doctor. Well, she's thirteen now, but she's had feet problems all her life.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What's been the problem with her feet?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, she had bilateral feet corrections when she was a year old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, how has she been since that procedure?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, just look at her heel, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I see. She has pretty significant calcaneal valgus deformity.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What does that mean, doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your heel is out of alignment, sweetie. Do you have pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I have a lot of pain, doctor.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What can we do about this, doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, given all of her symptoms, I think we should do a calcaneal osteotomy and Achilles lengthening procedure.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What does that procedure entail?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, in short, we'll go in there and straighten everything out, and get everything lined back up.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What's the risk of infection with the surgery, sir?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Actually, it's less than one percent, so it's extremely low.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: How is this possible, doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We use antibiotics to control for infection the entire time.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: That's great. Will she be asleep for this procedure?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, we'll use anesthesia the entire time. She won't feel a thing.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, that's good too. What about after the procedure? What's the protocol?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, I'll need your help. We have to be strict about her being nonweightbearing for six weeks at minimum.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Will she need a brace too?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, at least for six months, but if she does everything I ask of her, it will be only six months.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, yes, I think we should do the procedure. What do you think, honey?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I want to get back to playing sports with my friends.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The other risks include bleeding; changes in sensation in most of extremity; hardware failure; need for later hardware removal; possible nonunion; possible failure to correct all the deformity; and need for other surgical procedures.  I would not worry about these issues, though. It is quite rare. So, looking at her radiographs, the spinal arch is definitely collapsed. I think you guys are making the right decision.

reference_section: The patient is a 13-year-old female who had previous bilateral feet correction at 1 year of age.  Since that time, the patient has developed significant calcaneal valgus deformity with significant pain.  Radiographs confirmed collapse of the spinal arch, as well as valgus position of the foot.  Given the patient's symptoms, surgery is recommended for calcaneal osteotomy and Achilles lengthening.  Risks and benefits of surgery were discussed with the mother.  Risks of surgery include risk of anesthesia; infection; bleeding; changes in sensation in most of extremity; hardware failure; need for later hardware removal; possible nonunion; possible failure to correct all the deformity; and need for other surgical procedures.  The patient will need to be strict nonweightbearing for at least 6 weeks and wear a brace for up to 6 months.  All questions were answered and parents agreed to the above surgical plan.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: After he fell, how was he treated? Guest_family_1: We went to the E D right after he fell, and they said he had complete fractures of both bones in the arm.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I see that here, he also has shortening bayonet apposition. Guest_family_1: What can we do for this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: There's actually a few options here. First we can cast it and see how he heals, generally, children heal up very well from fractures. Guest_family_1: That's good, we like that option more than any kind of surgery.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: However, surgery is also an option here as well. Guest_family_1: Yeah, to be completely sure we fix this, I think we should opt for the surgery, what do you think, honey? Guest_family_2: Yes, I agree. What are the risks of infection for this surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The risk of infection is very low, generally less than one percent. We use antibiotics to control for infection. Guest_family_1: Will he be asleep for the surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Absolutely, he won't feel a thing. Other risks include bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremity, hardware failure, and need for later hardware removal, and cast tightness. I would not worry about these risks. We have great results with these surgeries. Guest_family_1: Then yes, we'd like to do the surgery.

reference_section: The patient is a 5-year-old male who sustained refracture of his right forearm on 12/05/2007.  The patient was seen in the emergency room.  The patient had a complete fracture of both bones with shortening bayonet apposition.  Treatment options were offered to the family including casting versus closed reduction and pinning.  The parents opted for the latter.  Risks and benefits of surgery were discussed.  Risks of surgery included risk of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremity, hardware failure, and need for later hardware removal, cast tightness.  All questions were answered, and the parents agreed to the above plan.

reference_section: This patient was injured on November 20, 2008.  He works at the Purdy Correctional Facility and an inmate had broken some overhead sprinklers, the floor was thus covered with water and the patient slipped landing on the back of his head, then on his back.  The patient said he primarily landed on the left side.  After the accident he states that he was generally stun and someone at the institute advised him to be evaluated.  He went to a Gig Harbor urgent care facility and they sent him on to Tacoma General Hospital.  At the Tacoma General, he indicates that a whiplash and a concussion were diagnosed and it was advised that he have a CT scan.  The patient describes that he had a brain CT and a dark spot was found.  It was recommended that he have a followup MRI and this was done locally and showed a recurrent acoustic neuroma.  Before, when the patient initially had developed an acoustic neuroma, the chiropractor had seen the patient and suggested that he have a scan and this was how his original acoustic neuroma was diagnosed back in October 2005.  The patient has been receiving adjustments by the chiropractor since and he also has had a few massage treatments.  Overall his spine complaints have improved substantially. After the fall, he also saw at Prompt Care in the general Bremerton area, XYZ, an Osteopathic Physician and she examined him and released him full duty and also got an orthopedic consult from XYZ.  She ordered an MRI of his neck.  Cervically this showed that he had a mild disc bulge at C4-C5, but this actually was the same test that diagnosed a recurrent acoustic neuroma and the patient now is just recovering from neurosurgical treatment for this recurrent acoustic neuroma and some radiation is planned. Since 2002 the patient has been seeing the chiropractor, XYZ for general aches and pain and this has included some treatments on his back and neck.

reference_section: The patient is a 54-year-old right-handed male who works as a phlebotomist and respiratory therapist at Hospital. The patient states that he was attempting to do a blood gas. He had his finger of the left hand over the pulse and was inserting a needle using the right hand. He did have a protective clothing including use of gloves at the time of the incident. As he advanced the needle, the patient jerked away, this caused him to pull out of the arm and inadvertently pricked the tip of his index finger. The patient was seen and evaluated at the emergency department at the time of incident and had baseline studies drawn, and has been followed by employee health for his injury. The source patient was tested for signs of disease and was found to be negative for HIV, but was found to be a carrier for hepatitis C. The patient has had periodic screening including a blood tests and returns now for his final exam.

turns.text: Yes, but what does that mean?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You have arthritis in both of your knees, sir.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Ah, yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had surgery on these knees?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I had surgery on both of these knees, let me check my notes. It was an, um, arthroscopy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When were these surgeries?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They were in the nineteen ninety one nineteen ninety two time frame, somewhere in there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have you managed this since the surgeries?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've taken antiinflammatories, had injections, and I've even used narcotics.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. If those haven't helped, I think you'd be a good candidate for knee replacements.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Can we do both at the same time?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No, let's do the left since that one hurts more. Do you have any other conditions I should know about?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've had a lot of back surgeries, I have spinal stenosis.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know what surgeries you've had?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Let me check my notes, um, I've had a spinal decompression and epidural steroids injection.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Who has prescribed you narcotics for this pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The pain is so bad, but Doctor X has handled those.

reference_section: The patient is a 57-year-old with severe bilateral knee DJD, left greater than right, with significant pain and limitations because of both. He is able to walk approximately a 1/2-mile a day but is limited because of his knees.  Stairs are negotiated 1 at a time.  His problems with bilateral knee DJD have been well documented.  He had arthroscopy in the 1991/199two time frame for both of these.  He has been on long-standing conservative course for these including nonsteroidals, narcotics, injections.  At this point because of his progressive and persistent limitations he has opted for total joint surgery on the left side.  He does have other arthritic complaints including multiple back surgeries for spinal stenosis including decompression and epidural steroids.  Significant pain is handled by narcotic medication.  His attending physician is Dr. X.

reference_section: The patient is a 64-year-old female referred to physical therapy following complications related to brain tumor removal.  The patient reports that on 10/24/08 she had a brain tumor removed and had left-sided weakness.  The patient was being seen in physical therapy from 11/05/08 to 11/14/08 then she began having complications.  The patient reports that she was admitted to Hospital on 12/05/08.  At that time, they found massive swelling on the brain and a second surgery was performed.  The patient then remained in acute rehab until she was discharged to home on 01/05/09.  The patient's husband, Al, is also present and he reports that during rehabilitation the patient did have a DVT in the left calf that has since been resolved.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: Overall, the patient has been doing reasonably well.  She is being treated for some hemorrhoids, which are not painful for her.  There has been a note that she is constipated. However, I also see one that is in the one teens and a couple in the 120s range. She is not bothered by cough or rib pain.  These are complaints, which I often hear about. Today, I reviewed Dr. Hudyncia's note from psychiatry.  Depression responded very well to Cymbalta, and the plan is to continue it probably for a minimum of 1 year. turns.text: The next patient we have is Miss Dey, we have been regularly following up with her for her hydrocephalus since two thousand and two.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Okay, then you asked her to follow up doctor X Y Z regarding her cervical spine M R I.

turns.text: Yes exactly! Let's go see her. Hello Miss Dey, how are you? This is my colleague doctor Jen, and she will be accompanying me today if that is okay with you?

turns.text: Hi Miss Dey.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, last week I had some urine issue, like had to pee frequently. I had few episodes of urgency.

turns.text: Okay and how do you feel this week?

turns.text: Okay good.

turns.text: That's good.

turns.text: Any headache?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope!

turns.text: Any changes in your walk or balance?

turns.text: Yes.

turns.text: Are you using cane at this point of time?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay good. Anything else you want to tell me?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Ah yes, in the beginning of May, I got a spell of severe cough and because of continuous coughing I think I developed pain in my hip which travels down to my legs.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh okay, do you feel any tingling or numbness.

turns.text: Yes! I feel constant tingling sensation and a feeling that something is pinching my never. Sometimes it's just so painful.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Doctor Jen did you take the notes of what she said?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay great, anything else Miss Dey?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Alright you take care. I will see you next time.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Bye!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Bye.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Take care Miss Dey, Bye!

reference_section: She has been followed for her hydrocephalus since 2002.  She also had an anterior cervical corpectomy and fusion from C3 though C5 in March 2007.  She was last seen by us in clinic in March 2008 and she was experiencing little bit of head fullness and ringing in the ears at that time; however, we decided to leave her shunt setting at 1.0.  We wanted her to followup with Dr. XYZ regarding the MRI of the cervical spine.  Today, she tells me that with respect to her bladder last week she had some episodes of urinary frequency, however, this week she is not experiencing the same type of episodes.  She reports no urgency, incontinence, and feels that she completely empties her bladder when she goes.  She does experience some leakage with coughing.  She wears the pad on a daily basis.  She does not think that her bladder has changed much since we saw her last.  With respect to her thinking and memory, she reports no problems at this time.  She reports no headaches at this time.  With respect to her walking and balance, she says that it feels worse.  In the beginning of May, she had a coughing spell and at that time she developed buttock pain, which travels down the legs.  She states that her leg often feel like elastic and she experiences a tingling radiculopathy.  She says that this tingling is constant and at times painful.  She feels that she is walking slower for this reason.  She does not use the cane at this time.  Most of the time, she is able to walk over uneven surfaces.  She is able to walk up and down stairs and has no trouble getting in and out of a car.

reference_section: 1.  Pneumonia.  He has had recurrent episodes of pneumonia, which started at approximately age 20.  These have been treated repeatedly over the years, and on average he has tended to have an episode of pneumonia once every five years, although this has been far more frequent in the past year.  He is usually treated with antibiotics and then discharged.  There is no known history of bronchiectasis, inherited lung disease or another chronic pulmonary cause for the repeated pneumonia. 2.  He has had a catheter placed for urinary retention, his urologist has told him that he thinks that this may be due to prostate enlargement.  The patient does not have any history of diabetes and does not report any other medical problems.  He has lost approximately 18 pounds in the past month. 3.  He had an appendectomy in the 1940s. 4.  He had an ankle resection in 1975.
