turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, miss. Before we begin your physical, could you verify your age and ethnicity for me, please?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm forty two years old and identify as white.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you. I also see that you're here for a follow up for your asthma, correct? How is your asthma?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's right. Oh, man. My asthma has been getting worse over the last three months. My allergies are also acting up again.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, no. Has anything changed that may have made your allergies worse?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, my husband has been hauling more corn in since it's busy season. I think that might have made it worse.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you taking any medications to alleviate your asthma and allergies?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm using my inhaler every day for my asthma. Here are the other medications and treatments I've been using. I know I wouldn't have remembered, so I put them on a paper for you to see.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let me take a look. I see you have been taking Allegra for your allergies. Has that been helping?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Eh. It kind of helps when I do take it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You don't take it every day then?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope. Only when I feel like I need to.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. What about the Flonase? Has that been helping?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm not taking that right now, but it helped me in the past.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I also see you took Advair in the past, correct? Do you still take it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I did, but I stopped taking it because it started to annoy my private area.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I understand. Speaking more on this. Let's begin your physical. Do you have anything you'd like to add that you're starting to notice more?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, yeah. I feel like I'm easily annoyed right before my period. It could also be my husband, but he likes to say it's because I'm about to start my period.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Do you see any other increased symptoms right before your menstrual cycle?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. I feel like I've seen an increase in all the signs before my period. I'm also getting more impatient around that time, but when I'm not on my period, I feel like my mood is better.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When do you see your mood change?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My husband says it's bad the week before I start my period, but I think it gets better a day after I start.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you seen any bleeding during your cycle?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not as much anymore. Just some spots here and there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. What about hot flashes or night sweats?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope. I feel fine most of the time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's good. I'm looking at your chart right now and it says you showed a U T I present, correct? Your test showed blood in your urine.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has your urine been checked since then?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. I'll order another urine test along with additional lab tests so that we can complete your physical.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I actually just had some lab work done because it was required for a life insurance application. Crazy, right? Here's the form with all the details for the lab work.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, perfect. I see they looked at your cholesterol and other areas. Could you send that to me when you get the results?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Of course. I'll get that sent to you A S A P.

reference_section: This is a 42-year-old white female who comes in today for a complete physical and follow up on asthma.  She says her asthma has been worse over the last three months.  She has been using her inhaler daily.  Her allergies seem to be a little bit worse as well.  Her husband has been hauling corn and this seems to aggravate things.  She has not been taking Allegra daily but when she does take it, it seems to help somewhat.  She has not been taking her Flonase which has helped her in the past.  She also notes that in the past she was on Advair but she got some vaginal irritation with that. She had been noticing increasing symptoms of irritability and PMS around her menstrual cycle.  She has been more impatient around that time.  Says otherwise her mood is normal during the rest of the month.  It usually is worse the week before her cycle and improves the day her menstrual cycle starts.  Menses have been regular but somewhat shorter than in the past.  Occasionally she will get some spotting after her cycles.  She denies any hot flashes or night sweats with this.  In reviewing the chart it is noted that she did have 3+ blood with what appeared to be a urinary tract infection previously.  Her urine has not been rechecked.  She recently had lab work and cholesterol drawn for a life insurance application and is going to send me those results when available.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, ma'am. What is the reason for your visit today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was referred by a doctor to come see you so that you could check up on my nasal problems. Here is my report from my previous doctor who referred me to you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you. Let me take a look.  I see here it says you had severe sinusitis two to three months ago, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Is that what they're calling my nasal problems?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, it is. Sinusitis is the inflammation of your nasal airways.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I see. Thank you for describing it to me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No problem. Would you be able to describe to me what you had been feeling two to three months ago?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I can. My face would feel uncomfortable, my nose was stuffy, my eyes hurt, and I felt something dropping in the back of my throat.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever been prescribed any medication?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Here's the list of medicine I was taking.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see you were given antibiotics, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was, but I don't know what those are. Could you explain them to me?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Antibiotics are usually used to fight infections.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had an infection? I thought I just had some nasal problems.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your report states you had a severe infection. Do you remember if the antibiotics helped?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not really. I felt like my symptoms were the same.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Did your doctor order any advanced imaging's?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. They did a C T scan of my nose. Here is the report from my C T scan.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let me take a look. It looks like you had some thickening of the mucosal layer in your right paranasal sinus. You also had some obstruction in your right ostiomeatal complex and excess growing of some of the bones in your nose. Uhm. Oh, one more thing. I see your nasal septum was shifted to the left.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, wow. Thank you for explaining everything to me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No problem. Going back to your list of medications, I know you took antibiotics for your infection, but did you take any medication for your sinuses?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I haven't. I did try this cream for my nose, but that didn't work either. Nothing worked!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Looks like the cream you used was a topical nasal corticosteroid. Are there any other symptoms that you have been experiencing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've had some trouble with my balance, and I feel like I've lost some of my hearing. I thought this was odd since I'm only fifty years old. I think my ears felt plugged or full of air, so they just needed to pop.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Let's perform an audiogram test to check your ears.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sounds good.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm seeing that you have some mild high frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Your tympanometry seems to be normal. Your speech discrimination was also normal.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's reassuring.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I want to ask a few more questions about your ears. Do you feel any fullness or pressure?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I don't feel anything like that right now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you hear any humming, buzzing, or roaring sounds?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope. I don't hear anything like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We checked your ears and now understand more about the problem, but I wonder why your balance is affected. When did you start noticing your balance was affected?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think it could have been to this one medicine that starts with an A. I forgot the name, but it didn't really help my nasal problems. It just made my balance worse.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Was the medicine called Allegra?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, yeah. That's what it was called. I thought I had some sort of allergy, so I thought it would help.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Did you ever feel any dizziness too?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I did.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I will have you do some movements to see if your dizziness occurs.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sounds good.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Could you look to the left and then look to the right.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, wow. That made me very dizzy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Looks like sudden movements and head turning make your dizziness worse.

reference_section: I had the pleasure of meeting and evaluating the patient referred today for evaluation and treatment of chronic sinusitis.  As you are well aware, she is a pleasant 50-year-old female who states she started having severe sinusitis about two to three months ago with facial discomfort, nasal congestion, eye pain, and postnasal drip symptoms.  She states she really has sinus problems, but this infection has been rather severe and she notes she has not had much improvement with antibiotics.  She had a CT of her paranasal sinuses identifying mild mucosal thickening of right paranasal sinuses with occlusion of the ostiomeatal complex on the right and turbinate hypertrophy was also noted when I reviewed the films and there is some minimal nasal septum deviation to the left.  She currently is not taking any medication for her sinuses.  She also has noted that she is having some problems with her balance and possible hearing loss or at least ear popping and fullness.  Her audiogram today demonstrated mild high frequency sensorineural hearing loss, normal tympanometry, and normal speech discrimination.  She has tried topical nasal corticosteroid therapy without much improvement.  She tried Allegra without much improvement and she believes the Allegra may have caused problems with balance to worsen.  She notes her dizziness to be much worse if she does quick positional changes such as head turning or sudden movements, no ear fullness, pressure, humming, buzzing or roaring noted in her ears.  She denies any previous history of sinus surgery or nasal injury.  She believes she has some degree of allergy symptoms.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Hello. Looks like you're having surgery today.

turns.text: Yeah, I am. I forgot what the surgery was, but it says it in my report.

turns.text: Okay and in one or both knees?

turns.text: Both.

turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi!

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hello!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you feeling now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am feeling okay.

turns.text: Yeah, looks like your condition is improving.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And who are we seeing today?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Hi Doctor, this my son J and that's my wife. Guest_family_2: Hi there

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, hello young man how are you feeling today? Guest_family_2: He has been complaining of severe tummy pain and was crying the whole time. We are worried as he is a special child. He has autism.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: For how long now? Guest_family_2: Autism?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No, I mean when did he start complaining of stomach pain? Guest_family_2: It started last night.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh okay, let me check him. Did he have any nausea or vomiting?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, he threw up a lot and is refusing to eat or drink anything.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And then he is complaining of tummy pain? Guest_family_2: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, the good part is he is not dehydrated.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any diarrhea? Guest_family_2: Yes, he went three to four times.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hm, but no blood or anything in the stools or vomit?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, nothing like that, we did not notice anything.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay good.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, let me run some tests but the signs and symptoms sound like he might have a stomach flu, also called as gastroenteritis in medical terms. I will start him on some medicines and hopefully that should help.

reference_section: 1.  Gastroenteritis. 2.  Autism.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, nice to meet you, miss. I will be taking care of you today. Before we start, can I get to know you a bit? I like to know who I am treating.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hello, nice to meet you. Of course. Um, what can I say? I am a recent widow. My husband passed when we were married for only eight years. I am also retired and loving every minute of it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am sorry to hear that, but I am glad you are happy after retirement. Do you celebrate your infinite days off with a drink or a cigarette?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I do not smoke. I drink occasionally, but it is very rare.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any children that you spend your time with?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have three wonderful children.

reference_section: She has no tobacco use.  She has rare alcohol use.  She has three children and is a widow.  Her husband died after they were married only eight years.  She is retired.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you use to treat your asthma?

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: Albuterol.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you eat three meals a day?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you think those meals add up to about two thousand calories a day?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I would say yes.

citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you still taking Micronase every morning?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I take um two point five M G once a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great. Continue taking Micronase by mouth every day. As for your infection, I want you to start taking Bactrim twice daily. I'll be prescribing you thirty pills. It'll be Bactrim four hundred M G and eighty M G tablets.

reference_section: Micronase 2.5 mg Tab PO QAM #30.  Bactrim 400/80 Tab PO BID #30.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you consume any kind of tobacco?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I've never done it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any kind of alcohol consumption?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

reference_section: She does not smoke or drink alcohol.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What seems to be the problem today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've been having headaches for a while now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long have you been having these headaches?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I had my first one about two months ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you suddenly start having them, or was it more gradual?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I'd say it was more gradual.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Where do you feel your headaches?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Right here, between my eyes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How would you describe your symptoms?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'd say it feels like a pressure sensation.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What's the intensity of these headaches?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, they're about moderately severe, I guess.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do these headaches interfere with your ability to do your activities?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, they do. My regular activities are significantly more difficult now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any sinus congestion?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I do. I also have some light sensitivity.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you stressed out at work?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I have a very stressful job, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you sleeping well?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, no not at all. I even try to have a little drink before bed, and it doesn't help.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any oral symptoms, like vomiting or pain in your jaw?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, nothing like that.

reference_section: The patient describes the gradual onset of a headache problem. The headache first began 2 months ago. The headaches are located behind both eyes. The pain is characterized as a sensation of pressure. The intensity is moderately severe, making normal activities difficult. Associated symptoms include sinus congestion and photophobia. The headache may be brought on by stress, lack of sleep and alcohol. The patient denies vomiting and jaw pain.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medical conditions that I should know about?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not that I know of.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, there's no history of depression, or cancer, or high blood pressure?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, it's not ringing any bells.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any hallucinations? Are you seeing hearing thing that is not real?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

reference_section: No headaches. No visual, hearing, or swallowing difficulties. No changes in bowel or urinary habits.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, which gender do you identify with?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good afternoon, doctor, thank you for asking, I identify as a female.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, thank you. Have you ever had surgery on this knee?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I actually had an A C L reconstruction done in March of two thousand eight. Um, it didn't go well, so they did a revision at the end of that year, in December.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see, thank you. What about your upper body? Is there any history of surgery there?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Actually, yes, I had surgery on my arm when I was six.

reference_section: She had an anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in 03/2008, and subsequently had a revision ACL reconstruction in 12/2008.  She has also had arm surgery when she was 6 years old.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Welcome in, sir.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you do for work?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am professor at the college up on the hill.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you teach?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I teach history and the bible.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you drink alcohol or use tobacco products?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I do not partake in either of those activities.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any major medical conditions that I should know about?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm seeing here that you have a history of allergies too, is that correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh yes, that's right too.

citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: How's the patient?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: He's stable. Heart rate sixty five. Normal rhythm. Oxygen ninety seven percent on room air.

reference_section: Stable.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Tell me about your past problems.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure. I just came into the hospital I think about three weeks back for recurrent urine infections.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes it says here that you have bladder problems from a long time, mostly related to tone and capacity.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes that is why they put catheter in me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay and you have recently had right side C V A?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, because of my heart problems they had to put pacemaker in.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Good.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have hereditary diabetes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay and your neural problem is associated to that as well.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You have pain on the right side now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, because of my stroke.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And you take thyroid medications too?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, for my hypothyroidism.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What surgeries have you had in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have had many surgeries. They took out my gall bladder, then colon cancer surgery was in nineteen ninety eight.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And now pacemaker placement, right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that is correct.

reference_section: Significant for recurrent UTIs as she was recently to the hospital about 3 weeks ago for urinary tract infection.  She has chronic incontinence and bladder atony, for which eventually it was decided for the care of the patient to put a Foley catheter and leave it in place.  She has had right-sided CVA.  She has had atrial fibrillation status post pacemaker.  She is a type 2 diabetic with significant neuropathy.  She has also had significant pain on the right side from her stroke.  She has a history of hypothyroidism.  Past surgical history is significant for cholecystectomy, colon cancer surgery in 1998.  She has had a pacemaker placement.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any major medical conditions running in your family history that you know about?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, there's nothing of note.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, there's no history of arthritis, or cancer that you're aware of?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not that I know of.

reference_section: Noncontributory.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, does high blood pressure run in your family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, no it's just me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay and this was your first time?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Because I am looking at your previous charts and I don't see it mentioned before.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh yeah first time it shot up this high. I never had a high blood pressure problem before.

reference_section: Noncontributory to the present condition and review of his previous charts.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Now, let's talk about your family history. Have any of them had cancer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Actually, yes, I know a few family members have, but I can't remember who had what kind.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's okay. What about heart disease? Can you remember anyone having that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that rings some bells.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you, has anyone in your family had a joint replacement?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I know that a lot of my family has had arthritis in the past, but I can't remember whether or not they had joint replacements, honestly.

reference_section: Family history is remarkable for a remote history of cancer. Family history of heart disease and osteoarthritis.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi, how are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am good, how about you?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, I am good too, thank you for asking. So, what brings you here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I have developed this painful ulcer on my hip.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, let me take a look. Which side?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: On my right hip.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, I see it. Looks like you have developed pressure ulcer.

reference_section: Pressure decubitus, right hip.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, tell me what's going on and what's brought you here.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I am her mother. She has this blister on the side of her head right above her ear, here. I was just worried and concerned about my baby.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old is the baby? When did you first notice it?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She is just fourteen days old. Let me tell you from the beginning. On Friday, when I was taking her for a bath, I noticed a blister near her umbilicus area. We went to our doctor on Saturday, and they did a test.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you get the test result?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I got it today. Here is the report.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let me have a look. It says she is having a growing M R S A.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, I've been diagnosed with that too. And I am on medications. I had it on my buttock area.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, so you know about it, and I don't have to explain it more.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So how is the blister on the umbilicus now?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She has been doing good. We put on some bacitracin ointment, and it almost healed up. But today I noticed that another small blister on her head. It really scared me, and I did not want to take any chance. That's why I reached out to the Infectious Disease center. I know it is private. But still, I don't want to take any chance with my baby's health. I called the center directly and they asked me to come to the hospital.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You did good. I will start the treatment. How are her eating and sleeping habits?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She hasn't missed any of her meals. She is taking around two ounces of milk in every feed. I don't think I have any issues with her eating or sleeping.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did she have any fever?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Not that I noticed.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has she been lethargic or crying more than normal?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any other changes in her daily routine that you might have noticed?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, I didn't notice any changes.

reference_section: A 14-day-old was seen by private doctor because of blister.  On Friday, she was noted to have a small blister near her umbilicus.  They went to their doctor on Saturday, culture was drawn.  It came back today, growing MRSA.  She has been doing well.  They put her on bacitracin ointment near the umbilicus.  That has about healed up.  However today, they noticed a small blister on her left temporal area.  They called the private doctor.  They direct called the Infectious Disease doctor here and was asked that they come into the hospital.  Mom states she has been diagnosed with MRSA on her buttocks as well and is on some medications.  The child has not had any fever.  She has not been lethargic or irritable.  She has been eating well up to 2 ounces every feed.  Eating well and sleeping well.  No other changes have been noted.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am in pain. I get these frequent episodes of pain and discomfort in my head.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is it in any side of head or is it overall?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sometimes it is overall and other times just on any one side. Doctor: This sounds like it is a migraine headache.

reference_section: Migraine headache.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, young man. Is this your mother?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi, doctor. Yes, this is my mom.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, can you tell me more about your son, ma'am?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Sure, well, he's six years old now, and we're here to follow up his A D H D medicines.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: He's been taking Adderall, correct? How long has he been taking this?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: It's been about a month now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How has he responded to the Adderall?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: The first day he took it, truthfully, he was wonderful. There's been a lot of improvement in his behavior, and he's really been doing well, so far.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's great!

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, but I have two concerns. When he takes the medicine first thing in the morning it seems to take a while to kick in, and then it wears off at about two P M and he has problems in the evening.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has he had problems with his appetite?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Um, he did at first, but it's been coming back. It's more of a problem in the morning when he first takes the medicine in the morning, not so much in the afternoon after it wears off.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you gotten any reports from his teachers?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: They have seen a dramatic improvement with it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has he taken every dose?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, I missed one last weekend, and he was just horrible.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, mommy, I thought I needed it, but you didn't give it to me.

reference_section: This is a 6-year-old male who comes in rechecking his ADHD medicines.  We placed him on Adderall, first time he has been on a stimulant medication last month.  Mother said the next day, he had a wonderful improvement, and he has been doing very well with the medicine.  She has two concerns.  It seems like first thing in the morning after he takes the medicine and it seems like it takes a while for the medicine to kick in.  It wears off about 2 and they have problems in the evening with him.  He was initially having difficulty with his appetite but that seems to be coming back but it is more the problems early in the morning after he takes this medicine than in the afternoon when the thing wears off.  His teachers have seen a dramatic improvement and she did miss a dose this past weekend and said he was just horrible.  The patient even commented that he thought he needed his medication.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome in. Let's get started, how old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good afternoon, doctor. I'm fifty two years old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: My nurse says that you're here for an independent evaluation, is that correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes sir, that is.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, what do you do for a living?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Right now, I'm a temporary employee for A B C A B C, I've worked for A B C D, too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you do there?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Mainly, I handle the loading and unloading of furniture and appliances for people's houses.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's hard work. When did you get hurt?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It was about two and a half weeks ago now, back in October.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have a history of back problems, like before this injury?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I've had back pain for a long time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What happened when you got hurt this time?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was unloading one of the A B C eighteen wheelers, when I bent down to pick up some boxes, and I felt the pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of pain did you feel?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I felt a sharp pain in my lower back right away when I tried to lift those boxes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does your pain go down your legs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it goes into the right side of my butt, and then all the way down the outside of my right leg, like into the knee.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have your symptoms progressed since they began?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Doctor, they've only gotten worse.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any pain in your left leg?

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: The patient is a 52-year-old male who is here for independent medical evaluation.  The patient states that he works for ABC ABC as a temporary worker.  He worked for ABCD too.  The patient's main job was loading and unloading furniture and appliances for the home.  The patient was approximately there for about two and a half weeks.  Date of injury occurred back in October.  The patient stating that he had history of previous back problems ongoing; however, he states that on this particular day back in October, he was unloading an 18-wheeler at ABC and he was bending down picking up boxes to unload and load.  Unfortunately at this particular event, the patient had sharp pain in his lower back.  Soon afterwards, he had radiating symptoms down his right buttock all the way down to the lateral part of his leg crossing his knee.  This became progressively worse.  He also states that some of his radiating pain went down to his left leg as well.  He noticed increase in buttock spasm and also noticed spasm in his buttocks.  He initially saw Dr. Z and was provided with some muscle relaxer and was given some pain patches or Lidoderm patch, I believe.  The patient states that after this treatment, his symptoms still persisted.  At this point, the patient later on was referred to Dr. XYZ through the workmen's comp and he was initially evaluated back in April.  After the evaluation, the patient was sent for MRI, was provided with pain medications such as short-acting opioids.  He was put on restricted duty.  The MRI essentially came back negative, but the patient continued to have radiating symptoms down to his lower extremity and subsequently the patient was essentially released by Dr. XYZ in June with maximum medical improvement. Unfortunately, the patient continued to have persistence of back pain and radiating symptoms down to his leg and went back to see Dr. XYZ again, and at this point, the patient was provided with further medication management and sent for Pain Clinic referral.  The patient also was recommended for nerve block at this point and the patient received epidural steroid injection by Dr. ABC without any significant relief.  The patient also was sent for EMG and nerve conduction study, which was performed by Dr. ABCD and the MRI, EMG, and nerve conduction study came back essentially negative for radiculopathy, which was performed by Dr. ABCD.  The patient states that he continues to have pain with extended sitting, he has radiating symptoms down to his lower extremity on the right side of his leg, increase in pain with stooping. He has difficulty sleeping at nighttime because of increase in pain.  Ultimately, the patient was returned back to work in June, and deemed with maximum medical improvement back in June.  The patient unfortunately still has significant degree of back pain with activities such as stooping and radicular symptoms down his right leg, worse than the left side.  The patient also went to see Dr. X who is a chiropractic specialist and received eight or nine visits of chiropractic care without long-term relief in his overall radicular symptoms.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, dear, how old are you?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you, yes, so this shows left patellar chondromalacia. Has she been to P T?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: We got a referral for P T, but they only wanted to do, um, let me look at my notes, patellar tracking exercises.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see, has she been wearing her brace?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, she has been. I've been making sure of it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's good, and how is your pain today, dear?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: P T only made the pain much worse, it hurts so much.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, she's in a lot of pain, is there anything else we can do, besides P T?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, we're in a pretty difficult spot here. The majority of my patients get significantly better by just going to P T.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Is there any surgery to fix this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Usually, we manage this for six months without surgery, and she hasn't reached that milestone yet. But, because her pain is getting so severe, I can do a lateral capsular release on this knee.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What is that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's a small procedure, minimally invasive, and we can do it outpatient. Her kneecap is partially dislocating, so this surgery will get everything back into alignment.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, what is the risk of infection?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The risk of infection is actually less than one percent. We use antibiotics to control for infection.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Will I be asleep for this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, you won't feel a thing.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Will I need to go back to P T?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, you'll need to go some after the surgery to make sure everything heals up okay. The other risks include bleeding, changes in sensation and motion extremity, failure of procedure to relieve pain, need for postoperative rehab, and significant postoperative swelling.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I think we'd like to do the surgery. What do you think, honey?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I think so too, I want to get back to playing soccer. Sp 3

reference_section: The patient is a 14-year-old girl who started having left knee pain in the fall of 2007.  She was not seen in Orthopedic Clinic until November 2007.  The patient had an outside MRI performed that demonstrated left patellar chondromalacia only.  The patient was referred to physical therapy for patellar tracking exercises.  She was also given a brace.  The patient reported increasing pain with physical therapy and mother strongly desired other treatment.  It was explained to the mother in detail that this is a difficult problem to treat although majority of the patients get better with physical therapy.  Her failure with nonoperative treatment is below the standard 6-month trial; however, given her symptoms and severe pain, lateral capsular release was offered.  Risk and benefits of surgery were discussed.  Risks of surgery including risk of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and motion extremity, failure of procedure to relieve pain, need for postoperative rehab, and significant postoperative swelling.  All questions were answered, and mother and daughter agreed to the above plans.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: This 46 y/o RHF presented with a 4 month history of right neck and shoulder stiffness and pain. The symptoms progressively worsened over the 4 month course. 2 weeks prior to presentation she began to develop numbness in the first and second fingers of her right hand and RUE pain. The later was described as a throbbing pain. She also experienced numbness in both lower extremities and pain in the coccygeal region. The pains worsened at night and impaired sleep. She denied any visual change, bowel or bladder difficulties and symptoms involving the LUE. She occasionally experienced an electric shock like sensation shooting down her spine when flexing her neck (Lhermitte's phenomena). She denied any history of neck/back/head trauma. She had been taking Naprosyn with little relief.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Here ya go.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you. And have you been watching your cholesterol intake since getting blood work done? Your labs show your cholesterol levels are a bit elevated. I'd like for you to monitor your cholesterol and go in for another set of labs before our next visit.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Do I need to fast for it again?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, you'll need to fast. I'd recommend going in early in the morning before eating any breakfast.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That sounds like a good plan.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And as for your sinusitis, how have you been feeling since finishing your course of antibiotics?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Much better. No more headaches and a stuffy nose.

reference_section: Followup on diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, and sinusitis.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: What brings you in today?

turns.text: Do you have any other symptoms?

turns.text: Do you have any history of kidney stones?

turns.text: Hello, doctor. Yes, I have been told that both eyes need cataract extraction. I came for a second opinion because I will only have surgery if necessary. I am nervous.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is the reason for the extraction?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am not exactly sure because the other doctors said a bunch of medical terms. I have had laser in my eyes though. That was for macular degeneration. Doctor X said I had neurovascular age-related macular degeneration.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know what laser you had on your eyes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I just know laser was done by Doctor X four times to the macula on the right and two times on the left.

reference_section: The patient seeks evaluation for a second opinion concerning cataract extraction.  She tells me cataract extraction has been recommended in each eye; however, she is nervous to have surgery.  Past ocular surgery history is significant for neurovascular age-related macular degeneration.  She states she has had laser four times to the macula on the right and two times to the left, she sees Dr. X for this.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.text: What do you do for work?

turns.text: I work in Human Resources for the State of Maryland.

turns.text: Do you live alone or with others?

turns.text: Do you smoke cigarettes?

turns.text: I used to smoke like a chimney. I quit smoking a while back. I had been smoking for about sixteen years.

turns.text: That's great! When did you quit?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I quit in nineteen eighty four. That is also the year I quit drinking.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What was the reason behind quitting drinking?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had a drinking problem. I am in A A. I have been in A A since I quit.

turns.text: That's great. Keep up the hard work.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any history of recreational or I V drug use?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. I used to take pills, but I never got into needle drugs. Thank God.  I went through treatment, all those years back. I started going to A A and got my life together.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any other risk factors for H I V? Like multiple sex partners?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I had my last H I V test over two years ago. I have been with the same guy for over two years.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: He lives alone.  He works full time in Human Resources for the State of Maryland.  He previously was an alcoholic, but quit in 1984.  He also quit smoking cigarettes in 1984, after 16 years of smoking.  He has a history of illicit drug use, but denies IV drug use.  He denies any HIV risk factors and states that his last HIV test was over two years ago.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, I am fifty eight now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, you are here today because you are having some vision difficulties? Tell me about what has been going on, ma'am.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. Okay. It all started a year ago. It started with losing the color in my vision.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Was the loss sudden or gradual?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Gradual. And now I am starting to have blurry vision.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did that start happening?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I noticed it two months ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is the blurred vision an all blur or is there a blind spot of blurred vision.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It is an all over vision blur and then I have on blind spot in my right eye.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any fluctuations in your symptoms in the last year? Have you gained any vision back?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Some days I feel like things are a little better but not much. I have basically been the same.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you experienced any weakness, dizziness, vertigo, nausea or vomiting?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any double vision or headaches?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any pain in or behind the eye at all?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any other health concerns or complains?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Just the vision problems.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Alright! Let me take a look here.

reference_section: 58 y/o female presents with a one year history of progressive loss of color vision. In the past two months she has developed blurred vision and a central scotoma OD. There are no symptoms of photopsias, diplopia, headache, or eye pain. There are no other complaints. There have been mild fluctuations of her symptoms, but her vision has never returned to its baseline prior to symptom onset one year ago.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you feeling today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have been having some trouble breathing.  I had tightness in my chest after walking up stairs.

turns.text: Let me listen to your lungs.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, ma'am. Before we begin, can you confirm your age for me, please?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure, I'm fifty six years old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, thank you. What seems to be the problem today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I have a history of systemic lupus erythematosus.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have you been treated for this in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I went to a rheumatologist about four months ago, I had discomfort in both of my hands.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which hand was worse?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My left was worse than my right at that time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you seen anyone else for this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I came in on October thirtieth two thousand seven. I was having the same problem.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What did they do for you at that time?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They have me a trial of Elavil because they thought it was, um, ulnar or radial neuropathy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did they give you any topical creams?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, they gave me a prescription for Zostrix but I couldn't fill it because of my insurance.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see, have your symptoms gotten worse since they began?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, especially here, at the base of my left hand, like around my wrist.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which fingers do you feel it in? If any?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Right here, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, these are your second, third, and fourth fingers. Do you have any other symptoms of note?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, actually yeah, I've been having some respiratory problems for the last three days or so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What symptoms have you been experiencing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I've had a dry cough and I feel like I've had a fever but I haven't taken my temperature.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any night sweats or chills?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not that I can remember.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any chest pain or discomfort?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about shortness of breath, or G I problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thankfully, no.

reference_section: The patient is a 56-year-old female with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus, who was last seen in rheumatology clinic approximately 4 months ago for bilateral hand discomfort, left greater than right.  The patient was seen on 10/30/07.  She had the same complaint.  She was given a trial of Elavil at bedtime because the thought was to see that represented ulnar or radial neuropathy.  She was also given a prescription for Zostrix cream but was unable to get it filled because of insurance coverage.  The patient reports some worsening of the symptoms especially involving at the dorsum of the left hand, and she points to the area that actually involves the dorsal aspect of the second, third, and fourth digits.  The patient recently has developed what sounds like an upper respiratory problem with a nonproductive cough for 3 days, although she reports that she has had subjective fevers for the past 3 or 4 days, but has not actually taken the temperature.  She has not had any night sweats or chills.  She has had no recent problems with chest pain, chest discomfort, shortness of breath or problems with GU or GI complaints.  She is returning today for routine followup evaluation.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you remember the name of the medication you are taking?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have two, but I do not remember their name or why I am taking it.

turns.text: That is fine, we will figure it out.

turns.text: I wanted to talk to you about your family medical history.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.text: Ready when you are.

turns.text: Do any of your siblings have it as well?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello. Looks like we are here for a six months follow up. How are we doing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have stayed relatively the same. My main complaint is that I feel tired throughout the day. The C P A P is doing fine and I wake up refreshed, but I don't like how I crash.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Alright. How are the thyroid issues?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I seem to be fine. My thyroid gland does not seem enlarged and I can breathe like normal. No fever or anything.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you experienced any of the following: temperature intolerance, palpitations, muscle weakness, tremors, nausea, vomiting, constipation, or diarrhea?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nothing of the kind.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How has you weight been?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It has been stable.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any muscle weakness closest to the body's center?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, nothing like that. Not bad for forty five.

reference_section: This is a return visit to the endocrine clinic for the patient with history as noted above.  She is 45 years old.  Her last visit was about 6 months ago.  Since that time, the patient states her health has remained unchanged.  Currently, primary complaint is one of fatigue that she feels throughout the day.  She states, however, she is doing well with CPAP and wakes up feeling refreshed but tends to tire out later in the day.  In terms of her thyroid issues, the patient states that she is not having signs or symptoms of thyroid excess or hypothyroidism.  She is not reporting temperature intolerance, palpitations, muscle weakness, tremors, nausea, vomiting, constipation, hyperdefecation or diarrhea.  Her weight has been stable.  She is not reporting proximal muscle weakness.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: So I understand you had a fainting episode yesterday?

turns.text: Yes, I did.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has this happened to you before?

turns.text: Yes. It happens whenever needles are involved.

turns.text: You had a Vasovagal Syncope. How are you feeling today?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi there, sir! I am Doctor Frankland.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi! It's nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What brings you into see me today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have had this pain in my finger and wrist for about a month. I have had some numbness too. The numbness started in the finger and is now in the wrist too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which wrist and finger is it that is hurting?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The left one and the middle finger, here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What was to time frame of the procreation of the numbness from the finger to the wrist?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It started when I woke up and then by the end of the day my wrist was numb too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did you start experiencing pain in the wrist area?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: A few days after the numbness started.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which hand is your dominate hand?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am left handed.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you do for work?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am a cook. I also cut the fish for the whole restaurant.  I cut fish for hours in the mornings and it has been a struggle and it is aggravating my finger and wrist.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am forty four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any history of injuring a neck injury?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any neck pain or weakness?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any difficulties with bowel movements or urination?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

reference_section: This 44 y/o LHM presented with a one month history of numbness and pain of the left middle finger and wrist. The numbness began in the left middle finger and gradually progressed over the course of a day to involve his wrist as well. Within a few days he developed pain in his wrist. He had been working as a cook and cut fish for prolonged periods of time. This activity exacerbated his symptoms. He denied any bowel/bladder difficulties, neck pain, or weakness. He had no history of neck injury.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good morning.  How are you feeling today?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you expensing any pain or discomfort?

turns.text: No. I feel fine.

turns.text: How are you doing with everything?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How's your wife doing? I think the last time I saw her was two weeks ago. She was telling me about the remodeling you've been doing around the house.

turns.text: She's doing well, thanks for asking. Oh yeah, the remodeling has been a lot. I didn't think it'd take as long as it has.

turns.text: Yeah, it can take some time. We remodeled our kitchen three years ago and it turned our lives upside down. So tell me, how's training going for you? I believe you were telling me that you have a five k coming up.

turns.text: Yeah, it's two weeks away. I've been jogging and doing cross country track about five times a week. I also lift twice a week on my better days.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's great! And no smoking or drinking, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How's work been treating ya?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Pretty darn well actually. I go into the allergy and immunology clinic four days outta the week. I like that my hours are flexible. My patients also haven't run away from me yet, which is always a good sign.

reference_section: The patient is married.  Wife is living and well.  He jogs or does Cross Country track 5 times a week, and weight training twice weekly.  No smoking or significant alcohol intake.  He is a physician in allergy/immunology.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: My nurse tells me you're thirty four years old, is that correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I just had my birthday, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You identify as African American, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You're here for a follow up? What brings you back in today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I don't really have a single acute complaint, but I have a muscle sprain in my upper back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there an injury associated with this pain, ma'am?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think it has to do with me lifting weights.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, that's common. Is this messing with your ability to work?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, it's not really.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you do for a living?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm a housekeeper, it's my profession.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you having trouble sleeping at night?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it's not severe, but I'm having some trouble.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: With ten being the worst pain imaginable, how would you rate your pain today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'd say it's usually a two out of ten.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When it's the worst, how would you rate it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: When that happens, I'd say it's a three or a four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you take any medicines for this pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Over the counter medications usually help the pain go away.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any other complaints?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, just this muscle pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any loss of balance when you hold something with this arm?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, my strength and everything is normal there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any signs of infection? That'd be anything like fever or chills, anything like that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I don't have anything like that.

reference_section: This is a 34-year-old African American female who comes today for routine followup.  She has no acute complaints.  She reports that she has a muscle sprain on her upper back from lifting.  The patient is a housekeeper by profession.  It does not impede her work in anyway.  She just reports that it gives her some trouble sleeping at night, pain on 1 to 10 scale was about 2 and at worse it is 3 to 4 but relieved with over-the-counter medication.  No other associated complaints.  No neurological deficits or other specific problems.  The patient denies any symptoms associated with opportunistic infection.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How can I help you today.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have been having irregular periods.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When was your last menstrual period?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My last period was on June first two thousand and four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you currently sexually active? Is there a possibility of pregnancy?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No! There is no possibility that I am pregnant.  I have not had sex in two years.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old where you when you had your first menstrual period?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was ten years old when I got my first period.  My cycle has never been regular. It runs in my mom's side of the family.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is your family history of reproductive health conditions on your mom's side of the family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My mom and my aunt have both had total hysterectomies.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there any other personal medical history I should know about?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I see Doctor X Y Z Allen for my abnormal heart valve condition.  I am on S B E prophylaxis.  I have to limit my activity because of my heart condition.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you avoid decongestants?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

reference_section: She denies sexual activities since two years ago.  Her last menstrual period was 06/01/2004.  Her periods have been irregular.  She started menarche at 10 years of age and she is still irregular and it runs in Mom's side of the family.  Mom and maternal aunt have had total hysterectomies.  She also is diagnosed with abnormal valve has to be on SBE prophylaxis, sees Dr. XYZ Allen.  She avoids decongestants.  She is limited on her activity secondary to her heart condition.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have you been feeling? How is your leg feeling?

turns.text: My right leg is in a lot of pain. The nurse just changed the bandage. I only have a rash where the bandage is.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It looks like we have you taking Vicodin for the pain. Is the medication not helping?

turns.text: The pain medication is horrible. I have been throwing up, off and on. I have been constipated since I have been here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'll note that. Vomiting since February nineteen of two thousand seven. I am sorry to hear that. I will make a change to the medication and get you something for the constipation issue.

turns.text: Thank you.

turns.text: Have you had any shortness of breath, chest pain or coughing up blood?

turns.text: Any joint pain, headaches or rashes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Just a rash where the bandages are like I said earlier. I also want to discuss this acne while I am here. I have had it for about two years. It's nothing big, just mild to moderate in severity.

reference_section: He has had emesis off and on related to Vicodin and constipation since 02/19/2007, also related to pain medication.  He has had acne for about two years, which he describes as mild to moderate.  He denied shortness of breath, chest pain, hemoptysis, dyspnea, headaches, joint pains, rashes, except where he has had dressings applied, and extremity pain except for the right leg pain.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: None.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you live with your husband?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, we live on a ranch about twenty miles away.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have children?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: We had six children all together, but two of them passed away suddenly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm so sorry to hear that. How old were they?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: One was forty years old and the other was forty five.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Wow, they were quite young. I offer you my sincerest condolences.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you. It's been really hard on my family, but we're trying our best to get by.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's all you can do. It's important to spend time with each other every chance you get.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.text: Go ahead.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke or drink?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Never.

reference_section: She is married, lives with her husband, has 2 children that passed away and 4 surviving children.  No history of tobacco use.  No history of alcohol use.  Family history is noncontributory.

turns.text: Hello, I am Doctor Rez. I will ask you a few questions about your personal and family history, okay?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did any one in your family get diagnosed with any medical conditions?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My mom has lumps in her breast but it is benign, however my granny on my father side had cancer.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of cancer, do you know?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, it was breast cancer don't know if there are types for it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No, that's fine. Did you ever have palpitations?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What do you mean by that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Um, Palpitations means the sensation when you feel that your heart is racing or pounding really fast even without doing any strenuous exercise or anything.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, got it. No, I never had that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about any uncontrolled urine leakage? Any accidents?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about any recent sudden hair loss or any other concerns?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, nothing like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any other treatments in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I recently got treatment for my sinus.

reference_section: Benign breast lump in her mother; however, her paternal grandmother had breast cancer.  The patient denies any palpitations, urinary incontinence, hair loss, or other concerns.  She was recently treated for sinusitis.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you tell me more about your family's medical history? Are there any conditions of note?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm so sorry to hear that, ma'am, how old were they?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, my father was eighty, and my mother was sixty seven.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm so sorry, do you have any siblings?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I had a brother, he passed away too, from bone and throat cancer.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm sorry, how old was he?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: He was seventy, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any children?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have four, two of each.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's wonderful, how are your sons doing?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's great, what about your daughters?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, they're sixty and fifty eight, and they both have cancer. They're real fighters.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm sorry, that must be so hard to deal with. Are there any other conditions you're aware of?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh yeah, we have it all, nervous condition, high blood pressure, kidney and lung disease, depression, it's all there.

reference_section: Her father died at the age of 80 from prostate cancer.  Her mother died at the age of 67.  She did abuse alcohol.  She had a brother died at the age of 70 from bone and throat cancer.  She has two sons, ages 37 and 38 years old who are healthy.  She has two daughters, ages 60 and 58 years old, both with cancer. turns.text: It looks like E M S found you in bad shape?

turns.text: What?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: My mother is hard of hearing. She is eighty five. They found her on the toilet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did your mother tell you anything about her condition before E M S arrived?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She said she threw up right before they came and she had diarrhea.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ma'am. How are you feeling now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have been sick to my stomach.  My belly has been hurting. I threw up.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How many times did you vomit ma'am?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't know.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you recall the color of the vomit? Did you see any blood or notice the color of the vomit?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't know.

reference_section: The patient is an 85-year-old female who presents with a chief complaint as described above. The patient is a very poor historian and is extremely hard of hearing, and therefore, very little history is available. She was found by EMS sitting on the toilet having diarrhea, and apparently had also just vomited. Upon my questioning of the patient, she can confirm that she has been sick to her stomach and has vomited. She cannot tell me how many times. She is also unable to describe the vomitus. She also tells me that her belly has been hurting. I am unable to get any further history from the patient because, again, she is an extremely poor historian and very hard of hearing.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: How's the little dude?

turns.text: He has fever and bad congestion for the last two days. He has had a fever for one. I try to suck the discharge out through nose.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am guessing he has some mild problems with breathing while feeding.

turns.text: Yes, that is correct. He is drinking milk every couple hours, only for ten minutes instead of twenty minutes.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: He has fever too, so she gave him Tylenol. Guest_family2: He is very fussy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is he sleeping well?

turns.text: Yes, he sleeps. But he is not able to breath well even with albuterol.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old is he? And, sorry this is odd, but what ethnicity do you identify as? I need it foe the paperwork.

turns.text: Twenty one days old Caucasian male.

turns.text: Do you notice him getting blue at all? Or does this area sink in when he tried to breathe?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, neither.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is he having any trouble breathing in general?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No.

reference_section: The patient is a 21-day-old Caucasian male here for 2 days of congestion - mom has been suctioning yellow discharge from the patient's nares, plus she has noticed some mild problems with his breathing while feeding (but negative for any perioral cyanosis or retractions).  One day ago, mom also noticed a tactile temperature and gave the patient Tylenol. Baby also has had some decreased p.o. intake.  His normal breast-feeding is down from 20 minutes q.2h. to 5 to 10 minutes secondary to his respiratory congestion.  He sleeps well, but has been more tired and has been fussy over the past 2 days.  The parents noticed no improvement with albuterol treatments given in the ER.  His urine output has also decreased; normally he has 8 to 10 wet and 5 dirty diapers per 24 hours, now he has down to 4 wet diapers per 24 hours.  Mom denies any diarrhea.  His bowel movements are yellow colored and soft in nature. The parents also noticed no rashes, just his normal neonatal acne.  The parents also deny any vomiting, apnea.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, with medication I feel it is better, but I want to be removed from the backboard.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let's get you off. Yeah, your C T scans of the abdomen appeared normal.  And there was no sign of bleeding.  I believe, you just have a contusion and abrasion to abdomen from the seatbelt and likely from the airbag as well.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's good that you can stand and walk through the emergency department without difficulty. I do not see any abrasions or lacerations.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, nothing like that and I can walk.

reference_section: The patient was removed from the backboard within the first half hour of her emergency department stay.  The patient has no significant bony deformities or abnormalities.  The patient is given a dose of Tylenol here in the emergency department for treatment of her pain.  Her pain is controlled with medication and she is feeling more comfortable and removed from the backboard.  The patient's CT scans of the abdomen appeared normal.  She has no signs of bleeding.  I believe, she has just a contusion and abrasion to her abdomen from the seatbelt and likely from the airbag as well.  The patient is able to stand and walk through the emergency department without difficulty.  She has no abrasions or lacerations.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Oh wow!

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And you mentioned that your mother had Alzheimer's?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: And she actually passed away in her eighties due to old age.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, how about your siblings, do they have any signs of Alzheimer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, they are fine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: Significant for lung, liver, and prostate cancer.  Her mother died in her 80s of "old age," but it appears that she may have had a mild dementing illness at that time.  Whatever that dementing illness was, appears to have started mostly in her 80s per the patient.  No one else appears to have Alzheimer disease including her brother and sister.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168
