turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Congratulations on your new baby! How are you doing today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm doing well, no headaches, and I'm breastfeeding well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any bleeding?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope, none.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you using a mini pad?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I use it twice a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any cramping or clotting?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, thankfully I don't.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What color is your discharge, ma'am?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, its turned from red to brown, and now its kind of yellowish.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, have you had sex again yet?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, we're waiting a little longer.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you going to the bathroom regularly?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Regularly? Yes, but I'm having some pain with it, and then every once in a while I have some bright red bleeding.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you constipated?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I'm not.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She hasn't been eating her vegetables like she should.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That'll also do it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, well, my seasonal allergies are back too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What symptoms do you have with your allergies?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I get itchy watery eyes, a runny nose, I can't stop sneezing, and I have a lot of pressure in my ears.

reference_section: She is doing well postpartum.  She has had no headache.  She is breastfeeding and feels like her milk is adequate.  She has not had much bleeding.  She is using about a mini pad twice a day, not any cramping or clotting and the discharge is turned from red to brown to now slightly yellowish.  She has not yet had sexual intercourse.  She does complain that she has had a little pain with the bowel movement, and every now and then she notices a little bright red bleeding.  She has not been particularly constipated but her husband says she is not eating her vegetables like she should.  Her seasonal allergies have back developed and she is complaining of extremely itchy watery eyes, runny nose, sneezing, and kind of a pressure sensation in her ears.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I just need to confirm some information before we begin sir, you're forty one, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes sir, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, so what happened?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I work at A B C, and about two days ago I slipped on some oil that had spilled.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did you fall?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I fell with both my arms outstretched, but I fell mostly on my left shoulder.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Where is your left shoulder pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Mostly, it's in the back of my shoulder.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Going backwards a little, how about the right shoulder?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It hurt really bad yesterday, but that's gone away now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, do you have any pain in the front of the shoulder?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No sir, I don't have anything there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, how about weakness? Is there any shoulder weakness?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, it's not really weak at all.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have your symptoms progressed over the last two days? Have they gotten better, or worse?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, overall, I'd say it's gotten better. I have a little better range of motion.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been able to do any activities?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was able to get in the swimming pool with my kids, and I didn't really have any trouble.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, what medicines have you taken for this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've just taken some Advil so far.

reference_section: The patient is a 41-year-old male presenting for initial evaluation of his left shoulder.  He works at ABC and two days ago was walking though an area, where there was some oil spilled on the floor.  He fell and landed on bilateral outstretched arms and then further fell landing primarily on his left shoulder.  He presents today reporting primarily posterior shoulder pain.  The right shoulder was bothersome yesterday, but is now asymptomatic.  He has no anterior shoulder pain.  He denies any feelings of weakness.  He reports some improvement over the last two days especially in his range of motion.  He was able to get into the swimming pool last night with his children without difficulty.  He has had no additional treatment other than over-the-counter Advil.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi there! It is good to see you both. How has everything been going for the both of you?

turns.text: Hi Doctor.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Things have been pretty good. She has been having some new emotional outbursts. I made an appointment with the down syndrome behavioral specialist that you recommended from the last time we were here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is great. Keep me updated on her progress.  Her bloodwork came back showing an underactive thyroid. This explains the recent weight gain and fatigue. I would like to start her on a medication called levothyroxine. We will need to check her bloodwork again in one month to see how her thyroid respond to the medication.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay.

turns.text: Is there any other concerns you have today?

turns.text: Let me look. Can you remove your socks for me?

turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is it this nail?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: This is very common. It is called Onychomycosis. It is nail fungus. Since only one nail is affected, I would recommend starting off with a topical treatment. I will send the drops to your pharmacy. You will put on drop on the affected nail, daily.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, miss. Today we're going to do a recheck for your hypertension. Sound good?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, of course.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I just want to check to see if you have any symptoms that can possibly raise alarm.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have been coming to you for the last fifteen of my seventy eight years on Earth. I know how a follow up works.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You are a seasoned veteran. Alright. So how is your chest? Any pains or tightness?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, luckily I do not have that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is your heart beating alright? Do you feel like it is beating too fast or hard?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I can't really feel my heart beat normally, but I guess that is better than feeling it beat constantly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You are correct. You shouldn't notice it. How is sleeping?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sleeping has been fine. I sleep through the night.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great. Any shortness of breath that causes you to wake up?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: None. I don't have shortness of breath at any other time of the day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are your legs doing well? Any swelling?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. No swelling.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, it's nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's nice to meet you as well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: My name is Doctor X and I will be taking care of you today.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I've been told that you'd like a refill on your Xanax prescription and something to help you break your smoking habit.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I feel like I've tried everything in the book and I still can't break the habit. One of my buddies was telling me about this medicine called Clantix or something like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I've heard of Chantix. We can look into it and see what's best fit.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, great. Since moving back home, I've ran out of Xanax.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long have you been taking it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Almost a year now. I usually take it on days where my anxiety is really bad.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see here that you also have mesothelioma in the lining of your stomach, is that correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I need to find a new cancer specialist that's closer to where I live.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you currently experiencing any pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not at the moment, but I do get pain when I eat sometimes. Other times it's when I'm not even doing anything. It's been chronic so nothing new.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you take anything for the pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I haven't in a while.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When were you diagnosed with mesothelioma?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: About six or so months ago.

reference_section: The patient presents today stating that she needs refills on her Xanax, and she would also like to get something to help her quit smoking.  She is a new patient today.  She states that she has mesothelioma in the lining of her stomach and that it does cause her some problems with eating and it causes some chronic pain.  She states that she is under the care of a cancer specialist; however, she just recently moved back to this area and is trying to find a doctor a little closer than his office.  She states that she has tried several different things to help her quit smoking and she has failed everything and had heard good results about Chantix and wanted to give it a try.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Are you allergic to anything?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Like any medications?

turns.text: Perfect!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Welcome to the clinic.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you. It is nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It is nice to meet you to. I hear an accent. Where are you from?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am from Denmark. I speak Danish as my first language. Me and my husband have been in the States for many many years. When we first got here, we did not speak a word of English.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Wow! Your English is excellent now.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I just turned seventy four last month.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Happy birthday!

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, your primary care physician sent you here for possible hydrocephalus.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Is that the water on brain thing?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Then, yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you tell me about the symptoms that you have been having.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think I have been walking funny lately. I have also been losing my balance.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How do you know that you have been walking funny?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My husband noticed that I have been walking funny. He noticed it about over six months ago or so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you notice about the way your wife's walk that has changed?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She walks wider then she used to, and I noticed that she stooped over. She walks much slower than she did before. She is often losing her balance. I have noticed her touching the walls and furniture to stabilize herself.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Have you noticed her stabilizing herself all of a sudden?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No. It has been happening more and more over the last six months or so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What else have you noticed about the way she walks?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I noticed that she is having trouble stepping up onto things like a scale. She seems very unbalanced. She also seems to take her time as she walks. She can't be hurried.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is good that you are taking your time. Do you use any devices to assist you to get around? Like a cane or a walker?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I must help her get in and out of the car. Not every time but sometimes. I am very concerned because she has been falling more and more recently.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have had one emergency room visit.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What happened that you had to go to the emergency room?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I fell. I was walking to the bedroom. I lost my balance so I put my hand out to brace myself against the wall and my hand slipped. I fell on my wrist.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She broke her wrist.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did this fall happen?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: March two thousand and seven.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She has fallen a few times since she broke her wrist. It makes me so nervous.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I can see why that would make you nervous. Have you had any headaches?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I never get headaches.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Aren't you lucky.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I guess so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any problems with your memory or cognitive abilities?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am still able to pay the bills on time. I don't feel as smart as I used to be.  I do feel like my thinking has slowed down over the last few months.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is your perspective on her memory and her cognitive abilities?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I have noticed some changes. She will occasionally start a sentence and then not know what words to use to finish the sentence.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has she ever had trouble finishing a sentence the in the past?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, she has always been very well spoken never has lost thoughts.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any fainting or vertigo episodes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have not fainted. I have had some dizzy spells in the past but not recently.

reference_section: The patient is a lovely 74-year-old woman who presents with possible adult hydrocephalus.  Danish is her native language, but she has been in the United States for many many years and speaks fluent English, as does her husband. With respect to her walking and balance, she states "I think I walk funny."  Her husband has noticed over the last six months or so that she has broadened her base and become more stooped in her pasture.  Her balance has also gradually declined such that she frequently touches walls and furniture to stabilize herself.  She has difficulty stepping up on to things like a scale because of this imbalance.  She does not festinate.  Her husband has noticed some slowing of her speed.  She does not need to use an assistive device.  She has occasional difficulty getting in and out of a car.  Recently she has had more frequent falls.  In March of 2007, she fell when she was walking to the bedroom and broke her wrist.  Since that time, she has not had any emergency room trips, but she has had other falls. With respect to her bowel and bladder, she has no issues and no trouble with frequency or urgency. The patient does not have headaches. With respect to thinking and memory, she states she is still able to pay the bills, but over the last few months she states, "I do not feel as smart as I used to be."  She feels that her thinking has slowed down.  Her husband states that he has noticed, she will occasionally start a sentence and then not know what words to use as she is continuing. The patient has not had trouble with syncope.  She has had past episodes of vertigo, but not recently.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: A 50-year-old female comes to the clinic with complaint of mood swings and tearfulness.  This has been problematic over the last several months and is just worsening to the point where it is impairing her work.  Her boss asks her if she was actually on drugs in which she said no.  She stated may be she needed to be, meaning taking some medications.  The patient had been prescribed Wellbutrin in the past and responded well to it; however, at that time it was prescribed for obsessive-compulsive type disorder relating to overeating and therefore her insurance would not cover the medication.  She has not been on any other antidepressants in the past.  She is not having any suicidal ideation but is having difficulty concentrating, rapid mood swings with tearfulness, and insomnia.  She denies any hot flashes or night sweats.  She underwent TAH with BSO in December of 2003.

turns.text: Before we begin today, sir, I just need a few pieces of background information. I see here on my chart that you're thirty years old, is that correct?

turns.text: Yes doctor, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, and which hand is your dominant hand?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Now, take me through the timeline of your symptoms, please. When did everything start?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was doing well until July of nineteen ninety three.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What were your initial symptoms?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I began having weakness in my right arm, and there was some neck pain too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, when these symptoms began, how did you manage them?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: At first, I went to a chiropractor, but after a while my arm started atrophying, and my right hand felt tight. I couldn't extend all my fingers out.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Once you noticed the atrophy and contractures, that's the tightness you were experiencing, how were you treated?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: After that, I went to a neurosurgeon close to my house, and he ordered an, um, C T scan of my neck.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, do you have the report of that C T Scan with you today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, doctor, I have it right here. They were one on the twenty fifth of September in ninety two.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you, okay, this shows an intramedullary lesion at C two three, and an extramedullary lesion at C six seven.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That means tumor, right?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes sir. Did you have neck surgery?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I have the op notes right here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, just so you know, you had a C six T one laminectomy, and they decompressed the spinal cord. How did you respond to this surgery?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, honestly, I improved for about three months following the operation, but after that I just got worse and worse.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Once your symptoms worsened, what happened?

reference_section: This 30 y/o RHM was in good health until 7/93, when he began experiencing RUE weakness and neck pain. He was initially treated by a chiropractor and, after an unspecified length of time, developed atrophy and contractures of his right hand. He then went to a local neurosurgeon and a cervical spine CT scan, 9/25/92, revealed an intramedullary lesion at C2-3 and an extramedullary lesion at C6-7. He underwent a C6-T1 laminectomy with exploration and decompression of the spinal cord. His clinical condition improved over a 3 month post-operative period, and then progressively worsened. He developed left sided paresthesia and upper extremity weakness (right worse than left). He then developed ataxia, nausea, vomiting, and hyperreflexia. On 8/31/93, MRI C-spine showed diffuse enlargement of the cervical and thoracic spine and multiple enhancing nodules in the posterior fossa. On 9/1/93, he underwent suboccipital craniotomy with tumor excision, decompression, and biopsy which was consistent with hemangioblastoma. His symptoms stabilized and he underwent 5040 cGy in 28 fractions to his brain and 3600 cGy in 20 fractions to his cervical and thoracic spinal cord from 9/93 through 1/19/94. He was evaluated in the NeuroOncology clinic on 10/26/95 for consideration of chemotherapy. He complained of progressive proximal weakness of all four extremities and dysphagia. He had difficulty putting on his shirt and raising his arms, and he had been having increasing difficulty with manual dexterity (e.g. unable to feed himself with utensils). He had difficulty going down stairs, but could climb stairs. He had no bowel or bladder incontinence or retention.

CV:  See history of present illness.  Denies chest pain, SOB supine, palpitations, edema, varicose veins or leg pains. RESPIRATORY:  He has a chronic cough.  Denies shortness of breath, wheezing, sputum production or bloody sputum. GI:  Denies heartburn, blood in stools, loss of appetite, abdominal pain or constipation. GU:  Denies painful/burning urination, cloudy/dark urine, flank pain or groin pain. MS:  Denies joint pain/stiffness, backaches, tendon/ligaments/muscle pains/strains, bone aches/pains or muscle weakness. NEURO:  Denies blackouts, seizures, loss of memory, hallucinations, weakness, numbness, tremors or paralysis. PSYCH:  Denies anxiety, irritability, apathy, depression, sleep disturbances, appetite disturbances or suicidal thoughts. INTEGUMENTARY:  Denies unusual hair loss/breakage, skin lesions/discoloration or unusual nail breakage/discoloration.

reference_section: The patient is a 33-year-old black male who comes in to the office today main complaint of sexual dysfunction.  Patient reports that he would like to try Cialis to see if it will improve his erectile performance.  Patient states that he did a quiz on-line at the Cialis web site and did not score in the normal range, so he thought he should come in.  Patient states that perhaps his desire has been slightly decreased, but that has not been the primary problem.  In discussing with me directly, patient primarily expresses that he would like to have his erections last longer.  However, looking at the quiz as he filled it out, he reported that much less than half the time was he able to get erections during sexual activity and only about half of the time he was able to maintain his erection after penetration.  However, he only reports that it is slightly difficult to maintain the erection until completion of intercourse.  Patient has no significant past medical history.  He has never had any previous testicular infections.  He denies any history of injuries to the groin and he has never been told that he has a hernia.

turns.text: Good to know, what about the lungs, any history there?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I know someone had C O P D.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know of anyone with dementia or Alzheimer's?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, my uncle has dementia right now, actually.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm sorry to hear that, that's a hard disease to see your family go through. What about diabetes, does anyone have that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you doctor, it's hard. Yes, my dad has the sugar.

reference_section: Remarkable for cervical cancer, heart disease, COPD, dementia, diabetes, and CHF.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you give me a quick run down of her medical history?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Sure. It's a bit long, sadly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm sorry to hear that.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She was recently diagnosed with dementia. She's also suffered from high blood pressure for some time now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When was she diagnosed with dementia?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Six months ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any history of heart disease, diabetes, or stroke?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, but she's not able to control her bladder well which leads to her having frequent accidents. Oh and she's had back pain for several years along with degenerative changes to her spine. Poor thing. I can't help but feel so bad for her situation. It definitely hasn't been easy.

reference_section: Include hypertension, dementia, urinary incontinence, chronic back pain, and degenerative joint disease of the spine.  No history of diabetes, stroke or coronary artery disease.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi, there. How are you both doing? What brings you two to the Emergency Department?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Hi, Doctor. We're both doing fine. I brought my daughter in today because she's been feeling sick.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Let me ask your daughter a few questions before we start. Hi, ma'am. I understand you feel sick. Before we begin I just want to confirm some information with you. Where is your primary residency?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My mom can give you the address. I still live with her.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you. One last question. Do you smoke?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope. My Mother has forbidden smoking in her home.

reference_section: Lives at home, here in the ED with the mother and there is no smoking in the home.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you married, sir?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I'm lucky to have, and live with my lovely wife.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's very nice. Did you speak with the nurse before I came in here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, she was lovely as well, I hope you're paying them well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We take good care of them. They'll be happy to hear that. Let me look, she should have left me some notes, um, yep, these look good, I agree with all of this. This looks good.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you, Doctor.

reference_section: The patient is married and lives with his wife. Nursing notes were reviewed with which I agree.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi. How are you doing, sir?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi. I am doing fine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The nurse told me that you are on disability from work now. What happened?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I got hurt at work and now I am on disability.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What did you do for work? How long ago was your injury?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I worked on the pipeline. The accident was five years ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which condition led to the disability?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't know really. I sent in all the notes for my doctor for evaluation and they approved the disability.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Do you live alone or with family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I live with my wife.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you a smoke or have you ever been?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I used to smoke. I quit years ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long ago did you quit?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, about twenty years ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How many years did you smoke? And how much did you smoke?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Probably twenty years. I was up to two packs a day. I feel way better now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's great. Any use of alcohol or illicit drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you do for fun? Do you have any hobbies?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't really do much these days. Work was my hobby.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: He previously worked with pipeline work, but has been on disability for five years.  He is unsure which symptoms led him to go on disability.  He has previously smoked about two packs of cigarettes daily for 20 years, but quit about 20 years ago.  He denies alcohol or illicit drug use.  He lives with his wife.  He does not really have any hobbies.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How're you doing today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Overall, pretty good.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any plans for the weekend?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not really. Just dog sitting my friend's golden.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Gotcha. That's still nice. We used to have a golden when I was a kid. They're the sweetest dogs.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They are very sweet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, so you're in for a follow up for your neck and back pain.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yessir.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been going to pain management?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I go once every week or so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How's your pain now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Manageable, I guess.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is the pain still keeping you up at night?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not like it used to.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, great to hear.

reference_section: Followup evaluation and management of chronic medical conditions.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's see. Are you taking any medications?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, none right now.

reference_section: None.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke cigarettes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. I smoke.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How much do you smoke per day?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: About a pack or two a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you drink alcohol?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. It is very rare that I will have a drink.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is your family medical history?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I don't know very much about my dad's side of the family but my dad did pass away from renal cancer.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am so sorry for your loss.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about your mother or siblings? Do they have any health conditions?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. They don't have any health problems. That I know of.

reference_section: 1-2 ppd cigarettes. rare ETOH use. Father died of renal CA.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, ma'am, what do you do for a living?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Actually, I'm retired, I don't work at all anymore.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Congratulations on your retirement. Where did you go to college?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, I didn't go to college, I stopped after high school.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's understandable. Do you have children?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, my husband and I were blessed with three wonderful children.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Fantastic, do they live at home?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope, we got them all out of there. They're all grown now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you drink or smoke?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I never had either.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about harder substances?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, absolutely not.

reference_section: The patient is retired.  She is married with three grown children.  Has a high school level education.  Does not smoke, drink, or utilize any illicit substances.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You are five feet four inches.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Weight one ninety seven.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your blood pressure is one twenty five over seventy five.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: VITAL SIGNS: Blood pressure is 125/75.  His weight is 197 with height 5 feet 4 inches.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke or drink?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Never smoked a cigarette a day in my life. As for alcohol, I'll drink socially with friends and family.

reference_section: Non-smoker. Social drinker.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How's he feeling today?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I think this is the worst he's been feeling all week.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm sorry to hear that he hasn't been feeling well. What symptoms has he been having?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: He's been very congested as of late and seems to be coughing a lot more than usual. He was also running a fever yesterday.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. What was his temperature?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: The thermometer was reading one hundred and one degrees Fahrenheit. Does he need to go to the hospital?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let me evaluate and see what we can do for him today.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Thank you, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I suspect that he has an upper respiratory infection, possible pertussis. Is he still experiencing apnea?

reference_section: Upper respiratory illness with apnea, possible pertussis.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let me quickly examine him. Mom do you give the permission? I will quickly check his genitalia. Can you pull his pants down?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Sure, you can check.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, everything looks fine, his penis and testes are normal shape and size for his age. No fluid accumulation or swelling in the scrotum area, no evidence of herniation there.

reference_section: EXTERNAL GENITALIA: Normal for age.  Normal penis with bilaterally descended testes that are normal in size, shape, and contour, and without evidence of hernia or hydrocele.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We can release you from the hospital today if we have a safe place for you to go. Is there a parent or guardian we can release you to?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am in foster care. My foster mom is going out of town on the nineteenth to the twenty third.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: In that case, we will have to keep you in the hospital until your foster mom returns from her trip.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Can my mom and grandmother come and visit me here on Thursday? That is the day they usually come to visit me at my foster home.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes. I think we can make some arrangements to make that happen.

reference_section: As mentioned, she is in foster care.  Foster mom is actually going to be out of town for a week the 19th through the 23rd, so she will probably be hospitalized in respite care because there are no other foster care situations that can handle the patient.  Biological Mom and Grandma do visit on Thursdays for about an hour.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know about any medical issues running in your family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, almost everyone had diabetes.

reference_section: Multiple family members have diabetes mellitus.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any past or present medical conditions?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

reference_section: None.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any family history of lung disease, thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism, stroke, or heart disease.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.  My parents are healthy with no medical issues.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How many children do you have?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have five kids.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do your children have any health condition?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My children are all healthy with no medical problems.

reference_section: She reported that her parents were healthy with no known medical problems. She had five healthy children with no medical problems. There was no family history of lung disease, thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism, stroke, or heart disease.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke or drink alcohol?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

reference_section: No tobacco or alcohol.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know of any medical problems that run in your family?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have no idea to be quite honest with you. My parents never shared their medical history with me and neither did their parents with them. I don't think they want any of us to worry.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh wow, I understand. It can be hard for many people to share intimate details about their health to others, even when it comes to disclosing medical info to their own children. For now, I'll put unknown but please let me know if anything changes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Will do. Thanks for understanding.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Of course. It's not totally uncommon for people to not know their family history.

reference_section: Unknown.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello again, how are you doing, miss?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm good. Thank you. How about you?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: All good here too. I know you are an established patient of dermatology here and was last seen in our office on July thirteenth, two thousand and four.  I will be asking you a few questions just to check whether the entry in our record is updated or not.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Twenty nine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Where are you from originally?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm from Vietnam.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am seeing you today as a referral from A B C for reevaluation.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, for my hand eczema.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, let's see what you have been treated with. Your record here says with Aristocort cream, Cetaphil cream, increased moisturizing cream and lotion. Does this sound right to you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you washing your hands in Cetaphil cleansing lotion?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I'm doing all that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What brings you here today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm having this flaring. My hands are all dry. I have these like cracks in my hands. I have been washing with the soap and the lotions that you prescribed, but still, it is happening. Maybe because of cracks or what, I don't know, but the Cetaphil cleansing lotion, whenever I'm applying that it is causing me a lot of burning pain. I have been wearing gloves though.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you married?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Still, a single. I'm not even looking for a husband yet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you working somewhere?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not currently.

reference_section: This is a 29-year-old Vietnamese female, established patient of dermatology, last seen in our office on 07/13/04.  She comes in today as a referral from ABC, D.O. for a reevaluation of her hand eczema.  I have treated her with Aristocort cream, Cetaphil cream, increased moisturizing cream and lotion, and wash her hands in Cetaphil cleansing lotion.  She comes in today for reevaluation because she is flaring.  Her hands are very dry, they are cracked, she has been washing with soap.  She states that the Cetaphil cleansing lotion apparently is causing some burning and pain because of the fissures in her skin.  She has been wearing some gloves also apparently.  The patient is single.  She is unemployed.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You have been diagnosed with allergic rhinitis, right? For how many years?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I would say around four years now. Oh my God it has been so, so many medications that I had to take for this.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, it's hard to control. Are you diabetic?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I don't have any such conditions.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So no hypertension or any kidney diseases?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Every been diagnosed with tuberculosis, asthma, or lung disease?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No I have not.

reference_section: Allergic rhinitis, which she has had for many years and treated with numerous medications. No history of diabetes, hypertension, or renal disease. No history tuberculosis, asthma, or upper airway disease.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hm how would you describe her diet?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does she eat solid food?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Mostly thin liquids and ground meat.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see.

reference_section: Regular with regular consistency with thin liquids and ground meat.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello there, I am Doctor Nathan.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hello.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am forty eight?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you get regular periods?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I didn't get any periods for the last year after my surgery.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any hot flashes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it's been happening for the last several months. Sometimes I feel hot even in a fully air conditioned room. Other times I just feel like opening the refrigerator and standing in front of it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any other symptoms?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am also experiencing a lot of mood swings for the last few weeks.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Based on all the symptoms my assessment would be mood swings along with postsurgical menopause. That would be the cause for your hot flashes.

reference_section: 1.  Postsurgical menopause. 2.  Mood swings.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any change in appetite?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, no.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any stomach pain or change in bowel movement?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any history of bowel issues?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not really.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any hernia problem?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any history of stomach ulcer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you notice any rectal bleeding?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any liver issues or jaundice?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, no.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: GASTROINTESTINAL: No history of rectal bleeding, appetite change, abdominal pain, hiatal hernia, ulcer, jaundice, change in bowel habits or liver problems, and no history of inflammatory bowel problems.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you drink alcohol?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope! I use to occasionally, very long time ago. But not anymore.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay and how bout cigarettes? Do you smoke or vape?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, none of those.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And no drugs and stuff, right? No snorting, I V or anything right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Right, I don't do drugs either, never did. Even though pot is legal here, I never ever felt like trying.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's a good thing.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah.

citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let me check your neck, it looks nice and symmetrical. Your thyroid looks normal it is not enlarged.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does it hurt you when I press on your neck?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Neck is nontender.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, I don't see any bulging of external jugular vein.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: These medical terms I don't understand.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, I am talking about the vein in your neck, it shows no bulging. No abnormal masses present. Can you turn your head from left to right and right to left, any pain in your neck or difficulty turning?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you rotate your head clockwise and anti clockwise.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let me just make a note here full range of motion with no pain.

reference_section: NECK: Supple and symmetric.  No masses. Thyroid midline, non enlarged.  No JVD.  Neck is nontender.  Full range of motion without pain.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, miss. It looks like you are here for your yearly physical. How is everything going?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Great, I think. I just got a mammogram and nothing showed up. I still am taking my multivitamin and low dose aspirin.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great to hear. Has there been any changes in drinking and smoking?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No changes. Check the chart, I answered that last time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great. Looks like drinking and smoking is off the menu. In regard to the mammogram, do you make sure to do self breast examinations? I believe I showed you how to do this last time.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I do not. I don't see a point if I come and do the mammogram.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I highly suggest you start doing so. Sometimes people do not get mammograms for a few years and it is important to make sure nothing is growing.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.text: Do you remember who diagnosed you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: A local doctor I was seeing at the time. A year before my diagnosis, I had a few falls and episodes of lightheadedness. I also noticed that I was staggering a lot more when walking.

turns.text: I'm sure that was difficult to experience.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.text: By slower, do you mean the movements of your arms and legs were slower and impaired?

turns.text: Yes. I was prescribed Sinemet back in September of nineteen ninety five.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you notice any improvement while taking it?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Noting that it's February thirteenth nineteen ninety six.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I felt weak in the morning and worse as the day went on.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

reference_section: This 67y/o RHF was diagnosed with Parkinson's Disease in 9/1/95, by a local physician. For one year prior to the diagnosis, the patient experienced staggering gait, falls and episodes of lightheadedness. She also noticed that she was slowly "losing" her voice, and that her handwriting was becoming smaller and smaller. Two months prior to diagnosis, she began experienced bradykinesia, but denied any tremor. She noted no improvement on Sinemet, which was started in 9/95. At the time of presentation, 2/13/96, she continued to have problems with coordination and staggering gait. She felt weak in the morning and worse as the day progressed. She denied any fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, HA, change in vision, seizures or stroke like events, or problems with upper extremity coordination.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, you first came to our Pulmonary Clinic, and you were suffering with dyspnea even on minimal exertion. turns.text: How would you compare your sleep here in the lab and at your home?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How do you feel when you wake up in the morning?

turns.text: Do you snore?

turns.text: Did you ever feel that you have difficulty breathing while you are asleep?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your current medications include Methadone, Trazodone, and Seroquel.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That sounds right.

reference_section: The patient presented initially to the Pulmonary Clinic with dyspnea on minimal exertion.  At that time, she was evaluated and found to have evidence for sleep disruption and daytime fatigue.  She also complained of nocturnal choking episodes that have since abated over the past several months.  In the meantime, she had been scheduled for an overnight sleep study performed to evaluate her for sleep apnea, returns today to review her study results. The patient's sleep patterns consist of going to bed between 9.00 and 10.00 p.m. and awakening in the morning between 5.00 and 6.00 a.m.  She reports difficulty in initiating sleep and then recurrent awakenings every 1 to 2 hours throughout the night.  She reports tossing and turning throughout the night and awakening with the sheets in disarray.  She reports that her sleep was much better quality in the sleep laboratory as compared to home.  When she awakens, she might have a dull headache and feels tired in the morning.  Her daughter reports that she has heard the patient talking during sleep and snoring.  There are no apneic episodes.  The patient reports that she used to cough a lot in the middle of the night, but has no longer been doing so in recent weeks. During the daytime, the patient reports spending a lot of sedentary time reading and watching TV.  She routinely dozes off during these sedentary activities.  She also might nap between 2.00 and 3.00 p.m., and nods off in the evening hours. The patient smokes perhaps one to two packs of cigarettes per day, particularly after dinner. She reports that her weight has fluctuated and peaked at 260 pounds approximately 1 year ago.  Since that time, her weight is down by approximately 30 pounds. The patient is managed in Outpatient Psychiatry and at her Maintenance Clinic.  She takes methadone, trazodone, and Seroquel.

My parents encouraged me to finish school and to go to college. I got my Bachelor of Science in Nursing at the State University in nineteen seventy nine.

turns.text: Did you have any problems in school such as learning disabilities, attentional problems, difficulty learning to read, failed grades, special help in school or behavioral problems?

turns.text: Are you married?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am so sorry.

turns.speaker: doctor

I was not sure why they let me go. I was given no explanation. And before that, I worked for Walter P. Carter Center for twenty one years. I also worked as an O B nurse.  Other than the two instances, I had never been fired or let go from a job.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you do in your spare time now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I enjoy reading, doing puzzles, playing computer games. I joined a women's support group for women my age. I keep myself, busy.

He completed third grade and died at 60 due to complications of diabetes.  Her mother is 93 years old.  Her last job was as a janitor.  She completed fourth grade.  She reported that she has no cognitive problems at this time.  Family medical history is significant for diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, thyroid problems, sarcoidosis, and possible multiple sclerosis and depression.  The patient completed a Bachelor of Science in Nursing through State University in 1979.  She denied any history of problems in school such as learning disabilities, attentional problems, difficulty learning to read, failed grades, special help in school or behavioral problems.  She was married for two years.  Her ex-husband died in 1980 from acute pancreatitis secondary to alcohol abuse.  She has two children ages 43 and 30.  Her son whose age is 30 lives nearby and is in consistent contact with her and she is also in frequent contact and has a close relationship with her daughter who lives in New York.  In school, the patient reported obtaining primarily A's and B's.  She said that her strongest subject was math while her worst was spelling, although she reported that her grades were still quite good in spelling.  The patient worked for Hospital Center for four years.  Prior to that, she worked for an outpatient mental health center for 2-1/2 years.  She was reportedly either terminated or laid off and was unsure of the reason for that.  Prior to that, she worked for Walter P. Carter Center reportedly for 21 years.  She has also worked as an OB nurse in the past.  She reported that other than the two instances reported above, she had never been terminated or fired from a job.  In her spare time, the patient enjoys reading, participating in women's groups doing puzzles, playing computer games.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, young man.

turns.text: Good afternoon, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you, sir?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm thirteen.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, what brings you in today?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, at first, we went to Sierra Pacific Orthopedic Group, and he had an M R I that showed, um, O C D in the left knee.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I see that from the report.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: So, we're here for a second opinion on that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, we should do surgery on this knee. There's gross instability of the fragment, and we don't want that get worse.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, that's about what we've heard so far. What are the risks of infection of the procedure?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's less than one percent. We use antibiotics to control for infection. Other risks include bleeding, changes in sensation of the limb, changes in motion, failure to relieve pain or restore the articular cartilage, the possible need for another procedure, and possible early arthritis. I would not worry, though. These things are rare.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, will he be asleep the entire time?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, he won't feel a thing.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, my husband agrees. We want to do the surgery.

reference_section: The patient is 13-year-old male with persistent left knee pain.  He was initially seen at Sierra Pacific Orthopedic Group where an MRI demonstrated unstable OCD lesion of the left knee.  The patient presented here for a second opinion.  Surgery was recommended grossly due to the instability of the fragment.  Risks and benefits of surgery were discussed.  The risks of surgery include risk of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and motion extremity, failure to relieve pain or restore the articular cartilage, possible need for other surgical procedures, and possible early arthritis.  All questions were answered and parents agreed to the above plan.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Hello, what brings you here today?

turns.text: How old are you?

turns.text: You don't ask age of a lady. She will never tell you the truth.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I know I'm in the wrong profession. I have to do that every time I meet someone. So how old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's true. I'm just teasing you. I'm fifty one.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you right handed or left handed?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am right handed.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, you said that your legs suddenly gave out. What happened exactly? Was it sudden? Or were you noticing some weakness before as well?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, I noticed weakness in my right leg before as well and sometimes, like, I have to give the support of my arm to actually move it. Sometimes during these episodes I just turn pale and it's like overall weakness. I feel so tired. My husband, he gives me some sugar, three teaspoons, and then it helps a little bit but not completely.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, is your weakness like overall in your legs or it is at any single point?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's overall. I remember in one of these episodes I was, like, in an odd fisted posture.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there any change in your sensations? Like if I touch you, is it like same before or was there any change?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, nothing like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there change in vision? Are you seeing double?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any difficulty in swallowing or eating? Any loss of consciousness?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any difficulty in speech? Slurring, or anything like that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You said that these episodes have been happening for some time, so did you see anyone for those before?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope. It's just that I fall and then fell again last night. I was feeling so weak. Nothing was helping me. That's when, in the morning, my husband brought me to the U I H C hospital for the evaluation on the fifth.

reference_section: This 51y/o RHF fell four times on 1/3/93, because her "legs suddenly gave out." She subsequently noticed weakness involving the right leg, and often required the assistance of her arms to move it. During some of these episodes she appeared mildly pale and felt generally weak; her husband would give her 3 teaspoons of sugar and she would appear to improve, thought not completely. During one episode she held her RUE in an "odd fisted posture." She denied any other focal weakness, sensory change, dysarthria, diplopia, dysphagia or alteration of consciousness. She did not seek medical attention despite her weakness. Then, last night, 1/4/93, she fell again ,and because her weakness did not subsequently improve she came to UIHC for evaluation on 1/5/93.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: What does that means?

turns.text: It means that you have something called Carpal tunnel syndrome, which explains your numbness and tingling sensation in your left hand. It also explains your pain in the middle part of your hand as it's caused due to pinching or compression of a nerve called median nerve.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, how did that happen?

turns.text: Well, it's possible that your repetitive hand motion could have caused it or sometimes it's just the anatomy of your wrist.

turns.text: Yeah.

reference_section: The patient is a 10-year-old boy who has been a toe walker since he started ambulating at about a year.  The patient had some mild hamstring tightness with his popliteal angle of approximately 20 degrees bilaterally.  He does not walk with a crouched gait but does toe walk.  Given his tightness, surgery versus observation was recommended to the family.  Family however wanted to correct his toe walking.  Surgery was then discussed.  Risks of surgery include risks of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremities, failure to resolve toe walking, possible stiffness, cast, and cast problems.  All questions were answered and parents agreed to above surgical plan.

reference_section: The patient is a 41-year-old female who presented to me with severe cervical spondylosis and myelopathy.  She was referred to me by Dr. X.  The patient underwent a complicated anterior cervical discectomy, 2-level corpectomy, spinal cord decompression and fusion with fibular strut and machine allograft in the large cervical plate.  Surgery had gone well, and the patient has done well in the last 2 days.  She is neurologically improved and is moving all four extremities.  No airway issues.  It was felt that the patient was now a candidate for a halo vest placement given that chance of going to the OR were much smaller.  She was consented for the procedure, and I sought the help of ABC and felt that a PMT halo would be preferable to a Bremer halo vest.  The patient had this procedure done at the bedside, in the SICU room #1.  I used a combination of some morphine 1 mg and Versed 2 mg for this procedure.  I also used local anesthetic, with 1% Xylocaine and epinephrine a total of 15 to 20 cc.

reference_section: Ms. ABC was admitted to the hospital.  She was seen by Dr. A.  He put her on an insulin drip.  Her sugars slowly did come down to normal down to between 115 and 134.  On the next day, she was then taken to the operating room, where she underwent her laparoscopic cholecystectomy.  She was noted to be a difficult intubation for the procedure.  There were some indications of chronic cholecystitis, a little bit of edema, mild edema and adhesions of omentum around the gallbladder.  She underwent the procedure.  She tolerated without difficulty.  She was recovered in the Postoperative Care Unit and then returned to the floor.  Her blood sugar postprocedure was noted to be 233.  She was started back on a sliding scale insulin.  She continued to do well and was felt to be stable for discharge following the procedure.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How're you today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not too bad. I'm hanging in there. My asthma has been acting up.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh no. How long has this been going on?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: For the past three months. I've been using my inhaler every day. I used to use it every now and again. This is definitely new for me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you experiencing any allergies alongside your asthma?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, actually. My husband has been hauling a lot more corn this season and it seems to be making my allergies much worse.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you take anything for your allergies?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not really. I'll sometimes take Allegra and that seems to help just a tiny bit. I was previously prescribed Flonase, but I can't remember the last time I took it. Oh and I was on Advair, too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did the Flonase or Advair help at all?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had to stop Advair because it started to bother my lady parts.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How so?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I noticed that it became more itchy as a result.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm sorry to hear that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Speaking of this, I wanted to also share that I've been experiencing a lot of P M S symptoms lately. I'm super impatient and moody.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you notice these symptoms are still there after you finish your cycle?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um lemme think. The symptoms start about a week before my period and tend to get less intense once I get over the first day of bleeding.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are your cycles generally regular?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: For the most part, yes. I feel like they don't last as long as they used to. I'm not sure why. I do, however, notice some spotting after my cycles end.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you get any night sweats or hot flashes while you're on your period?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any other medical troubles recently?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I did have a U T I and some blood in my urine because of it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you remember how many times you noticed blood in your urine?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hm about three times. I was prescribed antibiotics for it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any other urinary symptoms since? How about bdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or anything of the like?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nothing now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you gotten your urine rechecked recently?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not yet. I really should get it checked out again.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I can write an order for you if you'd like or you can make an appointment with your urologist. Do you have a specific urologist that you see?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I can call to make the appointment tomorrow. Do I also need to get blood work done?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, in fact I'd like to order some blood work while you're here.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had blood work done a few days ago for my life insurance application. I am forty two so thought I should get that going. My Swedish mother always used to nag about how I procrastinate on important things. Anyways, do I still need to get more blood work done?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know what they checked?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think the typical blood work with cholesterol added.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you happen to have a copy on hand or could you fax me the resulxts?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I can fax them to you once I get them back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That would be great. Thank you. Let me write down our fax number for you.

reference_section: This is a 42-year-old white female who comes in today for a complete physical and follow up on asthma.  She says her asthma has been worse over the last three months.  She has been using her inhaler daily.  Her allergies seem to be a little bit worse as well.  Her husband has been hauling corn and this seems to aggravate things.  She has not been taking Allegra daily but when she does take it, it seems to help somewhat.  She has not been taking her Flonase which has helped her in the past.  She also notes that in the past she was on Advair but she got some vaginal irritation with that. She had been noticing increasing symptoms of irritability and PMS around her menstrual cycle.  She has been more impatient around that time.  Says otherwise her mood is normal during the rest of the month.  It usually is worse the week before her cycle and improves the day her menstrual cycle starts.  Menses have been regular but somewhat shorter than in the past.  Occasionally she will get some spotting after her cycles.  She denies any hot flashes or night sweats with this.  In reviewing the chart it is noted that she did have 3+ blood with what appeared to be a urinary tract infection previously.  Her urine has not been rechecked.  She recently had lab work and cholesterol drawn for a life insurance application and is going to send me those results when available.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Hello there, how are you?

turns.text: I understand, so how old is she?

turns.text: And just wanted to confirm the ethnicity is Caucasian, right?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: It lasted about a minute.

turns.text: When did you first notice it?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: The first day when I was feeding her, she was barely a day old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you notice any interrupted breathing or bluish color around her mouth?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: While the episode occurs do you notice any color changes in the baby?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you happened to notice any arching of the back or eyes rolling back?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, it usually happens while she is sleeping, so I didn't notice her eye movements. But I am able to wake her up and stop the hand and leg movements.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Otherwise, is she feeding well and is active?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, absolutely! Although she falls asleep a lot during breast feeding but other than that everything is fine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And how often are you feeding her and for how long?

turns.text: I breast feed her every two to three hours for about fifteen to twenty minutes.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, her pee diapers have increased to up to eight and I would say about six to seven poopy diapers a day.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, it's like dirty yellowish color.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: The patient is a 10-day-old Caucasian female here for approximately 1 minute bilateral arm and leg jerks, which started at day of life 1 and have occurred 6 total times since then.  Mom denies any apnea, perioral cyanosis, or color changes.  These movements are without any back arching.  They mainly occur during sleep, so mom is unaware of any eye rolling.  Mom is able to wake the patient up during this periods and stop the patient's extremity movements. Otherwise, this patient has been active, breast-feeding well, although she falls asleep at the breast.  She is currently taking in 15 to 20 minutes of breast milk every 2 to 3 hours.  She is having increased diapers up to 8 wet and 6 to 7 dirty-yellow stools per day.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: This 34-year-old gentleman awoke this morning noting some itchiness to his back and then within very a short period of time realized that he had an itchy rash all over his torso and arms.  No facial swelling.  No tongue or lip swelling.  No shortness of breath, wheezing, or other associated symptoms.  He cannot think of anything that could have triggered this off.  There have been no changes in his foods, medications, or other exposures as far as he knows.  He states a couple of days ago he did work and was removing some insulation but does not remember feeling itchy that day.

turns.text: When was your last stroke?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, it was on January seventeenth. I had these episodes where I was like always so confused and looks like I lost everything. All my memory and everything. And then they did a scan. It was verified that I was having a stroke on the same day.

turns.text: Did they put you on some medications?

turns.text: They gave me an anticonvulsant and aspirin.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you taking them regularly?

turns.text: There have a few times like one or two days that I forgot to take my, uh, dyphenhydramine, but even when I'm taking it regularly, I'm still having all those symptoms or forgetfulness, confusion, and everything.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you feel anything else along with these episodes like a urine urgency, tendency to bite your tongue, headaches, any visual change, or your heart is beating very fast? Any kind of weakness or numbness or shortness of breath?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No nothing else, just the confusion and forgetfulness.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How frequent are these episodes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, they occur like two or three times in a week. Each one of the episodes lasts for like one or two minutes.

reference_section: This 65 y/o RHM reportedly suffered a stroke on 1/17/92. He presented locally at that time with complaint of episodic confusion and memory loss lasting several minutes per episode. The "stroke" was reportedly verified on MRI scan dated 1/17/92. He was subsequently placed on ASA and DPH. He admitted that there had been short periods (1-2 days duration) since then, during which he had forgotten to take his DPH. However, even when he had been taking his DPH regularly, he continued to experience the spells mentioned above. He denied any associated tonic/clonic movement, incontinence, tongue-biting, HA, visual change, SOB, palpitation, weakness or numbness. The episodes of confusion and memory loss last 1-2 minutes in duration, and have been occurring 2-3 times per week.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168
