turns.text: What about your mom? How old is she?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My mom is eighty years old. She does have sugar issues.

reference_section: Father with HTN and h/o strokes at ages 45 and 80; now 82 years old. Mother has DM and is age 80.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you currently living alone?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yep. Just me, myself, and I.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you do for a living?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've been working as a plumber for the last five years.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Nice. Where do you work?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Mostly in the city.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you drink, smoke, or do injection drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I drink and smoke here and there, but I've never tried hard drugs.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any recent travel?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was in Mexico earlier this year.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That sounds nice. How was your trip?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Relaxing. Much needed.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great to hear. I have a few more questions I need to ask so bear with me. How is your sexual history? Are you sexually active?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm sexually active with women, but my sex life isn't as good as it was in Japan. Over there, I would mix and mingle with prostitutes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you use protection?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't really remember.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been tested for S T D's?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yep. I'm negative for right now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever been incarcerated?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: One last question. Have you ever been in need of a blood transfusion?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, thank God.

reference_section: Patient is single and he lives alone. He is heterosexual and has a history of sexual encounter with prostitutes in Japan. He works as a plumber over the last 5 years. He smokes and drinks occasionally and denies any history of IV drug use. No blood transfusion. No history of incarceration. Recently traveled to Mexico .
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, champ, how you holding up?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good afternoon, Doctor, I have a lot of lower back pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh no, before we begin, how old are you, sir and which hand do you write with?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm seventy five now. Right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, so tell me, how long have you had this lower back pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's been about ten days now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have your symptoms improved at all since they began?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, they keep getting worse.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does the pain radiate into your legs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it started radiating down my right leg three days after the lower back pain began, and then the left leg three days after the right. The next day I could barely walk, the pain was so severe.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you remember the initial date of the beginning of your low back pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it was on December third nineteen ninety five.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you seen another doctor for this pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I saw my local physician, um, it was on December eleventh, but he wasn't able to pinpoint what was going on.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of treatments did he recommend?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: He gave me some antiinflammatories and sent me on my way.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you drive yourself?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I did.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did the antiinflammatories work?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, by the time I got home, I could hardly walk due to the back pain, and I had weakness in my legs. I was, however, able to feed my dogs, and I fixed myself some dinner.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Was there any leg numbness?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. Since December eleventh.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you seen an orthopedist for this pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I saw one the day after my primary care physician, but my legs gave out and I fell while walking to my car because of the leg weakness and back pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of imaging studies did that orthopedist do?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: He did a C T and x rays of my lower back, but he didn't see anything wrong. He recommended I follow up at U I H C. The imaging was on my L S Spine.

reference_section: This 75y/o RHM presented with a 10 day h/o progressively worsening LBP. The LBP started on 12/3/95; began radiating down the RLE, on 12/6/95; then down the LLE, on 12/9/95. By 12/10/95, he found it difficult to walk. On 12/11/95, he drove himself to his local physician, but no diagnosis was rendered. He was given some NSAID and drove home. By the time he got home he had great difficulty walking due to LBP and weakness in BLE, but managed to feed his pets and himself. On 12/12/95 he went to see a local orthopedist, but on the way to his car he crumpled to the ground due to BLE weakness and LBP pain. He also had had BLE numbness since 12/11/95. He was evaluated locally and an L-S-Spine CT scan and L-S Spine X-rays were "negative." He was then referred to UIHC.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Alright. So this is going to be a complex case. Your wound is complicated by methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus cellulitis.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Is there a treatment for my right leg?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: There is. It will be more aggressive, but we can do it.

reference_section: Complex open wound right lower extremity complicated by a methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus cellulitis.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good morning, young man. You're a patient of Doctor X Y Z, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes sir, that's right. I've seen him for years.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I just need to confirm some demographic information before we get started today. So, you're a twenty nine year old white male, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, doctor. That's all right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, thank you. So, what seems to be the problem today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I got stung by a Yellow Jacket Wasp yesterday.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have a lot of swelling?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it's in my right hand and right arm.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you every been stung by wasps before?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, this wouldn't be the first time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had similar reactions before?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I have. I have had one severe reaction. I came because I wanted to make sure it didn't get to that point again. I've never had, um, anaphylaxis, nothing super serious to date.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, that's good. Do you have any shortness of breath or difficulty with your throat?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, it's never felt like it was going to close up or anything like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any rapid heartbeat or anxiety?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I don't have anything like that either.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, it's just the localized swelling where you got stung?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's really all, doctor.

reference_section: He is a 29-year-old white male who is a patient of Dr. XYZ and he comes in today complaining that he was stung by a Yellow Jacket Wasp yesterday and now has a lot of swelling in his right hand and right arm.  He says that he has been stung by wasps before and had similar reactions.  He just said that he wanted to catch it early before he has too bad of a severe reaction like he has had in the past.  He has had a lot of swelling, but no anaphylaxis-type reactions in the past; no shortness of breath or difficultly with his throat feeling like it is going to close up or anything like that in the past; no racing heart beat or anxiety feeling, just a lot of localized swelling where the sting occurs.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: My nipples are cracked, and they are bleeding.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, I am so sorry to hear that.

turns.speaker: guest_family

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, no other issues.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Welcome to the clinic, Miss A.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's start with your medical history. What medical conditions do you have?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay. I have high blood pressure, asthma and sleep apnea. I had blood clots in my left leg about six months ago. I also have cancer.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of cancer do you have?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have stomach cancer. They also did a total abdominal hysterectomy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did they put you on an anticoagulant medication for the blood clotting?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. I took it for six months. I stopped taking it and then I had the stroke.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any other surgeries?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. I had a colonic resection to remove benign polyps. I had another benign lump removed from my breast.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you feeling today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am still having weakness in my left leg. That is why I still have to us my walker, but I have been able to get around easier.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been experiencing any daytime fatigue?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I have been falling asleep at work. I think it is from looking at my computer screen all day. My supervisor caught me snoring one day and forgot where I was at. My supervisor offered to give me a coffee. This has happened more than once.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: This could be due to your sleep apnea. Who is treating you for your sleep apnea?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Doctor X did a consult and had me do one of those sleep test about two years ago. I only get sleepy when I look at my computer screen.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did Doctor X recommend a C P A P machine to use at night?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, but I never used to use it. I had another follow up visit with her and she told me that I need to use it every night. I have been using it every other night.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How much uninterrupted sleep do you think that you get per night?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe two to five hours, on a good night.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is not enough sleep. No wonder you are falling asleep at work. I recommend following up again with Doctor X regarding your sleep apnea. You are at a much higher risk for obesity and high cholesterol if you continue to not address the issues you have been having with the lack of sleep and sleep apnea.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay. I will make a follow up visit with her.

reference_section: Ms. A continues to have some residual left leg weakness and continues to use a rolling walker for ambulation, but she reported that her motor functioning had improved significantly.  She was diagnosed with sleep apnea approximately two years ago and was recently counseled by Dr. X on the need to use her CPAP because she indicated she never used it at night.  She reported that since her appointment with Dr. X, she has been using it "every other night."  When asked about daytime fatigue, Ms. A initially denied that she was having any difficulties, but repeatedly indicated that she was falling asleep at work and thought that it was due to looking at a computer screen.  She reported at times "snoring" and forgetting where she is at and said that a supervisor offered to give her coffee at one point.  She receives approximately two to five hours of sleep per night.  Other current untreated risk factors include obesity and hypercholesterolemia.  Her medical history is also significant for hypertension, asthma, abdominal adenocarcinoma status post hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, colonic benign polyps status post resection, benign lesions of the breast status post lumpectomy, and deep vein thrombosis in the left lower extremity status post six months of anticoagulation (which she had discontinued just prior to her stroke).
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello. How are you doing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not doing that good. I'm here so that you can help me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Tell me how can I do that? What's bothering you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have gestational diabetes and I'm here for consultation related to my diet. No matter what I eat, I'm kind of scared that it will spike up my numbers.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hold on, hold on. First, tell me how old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sorry. I am thirty eight.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, now tell me what are you afraid of?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No matter what I eat, my number goes up and I just, I'm so afraid of eating anything now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you work?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I do, at Walmart. I try not to eat anything whenever I'm on the third shift.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Tell me about the eating habits. Do you prepare meals at home, or do you order from outside?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, before all this, I mean this gestational diabetes and pregnancy, I used to eat out a lot. Almost like every day. I like to eat rice a lot. It is like the staple food for me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You said you don't try to eat, so are you facing any symptoms because of not eating?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, whenever I'm on my late shift, I work from ten in the night to seven in the morning. I try to avoid eating. And then I feel very fatigued and tired all the time. I also have young kids at home, so after finishing my duty here at in the morning I go home and then there are young children who keep me busy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is your sleeping pattern? How much are you sleeping throughout the day?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Around two to four hours at a time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When do you test for ketones?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Normally, it is the first thing that I do when I reach back home from my shift in the morning.

reference_section: This is a 38-year-old female who comes for dietary consultation for gestational diabetes.  Patient reports that she is scared to eat because of its impact on her blood sugars.  She is actually trying not to eat while she is working third shift at Wal-Mart.  Historically however, she likes to eat out with a high frequency.  She enjoys eating rice as part of her meals.  She is complaining of feeling fatigued and tired all the time because she works from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. at Wal-Mart and has young children at home.  She sleeps two to four hours at a time throughout the day.  She has been testing for ketones first thing in the morning when she gets home from work.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you? What brings you here today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am fifty six years old. I am here for this pain in my legs. It hurts mostly in the night.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does changing positions helps you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, it helps. Whenever I stand it just goes away.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is it only in your legs or it starts there and goes somewhere else as well?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It normally starts in my hips and then it goes down my leg and sometimes into my ankles as well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did you first notice it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It all started after taking that medication. What is it called? Something with L? Yeah, Lipitor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever noticed any night sweats?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sometimes I do sweat at night.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any other issue? Anything else going on? Your body temperature is a little on the higher end.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I do feel feverish and have nausea as well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are your sugar numbers?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They have been low for quite some time. You know, I have started going to Genesis in Wichita and I've been doing water aerobics. And you know what? Surprisingly, I have lost thirty pounds.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's good. How much is your fasting sugar?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Anywhere between a hundred to one hundred and twenty. I check them one and a half hours after meals as well. They are, they have been one hundred and eighty five regularly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. I have a request to make. I will be coming for my diabetic checkup in one month. Can we do all the labs before that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, sure, that's a great idea. I should tell my assistant and they will call you for labs before your appointment for diabetes checkup.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Anything else going on? How is everything else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I tried to control my cholesterol with diet, but it didn't help. I cannot keep on dieting. It is just not my thing. I have started eating more meat though. I feel full after that.

reference_section: This is a 56-year-old female who has pain in her legs at nighttime and when she gets up it comes and goes, radiates from her buttocks to her legs, sometimes it is her ankle.  She has noticed it since she has been on Lipitor.  She has had some night sweats occasionally.  She has had a little bit of fever and nausea.  She has noticed her blood sugars have been low.  She has lost over 30 pounds after exercising doing water aerobics at Genesis in Wichita.  She has noticed her fasting blood sugars have been ranging from 100 to 120.  Blood sugars one and a half hours after meals have been 185.  She is coming in for a diabetic checkup in one month and wants lab prior to that time.  She has been eating more meat recently and has not been on a diet for cholesterol.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi there! I am Doctor Smith.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hello! It is nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's start with your family medical history.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My mother had breast cancer. My father had lung cancer that ended up taking his life. He was seventy nine when he passed. My mother also passed but not from an illness but from an infection she got after having an elective surgery.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am so sorry for your loss. How old was your mother when she passed?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you. She was eighty one when she passed. I am an orphan now. My only living sibling died at forty. He had a hard life. He struggled with mental illness.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did your brother pass away?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: He had pancreatitis. Oh, my dad had glaucoma.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You have had a lot of loss.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I have. My good friend passed away a year and a half ago. It has been a lot.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I have a support group I can refer you to for people to have been through loss. Would you be interested a referral, sir?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. I would like that. Thank you.

reference_section: Father died from CA at the age of 79.  Mother died from postoperative infection at the age of 81.  Brother died from pancreatitis at the age of 40 and had a prior history of mental illness.  Father also had a prior history of lung cancer.  Mother had a history of breast cancer.  Father also had glaucoma.  He does not have any living siblings.  Friend died a year and half ago.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I will ask some simple questions, okay?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hm

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you and how would you define yourself in terms of ethnicity?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I am forty seven and would proudly call myself as Latin American.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great. What brings you to the emergency room?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had a blood test before and then it came out to be high potassium. I also went to a regular clinic the other day as I was feeling very weak and extremely tired.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My potassium came out to be seven and it was highlighted in red. That really scared me, so I wanted to know everything what's going on inside me. I told the emergency doctors too that all these weakness and tiredness is going on for more than half a year.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you noticed any other symptoms other than weakness?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, there was the fever and chills. I was sweating a lot in the nights, and I also had weight loss of around twenty pounds. During that time, I sometimes have nausea and was throwing up a lot. I was not eating. I always felt dizzy every time I tried to stand.

turns.speaker: doctor

reference_section: A 47-year-old Latin American man presented to the emergency room after being told to come in for a high potassium value drawn the previous day. He had gone to an outside clinic the day prior to presentation complaining of weakness and fatigue. Labs drawn there revealed a potassium of 7.0 and he was told to come here for further evaluation. At time of his assessment in the emergency room, he noted general malaise and fatigue for eight months. Over this same time period he had subjective fevers and chills, night sweats, and a twenty-pound weight loss. He described anorexia with occasional nausea and vomiting of non-bilious material along with a feeling of light-headedness that occurred shortly after standing from a sitting or lying position. He denied a productive cough but did note chronic left sided upper back pain located in the ribs that was worse with cough and better with massage. He denied orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea but did become dyspneic after walking 2-3 blocks where before he had been able to jog 2-3 miles. He also noted that over the past year his left testicle had been getting progressively more swollen and painful. He had been seen for this at the onset of symptoms and given a course of antibiotics without improvement. Over the last several months there had been chronic drainage of yellowish material from this testicle. He denied trauma to this area. He denied diarrhea or constipation, changes in his urinary habits, rashes or skin changes, arthritis, arthralgias, abdominal pain, headache or visual changes.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm having these cramps in my feet, in my hand and I just wanted to get checked. It has been happening for like six months. I develop muscle contractions in my toes and both feet. It only happens in night.

turns.text: How frequent is it?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you do when you have these cramps?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I try to stand and it helps me relieve some of the discomfort. I noticed my toes are kind of extended. Whenever I step on the ground, it seems to pop into place. With all these cramps, I've started having pain in my calf. Sometimes because of that I could not sleep, or it wakes me up in the night. Similar to my toes, these cramps have also started coming up in my hands. They are not that strong or frequent. They're completely random and not in the nighttime. Sometimes my thumb gets so flexed that I have to move it to bring it to the right position and to relieve the cramp.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not like this.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have H I V for the last twenty one years and I was taking antiretroviral medications for it. I stopped those medications around six or seven years ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Why did you stop the medications?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I could not tolerate them. They were making my stomach weak.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know your C D four count?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It was three hundred and twenty six. I never developed autoimmune deficiency syndrome. I think I should restart my medicines.

reference_section: The patient is a 61-year-old right-handed gentleman who presents for further evaluation of feet and hand cramps.  He states that for the past six months he has experienced cramps in his feet and hands.  He describes that the foot cramps are much more notable than the hand ones.  He reports that he develops muscle contractions of his toes on both feet.  These occur exclusively at night.  They may occur about three times per week.  When he develops these cramps, he stands up to relieve the discomfort.  He notices that the toes are in an extended position.  He steps on the ground and they seem to "pop into place."  He develops calf pain after he experiences the cramp.  Sometimes they awaken him from his sleep. He also has developed cramps in his hands although they are less severe and less frequent than those in his legs.  These do not occur at night and are completely random.  He notices that his thumb assumes a flexed position and sometimes he needs to pry it open to relieve the cramp. He has never had any symptoms like this in the past.  He started taking Bactrim about nine months ago.  He had taken this in the past briefly, but has never taken it as long as he has now.  He cannot think of any other possible contributing factors to his symptoms. He has a history of HIV for 21 years.  He was taking antiretroviral medications, but stopped about six or seven years ago.  He reports that he was unable to tolerate the medications due to severe stomach upset.  He has a CD4 count of 326.  He states that he has never developed AIDS.  He is considering resuming antiretroviral treatment.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient returns for followup.  Since last consultation she has tolerated Lamictal well, but she has had a recurrence of her myoclonic jerking.  She has not had a generalized seizure.  She is very concerned that this will occur.  Most of the myoclonus is in the mornings.  Recent EEG did show polyspike and slow wave complexes bilaterally, more prominent on the left.  She states that she has been very compliant with the medications and is getting a good amount of sleep.  She continues to drive. Social history and review of systems are discussed  and documented on the chart.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: Patient is a 72-year-old white male complaining of a wooden splinter lodged beneath his left fifth fingernail, sustained at 4 p.m. yesterday.  He attempted to remove it with tweezers at home, but was unsuccessful.  He is requesting we attempt to remove this for him. The patient believes it has been over 10 years since his last tetanus shot, but states he has been allergic to previous immunizations primarily with "horse serum."  Consequently, he has declined to update his tetanus immunization.

reference_section: 71 y/o RHM developed a cataclysmic headache on 11/5/92 associated with a violent sneeze. The headache lasted 3-4 days. On 11/7/92, he had acute pain and loss of vision in the left eye. Over the following day his left pupil enlarged and his left upper eyelid began to droop. He was seen locally and a brain CT showed no sign of bleeding, but a tortuous left middle cerebral artery was visualized. The patient was transferred to UIHC 11/12/92.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm so sorry to hear that. I'm glad that you are here in one piece. Were you wearing your seatbelt?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I had my belt on and everything.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Unfortunately, the driver was drunk and ran a traffic signal.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you lose consciousness at all?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I briefly lost consciousness when help arrived at the scene. I felt an immediate headache when I regained consciousness. I also had lower back and neck pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you get out of the car by yourself?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I got out by myself. Once I made it out, the Rescue Squad drove me to Saint Thomas Memorial Hospital. I was seen in the emergency room and later discharged.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yessir.

reference_section: Date of incident: 1/15/2001. The patient was the driver of a small sports utility vehicle and was wearing a seatbelt. The patient's vehicle was proceeding through an intersection and was struck by another vehicle from the left side and forced off the road into a utility pole. The other vehicle had reportedly been driven by a drunk driver and ran a traffic signal. Estimated impact speed was 80 m.p.h. The driver of the other vehicle was reportedly cited by police. The patient was transiently unconscious and came to the scene. There was immediate onset of headaches, neck and lower back pain. The patient was able to exit the vehicle and was subsequently transported by Rescue Squad to St. Thomas Memorial Hospital, evaluated in the emergency room and released.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi, how are you doing?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you, young lady?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Eighty four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What brings you here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had a fall. And I was told to consult you for my heart conditions.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Um? Can you tell me a little detail about anything you experienced before or diagnosed before?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I have high blood pressure. And they also diagnosed me with other heart diseases. I cannot pronounce all the names I don't remember.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's fine. Let me go through your medical record first.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's see what we have here. Looks like you have your plate full. Your record says you had hypertension I mean, high blood pressure. Also, you have a history of severe tricuspid regurgitation with mild pulmonary hypertension, mild aortic stenosis, and previously moderate mitral regurgitation.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Wow! Those are a lot of fancy words that I can never remember.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ha ha. So, it says here they they want me to check you for atrial fibrillation. Yet another fancy word to add to your list.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What does it mean?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It means I must check if you have faster than normal heartbeat after your fall. In simple words, just to check if there are any irregularities in your heart beating, okay?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hm, okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So tell me what happened? How did you fall?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm not sure about how it happened, but yeah, I fell yesterday on my driveway and kind of hit a rock.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which side did you hit the rock?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um I think it was left side.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What happened in the emergency room?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They gave me some medicine. And they put something on my finger. They said that my heart rate was very high.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, in the record it says that they found rapid atrial tachyarrhythmia. So, according to this, they have given you Cardizem and they stopped it when your heart rate came to fifties.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let me review your electrocardiogram from emergency. It says that there was rapid heart rate. Your heart was really beating very fast and then there was one more electrocardiogram which showed that your pacemaker is acting weird.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They also did the same test this morning.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: One they did this morning shows normal rate with frequent early heartbeats. Looks like they also tested your blood. Your potassium level is three point one.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How was your heart feeling when you fell yesterday?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I felt that I just ran in a race. I could feel all the pain after that fall. It was ugly. My heart was pounding so fast it was ready to come out, I never felt like that before in my life.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you feel the same way afterwards as well?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, it was just after fall. It did not stay like that for long, I was normal later. I never felt it again after that incident.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is good. Do you have any pain or discomfort in your chest?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't think so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about before the fall? Did you have any pain or discomfort in your chest before the fall?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: how about shortness of breath?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not even before the fall. I'm able to walk and I'm sure I can climb stairs. Maybe two floors without any problems.

reference_section: The patient is an 84-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, severe tricuspid regurgitation with mild pulmonary hypertension, mild aortic stenosis, and previously moderate mitral regurgitation although not seen recently and I was asked to perform cardiology consultation for her because there was concern for atrial fibrillation after a fall.  Basically the patient states that yesterday she fell and she is not certain about the circumstances, on her driveway, and on her left side hit a rock.  When she came to the emergency room, she was found to have a rapid atrial tachyarrhythmia, and was put on Cardizem with reportedly heart rate in the 50s, so that was stopped.  Review of EKGs from that time shows what appears to be multifocal atrial tachycardia with followup EKG showing wandering atrial pacemaker.  An ECG this morning showing normal sinus rhythm with frequent APCs.  Her potassium at that time was 3.1.  She does recall having palpitations because of the pain after the fall, but she states she is not having them since and has not had them prior.  She denies any chest pain nor shortness of breath prior to or since the fall.  She states clearly she can walk and she would be able to climb 2 flights of stairs without problems.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor

reference_section: The patient is a 55-year-old gentleman, a patient of Mrs. A, who was referred to me because the patient developed iron deficiency anemia and he had blood in his stool.  The patient also has chronic diarrhea.  His anemia was diagnosed months ago when he presented with unusual pruritus and he got a CBC.  At that time he was discovered to have hemoglobin of 9 and MCV 65.  The patient also had multiple episodes of dark blood and bright blood in the stool for the last 5 months on and off.  Last colonoscopy was performed by Dr. X in Las Cruces 3 years ago.  At that time the patient had polyps removed from the colon, all of them were hyperplastic in nature.  The patient also was diagnosed with lymphocytic colitis.  He was not treated for diarrhea for more than 3 years.

reference_section: A 55-year-old white male who carries a diagnosis of polycythemia vera with secondary myelofibrosis.  Diagnosis was made some time in 2005/2006.  Initially, he underwent phlebotomy.  He subsequently transferred his care here.  In the past, he has been on hydroxyurea and interferon but did not tolerate both of them.  He is JAK-2 positive.  He does not have any siblings for a match-related transplant.  He was seen for consideration of a MUD transplant, but was deemed not to be a candidate because of the social support as well as his reasonably good health. At our institution, the patient received a trial of lenalidomide and prednisone for a short period.  He did well with the combination.  Subsequently, he developed intolerance to lenalidomide.  He complained of severe fatigue and diarrhea.  This was subsequently stopped. The patient reports some injury to his left leg last week.  His left leg apparently was swollen.  He took steroids for about 3 days and stopped.  Left leg swelling has disappeared.  The patient denies any other complaints at this point in time.  He admits to smoking marijuana.  He says this gives him a great appetite and he has actually gained some weight.  Performance status in the ECOG scale is 1.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient is a 5-year, 8-month-old male who presented to me direct from ED with distracted left lateral condyle fracture. reference_section: I am following the patient today for multiple issues.  He once again developed gross hematuria, which was unprovoked.  His Coumadin has been held.  The patient has known BPH and is on Flomax.  He is being treated with Coumadin because of atrial fibrillation and stroke.  This is the second time he has had significant gross hematuria this month.  He also fell about a week ago and is complaining of buttock pain and leg pain.  We did get x-rays of hips, knees, and ankles.  Clearly, he has significant degenerative disease in all these areas.  No fractures noted however.  He felt that the pain is pretty severe and particularly worse in the morning.  His sinuses are bothering him.  He wonders about getting some nasal saline spray.  We talked about Coumadin, stroke risk, etc. in the setting of atrial fibrillation.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I would like to get a detailed history of your inperforated anus and the curvature of the penis. It is a genetic condition. And do you know if you had surgery soon after birth?

turns.text: Do you know all the surgeries that you have had for this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, good you have a list.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. I was hospitalized in nineteen seventy for a U T I. That is when the problems started happening. It was a really bad infection.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: In nineteen eighty eight I the tissue removed from the anus. There was a blockage. They also did an operation in the shaft of the penis too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I bet things improved after that surgery.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It did. I have here in January of nineteen ninety one I had a cystoscopy to remove a blockage.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Um hum.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: In two thousand and one I had a colonoscopy that was normal. Later that year I had a biopsy of my prostate.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What did the biopsy show?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They said I had severe inflammation in the prostate. I was never told that cause of the inflammation.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Any other surgeries for your condition?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh yeah. I had that same procedure done again when I was twenty seven and twenty eight. The same one that I had as a newborn. I had a third surgery when I was seventy with just a correction of the shaft area.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Um hum. Any other surgeries unrelated to your condition?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. I have it written down here. In two thousand and one there was a left rotator cuff repair with acromioplasty and distal clavicle resection and in two thousand and three I had a left inguinal hernia repair with M E S H. That is what my notes say.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had any complications during any of your surgeries?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I did. I have a blood clot that apparently went into my lungs. I was very scary.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is very scary.

reference_section: Soon after birth for treatment of an inperforated anus and curvature of the penis.  At the age of 70 had another penile operation.  At the age of 27 and 28 he had repeat operations to correct this.  He did have complications of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism with one of those operations.  He has had procedures in the past for hypospadias, underwent an operation in 1988 to remove some tissue block in the anus.  In January of 1991 underwent cystoscopy.  He was hospitalized in 1970 for treatment of urinary tract infection.  In 2001, left rotator cuff repair with acromioplasty and distal clavicle resection.  In 2001, colonoscopy that was normal.  In 2001, prostate biopsy that showed chronic prostatitis.  In 2003, left inguinal hernia repair with MESH.

It is continuing the same way since then. I also feel like somebody is putting pins and needles on my legs approximately  halfway up the calf on both sides.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

reference_section: 21 y/o RHM complained of gradual onset numbness and incoordination of both lower extremities beginning approximately 11/5/96. The symptoms became maximal over a 12-24 hour period and have not changed since. The symptoms consist of tingling in the distal lower extremities approximately half way up the calf bilaterally. He noted decreased coordination of both lower extremities which he thought might be due to uncertainty as to where his feet were being placed in space. He denied bowel/bladder problems, or weakness or numbness elsewhere. Hot showers may improve his symptoms. He has suffered no recent flu-like illness. Past medical and family histories are unremarkable. He was on no medications.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Nurse, do you have a report on my patient?

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: I do. She has a two year history of small cell lung cancer, which spread to both femurs, lower lumbar spine, and pelvis.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, no. Did she get chemotherapy?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, ma'am. What is the reason for your visit today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I wanted to see if I could get some treatment for my pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of pain are you having?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I feel like it's a burning feeling? I don't know. I can feel it one spot and then it spreads down.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Where do you feel the pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I feel it mostly on my lower right side of my back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you feel it anywhere else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The back of my right leg and knee.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Would you said the pain radiates down from your back to your knee?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's it. Radiating. I forgot the word.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No problem. On a scale from zero to ten, with zero being no pain and ten being the worst pain of your life, how would you rate your back and leg?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They're both a ten.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, wow. Do you feel pain anywhere else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. Could you check my feet?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let me check them. I'll feel around your left foot. Let me know what you feel.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I feel like the bottom is numb. Ouch. It also feels sharp at times too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. The nurse stated here that you had some pain spreading to your mid back too. Let me feel it really quick. Let me know how that feels.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Ouch! It hurts a lot. I feel a sharp and dull pain. Most of the time, it's just aching.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. When do you feel like the pain in your body gets the worst?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'd say when I'm sitting in a car for a long time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, just sitting for long periods of time?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. When I stand and walk, too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever taken anything for the pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am on a load of narcotics for the pain.

reference_section: The patient is on my schedule today to explore treatment of the  complaints.  She has a two-year history of small cell lung cancer, which she says has spread to metastasis in both femurs, her lower lumbar spine, and her pelvis.  She states she has had numerous chemotherapy and radiation treatments and told me that she has lost count.  She says she has just finished a series of 10 radiation treatments for pain relief.  She states she continues to have significant pain symptoms.  Most of her pain seems to be in her low back on the right side, radiating down the back of her right leg to her knee.  She has also some numbness in the bottom of her left foot, and some sharp pain in the left foot at times.  She complains of some diffuse, mid back pain.  She describes the pain as sharp, dull, and aching in nature.  She rates her back pain as 10, her right leg pain as 10, with 0 being no pain and 10 being the worst possible pain.  She states that it seems to be worse while sitting in the car with prolonged sitting, standing, or walking.  She is on significant doses of narcotics.  She has had multiple CT scans looking for metastasis.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Even though you have been taking the medications without any issue, for about ten years, the methotrexate may be the cause of the mouth sores and the inflammation in the small intestines. These are both common side effects from the use of methotrexate. I am not as familiar with NSAID's causing mouth sores. Aspirin use can cause gastrointestinal upset. I think the most likely cause of the sores is the methotrexate not the use of Aspirin.

reference_section: Erosive stomatitis probably secondary to methotrexate even though the medication has been used for ten years without any problems.  Methotrexate may produce an erosive stomatitis and enteritis after such a use. The patient also may have an enteritis that at this point may have become more quiescent as she notes that she did have some diarrhea about the time her mouth problem developed. She has had no diarrhea today, however. She has noted no blood in her stools and has had no episodes of nausea or vomiting.   I am not as familiar with the NSAID causing an erosive stomatitis.  I understand that it can cause gastrointestinal upset, but given the choice between the two, I would think the methotrexate is the most likely etiology for the stomatitis.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: This is a 29-year-old Vietnamese female, established patient of dermatology, last seen in our office on 07/13/04.  She comes in today as a referral from ABC, D.O. for a reevaluation of her hand eczema.  I have treated her with Aristocort cream, Cetaphil cream, increased moisturizing cream and lotion, and wash her hands in Cetaphil cleansing lotion.  She comes in today for reevaluation because she is flaring.  Her hands are very dry, they are cracked, she has been washing with soap.  She states that the Cetaphil cleansing lotion apparently is causing some burning and pain because of the fissures in her skin.  She has been wearing some gloves also apparently.  The patient is single.  She is unemployed.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Remind me, how did he hurt himself? Guest_family_1: He was riding quads on October tenth two thousand seven when he got thrown off.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, and we did O R I F on his fracture dislocation of the left elbow. Guest_family_1: Yes, he also fractured the neck of his right glenoid, um, if I remember correctly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which hand does he write with? Guest_family_1: He writes with his right hand.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. That fracture appears to have healed very well; kids generally heal pretty well. How does it feel today? Guest_family_1: Yes, he's only ten. He's been pretty stiff, so he's been going to P T, and using his Dynasplint.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's good that he is already in P T. His left elbow fracture is healed, so we should do another surgery in order to remove that hardware. That may help decrease some of the irritation with elbow extension. He looks neurologically intact in terms of movement and reflexed in his wrist and hand. Guest_family_1: Yes, I agree. What is the risk of infection of this surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Historically, the risk of infection is less than one percent. Guest_family_1: Oh, wow, that's low, how is that possible?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We'll use prophylactic antibiotics, this controls for infection, and helps keep everything clean. Other Risks include bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremities, failure to remove hardware, failure to relieve pain, and continued postoperative stiffness. Guest_family_1: Wow, that's great, will be he asleep the entire time?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, we'll use anesthesia, he won't feel a thing. Guest_family_1: Will this fix his pain, for sure?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I can't guarantee it, he may still be in some pain. Guest_family_1: Okay, what about you, dear? What do you think? Guest_family_2: Yeah, I think we should do it, boys should be playing sports with their friends.

reference_section: The patient is a 10-year-old right-hand dominant male, who threw himself off a quad on 10/10/2007.  The patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation of his left elbow fracture dislocation.  The patient also sustained a nondisplaced right glenoid neck fracture.  The patient's fracture has healed without incident, although he had significant postoperative stiffness for which he is undergoing physical therapy, as well as use of a Dynasplint.  The patient is neurologically intact distally.  Given the fact that his fracture has healed, surgery was recommended for hardware removal to decrease his irritation with elbow extension from the hardware.  Risks and benefits of the surgery were discussed.  The risks of surgery included the risk of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremities, failure to remove hardware, failure to relieve pain, continued postoperative stiffness.  All questions were answered and the parents agreed to the above plan.

reference_section: The patient is a 58-year-old right-handed gentleman who presents for further evaluation of right arm pain.  He states that a little less than a year ago he developed pain in his right arm.  It is intermittent, but has persisted since that time.  He describes that he experiences a dull pain in his upper outer arm.  It occurs on a daily basis.  He also experiences an achy sensation in his right hand radiating to the fingers.  There is no numbness or paresthesias in the hand or arm. He has had a 30-year history of neck pain.  He sought medical attention for this problem in 2006, when he developed ear pain.  This eventually led to him undergoing an MRI of the cervical spine, which showed some degenerative changes.  He was then referred to Dr. X for treatment of neck pain.  He has been receiving epidural injections under the care of Dr. X since 2007.  When I asked him what symptom he is receiving the injections for, he states that it is for neck pain and now the more recent onset of arm pain.  He also has taken several Medrol dose packs, which has caused his blood sugars to increase.  He is taking multiple other pain medications.  The pain does not interfere significantly with his quality of life, although he has a constant nagging pain.

turns.text: We noticed it the week prior to Thanksgiving last year in nineteen ninety four. We have a family tradition where we play a game and this time, we were taking her to Vail, Colorado to play "Murder She Wrote" at one of our family gatherings. She was chosen to be the assassin.

turns.text: She seemed to be doing fine and stable throughout November and December, and we were visiting a local neurologist as well, who was evaluating her. He did a few blood tests and did uh, M R I of the brain. He gave us all clear. He said there's nothing there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, I see the working diagnosis of dementia of the Alzheimer's Type. When did these symptoms increase? Like when did you started noticing them more?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: One or two weeks ago, so end of December nineteen ninety four, she got lost in her own home. She was getting more sensitive and started saying that she is becoming a liability for everyone, which is not at all like her. Her walking was affected. She started walking like a bended form and also started veering to the right. She also did not recognize the location of where people were talking to her.

reference_section: This 73 y/o RHF presented on 1/12/95, with progressive memory and cognitive decline since 11/94. Her difficulties were first noted by family the week prior to Thanksgiving, when they were taking her to Vail, Colorado to play "Murder She Wrote" at family gathering. Unbeknownst to the patient was the fact that she had been chosen to be the "assassin." Prior to boarding the airplane her children hid a toy gun in her carry-on luggage. As the patient walked through security the alarm went off and within seconds she was surrounded, searched and interrogated. She and her family eventually made their flight, but she seemed unusually flustered and disoriented by the event. In prior times they would have expected her to have brushed off the incident with a "chuckle." While in Colorado her mentation seemed slow and she had difficulty reading the lines to her part while playing "Murder She Wrote." She needed assistance to complete the game. The family noted no slurring of speech, difficulty with vision, or focal weakness at the time. She returned to work at a local florist shop the Monday following Thanksgiving, and by her own report, had difficulty carrying out her usual tasks of flower arranging and operating the cash register. She quit working the next day and never went back. Her mental status appeared to remain relatively stable throughout the month of November and December and during that time she was evaluated by a local neurologist. Serum VDRL, TFTs, GS, B12, Folate, CBC, CXR, and MRI of the Brain were all reportedly unremarkable. The working diagnosis was "Dementia of the Alzheimer's Type." One to two weeks prior to her 1/12/95 presentation, she became repeatedly lost in her own home. In addition, she, and especially her family, noticed increased difficulty with word finding, attention, and calculation. Furthermore, she began expressing emotional lability unusual for her. She also tended to veer toward the right when walking and often did not recognize the location of people talking to her.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: This 21 month old male presented for delayed motor development, "jaw quivering" and "lazy eye." He was an 8 pound 10 ounce product of a full term, uncomplicated pregnancy-labor-spontaneous vaginal delivery to a G3P3 married white female mother. There had been no known toxic intrauterine exposures. He had no serious illnesses or hospitalizations since birth. He sat independently at 7 months, stood at 11 months, crawled at 16 months, but did not cruise until 18 months. He currently cannot walk and easily falls. His gait is reportedly marked by left "intoeing." His upper extremity strength and coordination reportedly appear quite normal and he is able to feed himself, throw and transfer objects easily. He knows greater than 20 words and speaks two-word phrases. No seizures or unusual behavior were reported except for "quivering" movement of his jaw. This has occurred since birth. In addition the parents have noted transient left exotropia.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: General:  No fevers, chills, or sweats.  No weight loss or weight gain. Cardiovascular:  No exertional chest pain, orthopnea, PND, or pedal edema.  No palpitations. ENT:  No allergy symptoms, such as rhinorrhea or sneezing. GI:  No indigestion, heartburn, or diarrhea.  No blood in the stools or black stools.  No change in bowel habits. GU:  No dysuria, hematuria, or pyuria.  No polyuria or nocturia.  Denies slow urinary stream. Psych:  No symptoms of depression or anxiety. Pulmonary:  No wheezing, cough, or sputum production. Skin:  No skin lesions or nonhealing lesions. Musculoskeletal:  No joint pain, bone pain, or back pain.  No erythema at the joints. Endocrine:  No heat or cold intolerance.  No polydipsia. Hematologic:  No easy bruising or easy bleeding.  No swollen lymph nodes.

reference_section: 23-year-old Hispanic male who presented for evaluation of chronic abdominal pain. Patient described the pain as dull, achy, constant and located at the epigastric area with some radiation to the back. There are also occasional episodes of stabbing epigastric pain unrelated to meals lasting only minutes. Patient noted that the pain started approximately six months prior to this presentation. He self medicated "with over the counter" antacids and obtained some relief so he did not seek medical attention at that time. Two months prior to current presentation, he had worsening of his pain as well as occasional nausea and vomiting. At this time the patient was found to be H. pylori positive by serology and was treated with triple therapy for two weeks and continued on omeprazole without relief of his pain. The patient felt he had experienced a twenty-pound weight loss since his symptoms began but he also admitted to poor appetite. He stated that he had two to three loose bowel movements a day but denied melena or bright red blood per rectum. Patient denied NSAID use, ethanol abuse or hematemesis. Position did not affect the quality of the pain. Patient denied fever or flushing. He stated he was a very active and healthy individual prior to these recent problems.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, miss X Y Z. Dr. X and I will go over your report with you to make sure everything is correct. Then, I will ask you a few questions.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sounds good to me. Doctor_2: Hi, ma'am. Could you confirm your age for me, please?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm seventy six years old. I'm also a resident of A S D F if that matters. Doctor_2: Thank you, ma'am.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Doctor A B  C requested for you to see us, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Perfect. Doctor X, could you go over her previous diagnoses? Doctor_2: She is diagnosed with hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease. Is this all correct, ma'am?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sounds about right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see she underwent a procedure. What was it, Doctor X? Doctor_2: She underwent a decompression for L three and L four. Did Doctor Stanley Gertzbein perform this procedure for your back?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: He did. He also did surgery on my lower legs. Doctor_2: Thank you for confirming.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see after the surgery, you had some pain in your right L four distribution, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Doctor X, did the M R I report of the outside lumbar come in? Doctor_2: It did. We also have a report of a lumbar C T myelogram, but no films came.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What does the C T myelogram say? Doctor_2: It says she has spondylolisthesis and L four and L 5 stenosis with right posterior surgical fusion changes at both levels.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. There are some notes from Doctor Reitman. What does it say? Doctor_2: It looks like she is being sent for an L four selective nerve root block to rule out if she would be a candidate for a T L I F at L four and L 5.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Could you review the M R I film as well? Doctor_2: The M R I reveal a grade two L four anterior spondylolisthesis without major canal stenosis. She does, however, have facet joint disease at this level and dorsal postoperative changes. She also has a foraminal disc protrusion on the right and a severely degenerated disc at L three and L four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you for that. So, miss. Where are you feeling pain today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I feel it in the font of my lower leg and right hip.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of pain are you feeling?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I told Doctor X about it. He could let you know. Doctor_2: She claimed she had a burning, shooting, aching, and constant pain in nature.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Is it worse when you do certain activities?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. When I walk and stand.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you able to walk at all?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I can walk around a block before it gets to the point where I get weak.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When does it feel better?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I feel more comfortable when I'm resting, sitting, sleeping, or getting a massage.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: From a scale of zero to ten, with ten being the worst pain, how would you rate the pain on average?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'd say like a nine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's the intensity on a daily level, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What's the lowest pain you've ever felt?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think it was a five.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Doctor X, did you ask her the series of questions about bowel function? Doctor_2: I did. She denied any bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle area hypoesthesia, numbness, tingling, weakness or Valsalva related exacerbation.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great. Have you taken any medication recently?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Uh. I think it starts with a T. Doctor_2: It states here you took Tylenol, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's correct.

reference_section: Ms. XYZ is a 76-year-old resident of ASDF.  She is seen at the request of Dr. ABC.  She carries a diagnosis of hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease.  She underwent an L3-4 decompression in Month DD, YYYY by Dr. Stanley Gertzbein for back and bilateral lower extremity pain.  Shortly after surgery, she began having pain in the right L4 distribution and is seen today with an outside lumbar MRI only.  I have a report of a lumbar CT myelogram as well, but no films.  She has apparently spondylolisthesis and L4-5 stenosis with right posterior surgical fusion changes evident at both levels.  According to Dr. Reitman's notes, she is being sent for an L4 selective nerve root block to rule out whether or not she would be a candidate for a TLIF at L4-5.  Her MRI films are reviewed.  These reveal grade 2 L4 anterior spondylolisthesis without significant canal stenosis, though she has facet joint arthropathy at this level and dorsal postoperative changes.  She has a foraminal disc protrusion on the right, as well as a severely degenerated disc at L3-4. The patient complains essentially of pain along the anterior tibia and along the right hip, which his burning, shooting, aching and constant in nature.  It is worse with standing and walking.  She can walk about a block before her symptoms become debilitating.  She is more comfortable in recumbency.  She denies bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle area hypoesthesia, numbness, tingling, weakness or Valsalva related exacerbation.  She rates her pain as 9/10 in average and her daily level of intensity and 5/10 for her least level of pain.  Alleviating factors include sitting, recumbency, sleeping, and massage.  She treats her pain with Tylenol currently.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, miss. How are you doing today? It looks like we are evaluating C O P D and emphysema.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, the last time I was seen in Pulmonary Medicine Clinic was March two thousand and four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It has been quite some time. How are you feeling?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have actually been hospitalized for psychiatric problems and now live in a nursing facility. Things have not been too great. I don't like living there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I understand the frustration. When you live in a nursing facility you lose a lot of your freedom.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I want to live back in my apartment, but I know I am too ill to care for myself.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: In spite of all of that how are your respiratory issues?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I feel pretty stable. I still have shortness of breath when I do activities, but with my condition I feel like that is something I will have to live with.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Unfortunately, that is the nature of the disease. I am happy to see that the pulmonary disease has not changed significantly since your last visit.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The only thing that seems to have changed is that I have a small cough and produce some mucus.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Do you have any fever or chills?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, none of that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you experience any chest pains? I want to check especially since you have been coughing up some mucus.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I luckily do not have any chest pains.

reference_section: The patient returns to the Pulmonary Medicine Clinic for followup evaluation of COPD and emphysema.  She was last seen in the clinic in March 2004.  Since that time, she has been hospitalized for psychiatric problems and now is in a nursing facility.  She is very frustrated with her living situation and would like to return to her own apartment, however, some believes she is to ill to care for herself. At the present time, respiratory status is relatively stable.  She is still short of breath with activity, but all-in-all her pulmonary disease has not changed significantly since her last visit.  She does have occasional cough and a small amount of sputum production.  No fever or chills.  No chest pains.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you confirm your age for me, ma'am?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure, I'm fifty six years old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, so what brings you in to see me today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I'm peeing a lot, and I'm having  a little bit blood in that urine as well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had a cystoscopy?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor

reference_section: The patient is a 56-year-old noted to have microscopic hematuria with overactive bladder.  Her cystoscopy performed was unremarkable.  She continues to have some episodes of frequency and urgency mostly with episodes during the day and rare at night.  No gross hematuria, dysuria, pyuria, no other outlet obstructive and/or irritative voiding symptoms.  The patient had been previously on Ditropan and did not do nearly as well.  At this point, what we will try is a different medication.  Renal ultrasound is otherwise unremarkable, notes no evidence of any other disease.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello sir, how are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't know, I don't know whether I am good, or my problem is getting worse and that is the reason I got myself to your clinic for a neurological consult.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hm, don't worry! We will take care of you, let me start by taking some details.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So were you referred by someone or-

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, no I referred myself to your clinic.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. And what is your age?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am sixty four years young!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ah, that's clever, you certainly look very young. And which is your dominant hand? Are you left handed, or right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am right handed.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, tell me what is going on with you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, lately I am having difficulty remembering names and phone numbers or even events.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, it's not uncommon.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I know, but I am usually very good at remembering things. I would have not worried that much, but it was brought to my attention by my clerical staff.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, okay. What do you do?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I was the catholic priest at my parish, like we have our own small administrative district and church.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, and when did you notice first that you are forgetting things?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Around twelve months back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And did it cause any problem at work or any mishaps?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not at all! No social or professional faux pas whatsoever.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, I have my notes let me put the date, oh what is the date-

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's twenty eighth of February.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you!

reference_section: This 64 y/o RHM had had difficulty remembering names, phone numbers and events for 12 months prior to presentation, on 2/28/95. This had been called to his attention by the clerical staff at his parish--he was a Catholic priest. He had had no professional or social faux pas or mishaps due to his memory. He could not tell whether his problem was becoming worse, so he brought himself to the Neurology clinic on his own referral.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi there! Welcome to the Neurology clinic, sir.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi! Thank you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What brings you in to the clinic today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was diagnosed with binocular diplopia twenty five years ago but I haven't had much of an issue with it until about a year ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What did you notice as far as symptoms?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Suddenly, I started having double vision.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did the double vision happen more than one time?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It has been happening almost every day off and on through out the day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long do the episodes last?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They last for only a few minutes at a time. When I was first diagnosed years ago it happened for a year and then it stopped happening. It was not happening as often as it is now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you ever receive any treatment for your binocular diplopia?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. It spontaneously resolved and so I didn't need to seek any treatment. Back when all this was happening it had two episodes of a drooping eyelid. I thought I had myasthenia gravis but I was told that that was probably not the case.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What eyelid was drooping?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't remember?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is your dominate hand?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am right handed.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And how old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am sixty seven.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Involving the double vision, does it become worse when looking at distant objects?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When you look at objects off to either side of midline does it become worse?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. That makes it worse too. When I put my hand over one eye is goes away.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any other symptoms related to the vision issues?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

reference_section: This 67 y/oRHM first began experiencing horizontal binocular diplopia 25 years prior to presentation in the Neurology Clinic. The diplopia began acutely and continued intermittently for one year. During this time he was twice evaluated for myasthenia gravis (details of evaluation not known) and was told he probably did not have this disease. He received no treatment and the diplopia spontaneously resolved. He did well until one year prior to presentation when he experienced sudden onset horizontal binocular diplopia. The diplopia continues to occur daily and intermittently; and lasts for only a few minutes in duration. It resolves when he covers one eye. It is worse when looking at distant objects and objects off to either side of midline. There are no other symptoms associated with the diplopia.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old is your son?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: He is almost five and a half years old now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What seems to be the problem?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: He has a lot of pain about both feet, and if you look at it, it looks like his feet rotate inwards.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let me see, okay, um, he has rocker bottom feet.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I believe he would benefit from a subtalar arthrodesis, possible autograft, and lengthening of the Achilles. I'll go over the details of that procedure right now.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Can we do the surgery soon?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes we can. But we'll probably need to do another procedure until his foot matures some more.   This is a stabilizing measure.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What are the risks of infection if we do the surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Historically, the risk of infection is very low, usually less than one percent.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: How do you get the risk so low?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We use prophylactic antibiotics to minimize the infection risk.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Will he be able to walk again right after the surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No, he'll need to stay off it for a while, we call this nonweightbearing. It will only be for some time after the procedure, it's not permanent.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What are the rest of the risks?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The total risks of surgery include risks of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremity, hardware failure, need for other surgical procedures, need to be nonweightbearing for some time. I would not worry about these risks, though. The risk is low.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay. Let's do the surgery.

reference_section: The patient is a 5-year-4-month-old male who presents for evaluation of feet.  He has been having significant feet pain with significant planovalgus deformity.  The patient was noted to have flexible vertical talus.  It was decided that the patient would benefit by subtalar arthrodesis, possible autograft, and Achilles lengthening.  This was explained to the mother in detail.  This is going to be a stabilizing measure and the patient will probably need additional surgery at a later day when his foot is more mature.  Risks of surgery include risks of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremity, hardware failure, need for other surgical procedures, need to be nonweightbearing for some time.  All questions were answered and the mother agreed to the above plan.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Welcome back to the clinic.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: patient
