turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am required to ask some specific questions for the L and I paperwork. What is your ago, ethnicity and gender?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am a thirty one year old, white, female.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had a prior injury to your right shoulder?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are right or left hand dominant?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Other then your shoulder injury, do you have any other chronic health problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you experiencing any fever, chills or illnesses?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let discuss some of the previous treatments and test that you have been done for your shoulder.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okey. I have done a lot of different treatments.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What treatments have you done?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I tried physical therapy. They did a subacromion decompression treatment in November, two thousand and two.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did either of those treatments help?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not much. I went and saw Doctor Lin and he said that I might have a nerve fiber injury. I forget what he called it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Brachial plexopathy?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. That sounds right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, I see his notes in your chart. It says that he felt like you had a right superficial radial neuritis and blocked this with resolution of your symptoms. Then it looks like he sent you to get E M G testing at Valley Medical. Let me look for those results.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okey. They should be in my chart. I had Doctor Lin send over all my records.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Here it is. It says that the right suprascapular neuropathy although a C5 radiculopathy could not be ruled out.  MRI testing on the cervical spine was then done which was negative for disk herniation and underwent suprascapular nerve decompression of the scapular notch on December eighteenth, two thousand and three.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Whatever that means? I ended up getting a nerve block because I was still in pain. Doctor Lin did one in the frount of my shoulder and then another in the back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: This has been a long drawn out course of treatments for you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it has been.

reference_section: The patient is a pleasant, 31-year-old, right-handed, white female who injured her shoulder while transferring a patient back on 01/01/02.  She formerly worked for Veteran's Home as a CNA.  She has had a long drawn out course of treatment for this shoulder.  She tried physical therapy without benefit and ultimately came to a subacromion decompression in November 2002.  She had ongoing pain and was evaluated by Dr. X who felt that she had a possible brachial plexopathy.  He also felt she had a right superficial radial neuritis and blocked this with resolution of her symptoms.  He then referred her to ABCD who did EMG testing, demonstrating a right suprascapular neuropathy although a C5 radiculopathy could not be ruled out.  MRI testing on the cervical spine was then done which was negative for disk herniation and she underwent suprascapular nerve decompression of the scapular notch on 12/18/03.  She finally went to an anterior axillary nerve block because of ongoing pain in the anterior shoulder again by Dr. X.  She comes to me for impairment rating.  She has no chronic health problems otherwise, fevers, chills, or general malaise.  She is not working.  She is right-hand dominant.  She denies any prior history of injury to her shoulder.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: So, tell me what's going on? What brings you to the emergency?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I felt like my heart will explode. I have never felt palpitations like this. I am feeling so weak.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did it start?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: This afternoon.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hm, so your blood pressure is one ninety five by eighty three and your heart rate is one twenty one which is quite high.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We have started you on I V Metoprolol. This will help to bring your heartrate down.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And you said you are sixty six?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: My mom has stopped taking her medications.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I can tell from her reports. Her blood pressure is quite high.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: It's been several months since she last took her medicines.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, that's not good!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And does she drink and smoke?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, both.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How much do you drink Ma'am? Is it occasional?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She drinks a lot!

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I drink about four to five glasses of wine every day. I drank last night.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, I think you need to cut down on it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am trying doctor and honestly these are all withdrawal symptoms. I have never felt like this before.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hm, I understand. For now I have put you on five M G of Metoprolol and looks like your blood pressure is under control and your heart rate has come down to seventy.

reference_section: This 66-year-old patient has history of hypertension and has not taken medication for several months.  She is a smoker and she drinks alcohol regularly.  She drinks about 5 glasses of wine every day.  Last drink was yesterday evening.  This afternoon, the patient felt palpitations and generalized weakness and came to the emergency room.  On arrival in the emergency room, the patient's heart rate was 121 and blood pressure was 195/83.  The patient received 5 mg of metoprolol IV, after which heart rate was reduced to the 70 and blood pressure was well controlled.  On direct questioning, the patient said she had been drinking a lot.  She had not had any withdrawal before.  Today is the first time she has been close to withdrawal.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient presents today for followup, history of erectile dysfunction, last visit started on Cialis 10 mg.  He indicates that he has noticed some mild improvement of his symptoms, with no side effect.  On this dose, he is having firm erection, able to penetrate, lasting for about 10 or so minutes.  No chest pain, no nitroglycerin usage, no fever, no chills.  No dysuria, gross hematuria, fever, chills.  Daytime frequency every three hours, nocturia times 0, good stream.  He does have a history of elevated PSA and biopsy June of this year was noted for high grade PIN, mid left biopsy, with two specimens being too small to evaluate.  PSA 11.6.  Dr. X's notes are reviewed.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: She was brought to emergency by her son. Apparently, she is doing fine, no distress. She is alert, and I was able to communicate with her and take her history, she was cooperative and calmy responded to all my questions.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, that's good.

reference_section: GENERAL: Alert and in no apparent distress, calm, cooperative, and communicative.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is your family medical history?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My family has high blood pressure and diabetes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any family history of nervous system disorder or disease such as multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, epilepsy, or stroke?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any children, miss?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. I have a son, he was born on October thirty first, two thousand and eight.

reference_section: There is a family history of diabetes and hypertension.  There is no family history of a neuropathy or other neurological disease.  She has one child, a son, born on October 31, 2008.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had any heart problems in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I remember I did have something heart related but I don't know what that was. I do not understand any medical terms.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay that's fine, I completely understand. We will try to look for your  past medical history.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I do have hypertension and diabetes, you know that right?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, type two diabetes. Do you know of any other things that you had in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, four years back I had lung embolism. I also get frequent urine infections.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. And I can see on the file that you have high cholesterol and a gastric ulcer too.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's about right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. What surgeries have you had in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have had my appendix taken out, then C Section, cataract surgery and hernia repair done in the past.

reference_section: She has had a fairly extensive past medical history but is a somewhat poor historian and is unable to provide details about her history.  She states that she has underlying history of heart disease but is not able to elaborate to any significant extent.  She also has a history of hypertension and type II diabetes but is not currently taking any medication.  She has also had a history of pulmonary embolism approximately four years ago, hyperlipidemia, peptic ulcer disease, and recurrent urinary tract infections.  Surgeries include an appendectomy, cesarean section, cataracts, and hernia repair.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good afternoon, ma'am.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good afternoon, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, are you married?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, happily to my husband.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's wonderful, um, what do you do for a living?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I work as an office manager right now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I do. I've smoked a pack a day for the last twenty years.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you drink?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Actually, yes, I drink daily.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How much do you drink every day?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, it varies, but usually about anywhere from three to five drinks a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, do you do any illicit drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, absolutely not.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you do for exercise?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I go for walks, and like low impact cardio. But, I do like playing softball with my friends too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Very nice, how often do you exercise?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I work out a few times a month.

reference_section: The patient is married.  She is employed as an office manager.  She does smoke cigarettes, one pack per day for the last 20 years.  She consumes alcohol 3 to 5 drinks daily.  She uses no illicit drugs.  She exercises monthly mainly walking and low impact aerobics.  She also likes to play softball.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: I'm going to run down a list of symptoms and I'd like you to tell me if you've experienced any.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.text: Headache?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No headaches.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: None.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, sir. Looks like we are here for a general wellness check?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, sir. In my seventy eight years on this Earth, I have learned to take my health more seriously. I need to start catching things before they come, not after.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I could not agree more. From your last checkup notes, it looks like you had right knee surgery and back surgery about eighteen months ago. How is that going? Any pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I had a right knee replacement. I am doing great so far. Nothing to complain about. I can do almost anything I desire now. It is such a good lifestyle change from before surgery.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you do with your new body?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I travel every chance I get. I just got back from a cruise.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I hope to be as agile as you when I get to retirement. Now let's check the other systems. Do you feel any type of chest pain? Any heaviness, tightness or pressure?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, nothing like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about shortness of breath?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I only get short of breath when I walk up the stairs.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is decently normal. I get out of breath when walking from floor to floor in this hospital too.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I thought so. I remember being young and still struggling with stairs.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Unfortunately, some things are just with us for life. Do you have any coughing fits or irregular heart beating?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great! You are getting a clean bill of health from me today. On the notes it says you have Crohn's disease. Are you getting regularly checked for that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. Doctor Ferguson takes care of me for that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Excellent. Are you scheduled for a prostate check?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I go to Doctor Roszhart.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You are wonderfully on top of it. What a breath of fresh air. From all of your travelling, how are your ankles? Have you noticed any swelling?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Surprisingly, from all the walking I do, I do not have any swelling. After quitting smoking ten years ago I had to get addicted to something else and that was walking and travelling.

reference_section: This is a 78-year-old male who recently had his right knee replaced and also back surgery about a year and a half ago.  He has done well with that.  He does most of the things that he wants to do.  He travels at every chance he has, and he just got back from a cruise.  He denies any type of chest pain, heaviness, tightness, pressure, shortness of breath with stairs only, cough or palpitations.  He sees Dr. Ferguson.  He is known to have Crohn's and he takes care of that for him.  He sees Dr. Roszhart for his prostate check.  He is a nonsmoker and denies swelling in his ankles.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you, sir?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: One less than sixty.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, what happened?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I was visiting my son in Cheyenne, Wyoming, then I on October tenth when I was taking a shower, I felt a pop in my head. I don't know what happened after that.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: We thought he was having a long shower that day. Then about one and a half hours later my son suspected something is not right and we went up to check. There we found him unconscious on the shower floor. Our son, he then drove us back to Iowa and since then he is complaining of these headaches and that he's not feeling well. He gets unconscious or falls asleep I don't know but it is happening a lot of the time. We got him to local hospital today in the morning. It is three days after that shower incident.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, his report says he got a hemorrhage, I mean, blood clot in his brain.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, after that report they transferred us to this hospital.

reference_section: 59y/o male experienced a "pop" in his head on 10/10/92 while showering in Cheyenne, Wyoming. He was visiting his son at the time. He was found unconscious on the shower floor 1.5 hours later. His son then drove him Back to Iowa. Since then he has had recurrent headaches and fluctuating level of consciousness, according to his wife. He presented at local hospital this AM, 10/13/92. A HCT there demonstrated a subarachnoid hemorrhage. He was then transferred to UIHC.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.text: Good morning, sir. Before we begin, how old are you?

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not at all.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see here that you've been feeling more short of breath.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, for three days now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is it worse when you exert yourself?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um no, not really. I've had a terrible cough along with frequent headaches and chest congestion. I have also had a low fever.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did these symptoms start around the same time?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Where does your chest feel most congested? And how would you rate the pain right now? Ten being the worst.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Both sides. I'd say it's at a three currently.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does it send pain or numbness or tingling down your arms? How about any jaw pain as a result?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, but it does get worse whenever I cough.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is this your first time experiencing this type of congestion?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh no. I had something like it about ten months ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did that improve on its own?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It would come and go, but over the past few days it's gotten worse. I am a strong German man so I held out coming to the doctor as long as I could.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You are very strong! You are sixty nine though, so I don't think anyone would see it as weak if you came to the doctor more often.

He also admits to having intermittent headaches and bilateral chest pain that does not radiate to upper extremities and jaws but worse with coughing.  Patient initially had this type of episodes about 10 months ago but has intermittently getting worse since.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, sir how can I help you? Looks like we are talking about snoring today.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I need to get this loud and obnoxious snoring under control. I keep waking up my partner. I have a C P A P right now because I was told I have almost severe sleep apnea.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I see on your chart that you were given ten centimeters of H two O nasal pressure and that you predominately suffer from hypopnea. Hypopnea is shallow breathing. How has the device been working?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It definitely has reduced my snoring, but my partner keeps waking me up in the middle of the night because the mask pops off. I wear it around five to seven nights a week, but for some reason it falls off or I take it off randomly in the night. My wife usually must remind me to put it back on.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So what is your sleep pattern now? When do you usually go to bed and wake up?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Usually I sleep around eleven or eleven thirty and wake up at six or seven on the weekends. I'll sleep in until eight or nine on the weekdays. On Saturday's I might go to sleep around midnight because I usually watch a show with my family. I feel good when I wake up though. Much less tossing and turning. The sheets are always on the bed still.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's some good news. I see you have lost a bit of weight too. Around fifteen to eighteen pounds is something to be proud of.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thanks. It has been a lot of exercising and dieting. I am motivated because I want to stop snoring.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How has work been? Do you think it has been stressful at all?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I still work at Smith Barney in downtown Baltimore. I work from around eight or eight thirty to five or five thirty. I deal with training on how to sell managed funds and accounts. I do not think I have been stressed because I am able to stay awake through my shift and even when I come home at night. I may get a little tired during hay fever season, but that is rare.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I see that you have hay fever. Fatigue is a common symptom from the allergy.

reference_section: The patient initially presented with loud obnoxious snoring that disrupted the sleep of his bed partner.  He was found to have moderate-to-severe sleep apnea (predominantly hypopnea), was treated with nasal CPAP at 10 cm H2O nasal pressure.  He has been on CPAP now for several months, and returns for followup to review his response to treatment. The patient reports that the CPAP has limited his snoring at night.  Occasionally, his bed partner wakes him in the middle of the night, when the mask comes off, and reminds him to replace the mask.  The patient estimates that he uses the CPAP approximately 5 to 7 nights per week, and on occasion takes it off and does not replace the mask when he awakens spontaneously in the middle of the night. The patient's sleep pattern consists of going to bed between 11:00 and 11:30 at night and awakening between 6 to 7 a.m. on weekdays.  On weekends, he might sleep until 8 to 9 a.m.  On Saturday night, he might go to bed approximately mid night. As noted, the patient is not snoring on CPAP.  He denies much tossing and turning and does not awaken with the sheets in disarray.  He awakens feeling relatively refreshed. In the past few months, the patient has lost between 15 and 18 pounds in combination of dietary and exercise measures. He continues to work at Smith Barney in downtown Baltimore.  He generally works from 8 to 8:30 a.m. until approximately 5 to 5:30 p.m.  He is involved in training purpose to how to sell managed funds and accounts. The patient reports no change in daytime stamina.  He has no difficulty staying awake during the daytime or evening hours. The past medical history is notable for allergic rhinitis.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay I will investigate it. Are you experiencing any chest pain or shortness of breath?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay great!

turns.text: How about your back pain?

turns.text: Um, it is improving as well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, cool.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah.

reference_section: ABC is in today for a followup of her atrial fibrillation.  They have misplaced the Cardizem.  She is not on this and her heart rate is up just a little bit today.  She does complain of feeling dizziness, some vertigo, some lightheadedness, and has attributed this to the Coumadin therapy.  She is very adamant that she wants to stop the Coumadin.  She is tired of blood draws.  We have had a difficult time getting her regulated.  No chest pains.  No shortness of breath.  She is moving around a little bit better.  Her arm does not hurt her. turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good morning, young man.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good morning, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Who is this young lady, is this your grandmother, or sister?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Oh doctor, yes, I am his grandmother.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, my chart says that you're fourteen years old. Is that correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes sir.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, so what seems to be the problem today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've been having pain in this knee for about a month now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you remember a specific injury to this knee?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, yeah, I was playing basketball when I jumped, and then when I landed I felt this knee pop.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you remember the date of your injury, young man?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Um, it was on December twenty second two thousand seven.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, so how have you been treated for this so far?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: We went to another clinic first, and they put me in a splint.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, and then they referred us over to Children's.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have they taken x rays yet?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I got back a few minutes ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's have a look. Well, you broke your leg.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What, where? Can you show me?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Right here, this is a tibial tubercule avulsion fracture with patella alta.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What does that mean, doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, he's broken his leg, and pulled some bone off by doing so. We'll need to do surgery on this.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Oh no, what's the name of the procedure?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's called an O R I F. We'll go in there with some hardware to put everything back together, and he can get on the road to healing.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Let me call his father while we discuss this. What's the risk of infection from this surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Historically, it's less than one percent. We use antibiotics to control for infection.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, will he be asleep for this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, he won't feel a thing.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: That's good too. Will he need this hardware out in the future?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We can remove everything once he has healed up nicely. Other risks include bleeding, changes in the sensation of the leg, hardware failure, need for post op rehab, need for hardware removal, and failure to restore extensor mechanism tension. But I would not worry about these things. I have been doing these surgeries for years and things like this rarely happen.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes, his father agrees. We're going to do the surgery.

reference_section: The patient is a 14-year-old male who reported having knee pain for 1 month.  Apparently while he was playing basketball on 12/22/2007 when he had gone up for a jump, he felt a pop in his knee.  The patient was seen at an outside facility where he was splinted and subsequently referred to Children's for definitive care.  Radiographs confirmed comminuted tibial tubercle avulsion fracture with patella alta.  Surgery is recommended to the grandmother and subsequently to the father by phone.  Surgery would consist of open reduction and internal fixation with subsequent need for later hardware removal.  Risks of surgery include the risks of  anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes on sensation in most of the extremity, hardware failure, need for later hardware removal, failure to restore extensor mechanism tension, and need for postoperative rehab.  All questions were answered, and father and grandmother agreed to the above plan.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: This is a 61-year-old woman with a history of polyarteritis nodosa, mononeuritis multiplex involving the lower extremities, and severe sleep apnea returns in followup following an overnight sleep study, on CPAP and oxygen to evaluate her for difficulty in initiating and maintaining sleep. reference_section: Dr. X has cared for her since 2002.  She has a Codman-Hakim shunt set at 90 mmH2O. reference_section: This 59 y/o RHM was seen and released from an ER 1 week prior to this presentation for a 3 week history of progressive sensory and motor deficits in both lower extremities. He reported numbness beginning about his trunk and slowly progressing to involve his lower extremities over a 4 week period. On presentation, he felt numb from the nipple line down. In addition, he began experiencing progressive weakness in his lower extremities for the past week. He started using a cane 5 days before being seen and had been having difficulty walking and traversing stairs. He claimed he could not stand. He denied loss of bowel or bladder control. However, he had not had a bowel movement in 3 days and he had not urinated 24 hours. His lower extremities had been feeling cold for a day. He denied any associated back or neck pain. He has chronic shortness of breath, but felt it had become worse. He had also been experiencing lightheadedness upon standing more readily than usual for 2 days prior to presentation.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Before we begin, how old are you? And which gender do you identify?

turns.text: How far did you fall?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, yes, I see. I have some good news for you, there's no gross deformity in this ankle.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What does that mean, exactly?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I don't see any ankle dislocation, which is good.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, that's good news.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had your x rays taken yet?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, the tech just brought me back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, let me pull them up here. Okay, um, if you look here, you'll see a fracture of your talus.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Which bone is that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's your heel, to be specific, it's a grade I V Hawkins fracture of the left talus. You are still neurovascularly intact in the distal region.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What are we going to do about this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any other pain from the fall, aside from the ankle?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, the ankle really took all of the weight of the fall.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, I think we should do surgery in order to repair this ankle.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Why is that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: There is very weak blood flow to the body of this bone, there's a risk for avascular necrosis, which is bone death.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, you're right. What are the risks of this infection with this surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Overall, the risks of infection are less than one percent. We'll use antibiotics to keep everything clean.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Will I be asleep for this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, you'll be under anesthesia.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, yes, um, I'd like to go forward with the surgery.

reference_section: This is a 50-year-old male who presented to ABCD General Hospital Emergency Department with complaints of left ankle pain and disfigurement.  There was no open injury.  The patient fell approximately 10 feet off his liner, landing on his left foot.  There was evidence of gross deformity of the ankle.  An x-ray was performed in the Emergency Room, which revealed a grade IV Hawkins classification talus fracture.  He was distal neurovascularly intact.  The patient denied any other complaints besides pain in the ankle. It was for this reason, we elected to undergo the  procedure in order to reduce and restore the blood supply to the talus body.  Because of its tenuous blood supply, the patient is at risk for avascular necrosis.  The patient has agreed to undergo the above-named procedure and consent was obtained.  All risks as well as complications were discussed.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, yes, I'd like to do the surgery.

reference_section: This is a 69-year-old male with complaints of bilateral knee pain for several years and increased intensity in the past several months where it has affected his activities of daily living.  He attempted conservative treatment, which includes anti-inflammatory medications as well as cortisone and Synvisc.  This has only provided him with temporary relief.  It is for that reason, he is elected to undergo the above-named procedure. All risks as well as complications were discussed with the patient, which include, but are not limited to infection, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, need for further surgery, and further pain.  He has agreed to undergo this procedure and a consent was obtained preoperatively.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: After doing the exam I see his ulnar, median, and radial nerves are intact. I couldn't do the entire exam because the pain might be too much for him.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Thank you so much for your help.

reference_section: This is a 4-year-old white male, apparently dominantly right-handed who suffered a severe injury to his left distal humerus after jumping off of a swing.  He apparently had not had previous problems with his left arm.  He was seen in the Emergency with a grossly deformed left elbow.  His parents' were both present preoperatively.  His x-ray exam as well as physical exam was consistent with a closed type-III supracondylar fracture of the left distal humerus with rather severe puckering of the skin anteriorly with significant ecchymosis in the same region.  Gross neurologic exam revealed his ulnar, median, and radial nerves to be mostly intact, although a complete exam was impossible.  He did have a radial pulse palpable.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

He was normally rushing to the restroom and every time used to say he didn't want to pee as it hurt him. He also had a few accidents in the last few days where he wet himself.

reference_section: The patient is a pleasant but demented 80-year-old male, who lives in board and care, who presented with acute onset of abdominal pain.  In the emergency room, the patient was found to have a CT scan with dilated bladder with thick wall suggesting an outlet obstruction as well as bilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureter.  The patient is unable to provide further history.  The patient's son is at the bedside and confirmed his history.  The patient was given IV antibiotics in the emergency room.  He was also given some hydration.

reference_section: This is a 39-year-old female who has sustained a twisting injury to her knee while on trampoline in late August.  She was diagnosed per MRI.  An MRI confirmed the clinical diagnosis of anterior cruciate ligament tear.  She states she has had multiple episodes of instability to the patellofemoral joint throughout the years with multiple dislocations.  She elected to proceed with surgery to repair the anterior cruciate ligament as well as possibly plicate the medial retinaculum to help prevent further dislocations of the patellofemoral joint.  All risks and benefits of surgery were discussed with her at length.  She was in agreement with the treatment plan.

reference_section: The patient is a 44-year-old man who was seen for complaints of low back and right thigh pain.  He attributes this to an incident in which he was injured in 1994.  I do not have any paperwork authenticating his claim that there is an open claim.  Most recently he was working at Taco Bell, when he had a recurrence of back pain, and he was seen in our clinic on 04/12/05.  He rated pain of approximately 8/10 in severity. He took a Medrol Dosepak and states that his pain level has decreased to approximately 4-5/10.  He still localizes it to a band between L4 and the sacrum.  He initially had some right leg pain but states that this is minimal and intermittent at the present time.  His back history is significant for two laminectomies and a discectomy performed from 1990 to 1994.  The area of concern was L4-L5. The patient's MRI dated 10/18/04 showed multi-level degenerative changes, with facet involvement at L2-L3, L3-L4 and L5-S1.  There was no neural impingement.  He also had an MR myelogram, which showed severe stenosis at L3-L4, however it was qualified in that it may have been artifact, rather than a genuine finding.

reference_section: Mr. ABC is a 2-year-old boy, who is brought in by parents, stating that the child keeps complaining of belly and back pain.  This does not seem to be slowing him down.  They have not noticed any change in his urine or bowels.  They have not noted him to have any fevers or chills or any other illness.  They state he is otherwise acting normally.  He is eating and drinking well.  He has not had any other acute complaints, although they have noted a foul odor coming from his nose.  Apparently, he was seen here a few weeks ago for a foreign body in the right nose, which was apparently a piece of cotton; this was removed and placed on antibiotics.  His nose got better and then started to become malodorous again.  Mother restarted him on the remainder of the antibiotics and they are also stating that they think there is something still in there.  Otherwise, he has not had any runny nose, earache, no sore throat.  He has not had any cough, congestion.  He has been acting normally.  Eating and drinking okay.  No other significant complaints.  He has not had any pain with bowel movement or urination, nor have they noted him to be more frequently urinating, then again he is still on a diaper.

turns.text: Please, tell me a little more about your son.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: He previously had a lot of trouble straightening out both of his legs, and since the right was worse than the left he had an operation on the inside part of the back of that leg.

turns.text: It was in February of two thousand seven.

turns.text: What seems to be the problem today?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Now, his left knee is getting really bad, it's like how the right knee was. He can't straighten this leg. I think we should do the same operation again on the left knee.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I think we'll have to do surgery.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What is the risk of infection with the surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Historically, it's been less than one percent, we use prophylactic antibiotics in order to minimize infection risk.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What's the name of this procedure?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's called a distal medial hamstring release.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: This is the same procedure he had in two thousand seven, right?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes ma'am, the exact same one.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, that sounds good, we want to go through with the procedure.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, here is my surgical scheduler's business card, give them a call, and they can walk you through everything.

reference_section: The patient is a 12-year-old boy born at a 32-week gestation and with drug exposure in utero.  The patient has diagnosis of autism as well.  The patient presented with bilateral knee flexion contractures, initially worse on right than left.  He had right distal medial hamstring release performed in February 2007 and has done quite well and has noted significant improvement in his gait and his ability to play.  The patient presents now with worsening left knee flexion contracture, and desires the same procedure to be performed.  Risks and benefits of the surgery were discussed.  The risks of surgery include risk of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of extremity, failure to restore normal anatomy, continued contracture, possible need for other procedures.  All questions were answered and mother and son agreed to above plan.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Good afternoon, who's the victim today, sir? Is it you, or your daughter?

turns.text: Before seeing me, have you seen anyone else?

turns.text: Yeah, we went to an Urgent Care and she had an x ray there.

turns.text: What else did they do?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have those x rays with you right now?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, I have them right here, take a look, please.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, these x rays show an incarcerated medial epicondyle fracture, as well as a mildly angulated radial shaft break.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What does that mean?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, in short, you broke the inside part of your elbow. In addition to the pain, do you have any burning or tingling feelings in that arm?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I do.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you have this before they tried to do a reduction?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I didn't, this is new.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is this feeling getting worse?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it is.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, guys, there is a lot of pressure on that ulnar nerve because of the break and the attempted reduction.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: What should we do?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We need to do an O R I F procedure A S A P. I'll reduce that radial shaft fracture at the same time.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: O R I F? What's that

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'll put some pins in the elbow, in order to stabilize the break, and we can start the healing process.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Will this not heal on its own?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No, we need to do the surgery.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, what are the risks of infection with the surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Historically, its less than one percent.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: How is this possible?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We use prophylactic antibiotics, this helps us control for infection the entire time.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Will she be asleep for this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, she won't feel a thing.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Will she need this hardware taken out in the future?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, in about a year or two, after everything is healed up nicely. The other risks include bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremity, and hardware failure. I see good results from my surgeries so I would not worry about these things, but I must disclose.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Okay, yes, we'd like to do the surgery.

reference_section: The patient is a 13-year-old right-hand dominant girl, who fell off a swing at school around 1:30 today.  The patient was initially seen at an outside facility and brought here by her father, given findings on x-ray, a closed reduction was attempted on the left elbow.  After the attempted reduction, the patient was noted to have an incarcerated medial epicondyle fracture as well as increasing ulnar paresthesias that were not present prior to the procedure.  Given this finding, the patient needed urgent open reduction and internal fixation to relieve the pressure on the ulnar nerve.  At that same time, the patient's mildly angulated radial shaft fracture will be reduced.  This was explained to the father.  The risks of surgery included the risk of anesthesia, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremity, hardware failure, need for later hardware removal, and possible continuous nerve symptoms.  All questions were answered.  The father agreed to the above plan.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

The patient states that she tripped over her dog toy and fell with her left foot inverted.  The patient states that she received a series of x-rays and MRIs that were unremarkable.  After approximately 1 month, the patient continued to have significant debilitating pain in her left ankle.  She then received a walking boot and has been in the boot for the past month.

turns.text: As for my mom, she had a long history of mini strokes. She didn't have any memory problems or dementia when she passed at eighty five. They believe she passed due to old age.

reference_section: Reportedly significant for TIAs in his mother, although the patient did not report this during our evaluation and so that she had no memory problems or dementia when she passed away of old age at the age of 85. turns.text: Hi, there.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi.

turns.text: Hi! It is nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It is nice to meet you as well. You are the husband, correct?

turns.text: Yes. I am the husband.

turns.text: Do you live in the same household?

turns.text: Yes.

turns.text: I would like your recommendations for both.

turns.text: Are you working currently?

turns.text: No, I am not. I used to work as a registered nurse. It has become too much for me right now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you drink alcohol or use any recreational drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't do any drugs. I drink very rarely. I only drink is social situations.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever taken any prescription drugs, muscle relaxants or sedative medications?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: I don't think that she has ever taken muscle relaxants or sedative medications without prescriptions. I give her, her medications every day so she doesn't forget.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, okay.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She does have a pattern of self-prescribing for minor illness. She loves WebMD.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. How have you been feeling lately? Have you been participating in social activities?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Since this last March I have been feeling more social and have been doing things on my own more.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She used to never leave the house unless I go with her. She has defiantly been more independent lately. She even went and met a friend for coffee the other day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is great to hear.

reference_section: The patient lives with her husband of 48 years.  She used to be employed as a registered nurse.  Her husband states that she does have a pattern of self-prescribing for minor illness, but does not think that she has ever taken muscle relaxants or sedative medications without prescriptions.  She rarely drinks socially.  She denies any illicit substance usage.  Her husband reportedly gives her medication daily.  Has been proactive in terms of seeking mental health care and medical care.  The patient and husband report that from March 2009, she has been relatively independent, more socially active.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello Miss Jane, how are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am good, thank you for asking.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, tell me what brings you here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have so many issues and problems, where do I start?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Start by telling the one troubling you the most.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have this pain in my toes on the right side and I also feel this numbness there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay and do you feel any tingling sensation? Or feeling like your leg is giving away?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I feel the tingling and sometimes. I feel like my leg has fallen asleep.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hm, tell me about your pain. Is it mild, moderate, or severe?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I will say it's moderate.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Would you define it as sharp shooting pain or dull kind of radiating pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe sharp pain but I am not sure how to describe it. But it radiates up the leg.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. How long have you had this problem?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's been there for almost one year but now it started to get worst.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see, does it get worse when you walk?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, mostly when I am in bed. And sometimes I feel it on my left toe as well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It looks like you have paresthesia in the toes of your right foot and I feel your left toe also has the same problem.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I thought so. I read over the internet. But anyways, I am also having this shoulder pain on both sides, plus I am not able to sleep at night.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have high blood pressure and hypothyroidism.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well-

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, that's not it. I have thrombo-

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thrombocythemia.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are your allergies by the way?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have no sinus allergies, thankfully.

reference_section: The patient is in with several medical problems.  She complains of numbness, tingling, and a pain in the toes primarily of her right foot described as a moderate pain.  She initially describes it as a sharp quality pain, but is unable to characterize it more fully.  She has had it for about a year, but seems to be worsening.  She has little bit of paraesthesias in the left toe as well and seem to involve all the toes of the right foot.  They are not worse with walking.  It seems to be worse when she is in bed.  There is some radiation of the pain up her leg.  She also continues to have bilateral shoulder pains without sinus allergies.  She has hypothyroidism.  She has thrombocythemia, insomnia, and hypertension.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Good afternoon, sir. Is this your mother?

turns.text: Good afternoon, doctor. Yes, this is my mom.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, please, give me some background information on your history.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I used to live here in the city when I went to college, but I wanted to get away from a bad crowd, so I came back to live with my mom.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you mean, bad crowd?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I got addicted to drugs out there, and I used to inject heroin.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you see a doctor for this addiction?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I saw another doctor in the city.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did they treat you at that time?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They prescribed me methadone for a while.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did that help at all?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Honestly, no, it didn't help at all.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you remember the dosage that you were given?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it was ten M G.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long did you take methadone for?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it was for three or four months.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you ever try to decrease your dosage?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, um, I tried to wean off it for a while, but I was never really successful.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been using heroin since?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, yeah, I've been using it occasionally.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Were you roommates at school using drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, so it's hard to get away from the stuff, it was all over the house.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Well, he can now, especially because he lives with me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, when was the last time you used heroin?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it's been about eight days now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, congratulations. When was the last time you had methadone?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it's been about a week for that now, too. Am I able to get more today?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We can discuss that. Have you had any feelings of depression recently?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, what about delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized thoughts or behaviors?

turns.text: No, nothing like that either, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medical conditions in the past that I should know about?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not that I know of.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No, he hasn't been treated for anything before, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You completed your family and social history earlier with the nurses, is there anything you want to add to that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, everything there is complete.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any allergies?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I don't have any.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, and do you take any medications right now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, doctor. I don't take anything.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any surgeries in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I voluntarily donated my left kidney.

reference_section: This patient presents to the office today with his mom for checkup.  He used to live in the city.  He used to go to college down in the city.  He got addicted to drugs.  He decided it would be a good idea to get away from the "bad crowd" and come up and live with his mom.  He has a history of doing heroin.  He was injecting into his vein.  He was seeing a physician in the city.  They were prescribing methadone for some time.  He says that did help.  He was on 10 mg of methadone.  He was on it for three to four months.  He tried to wean down on the methadone a couple of different times, but failed.  He has been intermittently using heroin.  He says one of the big problems is that he lives in a household full of drug users and he could not get away from it.  All that changed now that he is living with his mom.  The last time he did heroin was about seven to eight days ago.  He has not had any methadone in about a week either.  He is coming in today specifically requesting methadone.  He also admits to being depressed.  He is sad a lot and down.  He does not have much energy.  He does not have the enthusiasm.  He denies any suicidal or homicidal ideations at the present time.  I questioned him on the symptoms of bipolar disorder and he does not seem to have those symptoms.  His past medical history is significant for no medical problems.  Surgical history, he voluntarily donated his left kidney.  Family and social history were reviewed per the nursing notes.  His allergies are no known drug allergies.  Medications, he takes no medications regularly.

reference_section: The patient comes in for a neurology consultation regarding her difficult headaches, tunnel vision, and dizziness.  I obtained and documented a full history and physical examination.  I reviewed the new patient questionnaire, which she completed prior to her arrival today.  I also reviewed the results of tests, which she had brought with her. Briefly, she is a 60-year-old woman initially from Ukraine, who had headaches since age 25.  She recalls that in 1996 when her husband died her headaches became more frequent.  They were pulsating.  She was given papaverine, which was successful in reducing the severity of her symptoms.  After six months of taking papaverine, she no longer had any headaches.  In 2004, her headaches returned.  She also noted that she had "zig-zag lines" in her vision.  Sometimes she would not see things in her peripheral visions.  She had photophobia and dizziness, which was mostly lightheadedness.  On one occasion she almost had a syncope.  Again she has started taking Russian medications, which did help her.  The dizziness and headaches have become more frequent and now occur on average once to twice per week.  They last two hours since she takes papaverine, which stops the symptoms within 30 minutes.

turns.text: I am having this chest pain. I was hospitalized last year in October and at that time they put this catheter in my heart. I also underwent a heart scan. It's here in this report.

turns.text: Yeah, I see that you got nuclear and myocardial perfusion scan, which was normal. They were looking for some heart artery lesion but then it was thought to be due to spasm.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It is also mentioned here that you have hyperlipidemia.

turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: Hyperlipidemia, smoking history, and chest pain.  He has been, in October of last year, hospitalized.  Subsequently underwent cardiac catheterization.  The left system was normal.  There was a question of a right coronary artery lesion, which was thought to be spasm.  Subsequently, the patient did undergo nuclear and myocardial perfusion scan, which was normal.  The patient continues to smoke actively since in last 3 to 4 days especially when he is stressed.  No relation to exertional activity.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Tell me what brings you here today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm having some issues with my right hand.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of issues?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm having these pins and needles kind of feeling in my hand and it has been going on for several weeks. Sometimes I feel it gets numb. I think it might be carpal tunnel, but I'm not sure. I'm just worried.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you do anything for it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: At work I recently moved my keyboard down. I just hope it will help. You know, I do a lot of the same kind of activities all the time. All of it I typing based.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What is more difficult, day or night?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It gets worse at night. If I sleep on it, like in a certain way, it will just wake me up and it starts hurting. These tingling sensations are the worst. It helps if I shake it then the sensation goes away. It irritates me all the time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is it complete hand or is there any part of hand that is worse than others?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It is mostly my middle finger, but maybe my first or second finger of the hand also, but mostly my middle finger.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there pain anywhere else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: In my thumb as well. I'm just afraid it can be arthritis. I don't want that, too, on my plate.

reference_section: This patient presents to the office today because of some problems with her right hand.  It has been going tingling and getting numb periodically over several weeks.  She just recently moved her keyboard down at work.  She is hoping that will help.  She is worried about carpal tunnel.  She does a lot of repetitive type activities.  It is worse at night.  If she sleeps on it a certain way, she will wake up and it will be tingling then she can usually shake out the tingling, but nonetheless it is very bothersome for her.  It involves mostly the middle finger, although, she says it also involves the first and second digits on the right hand.  She has some pain in her thumb as well.  She thinks that could be arthritis.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: He had a broken ankle in the past.  They questioned the patient who is a truck driver whether he has had an auto accident in the past, he said that he has not had anything major. turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you feeling?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've been having a lot more joint pain lately.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You're seventy seven, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Don't remind me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did you first start experiencing joint pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Couple years ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: In what ways has it worsened?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's caused me to become less active in general. My hands and wrists aren't as mobile.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you noticed any increased swelling?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, but it's all gotten to be a little too uncomfortable.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see here that you take the generic of Daypro. Is that helping?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And no redness to the area, right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Fever or chills?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had diarrhea for a few days, but it's gotten much better. I was also having trouble holding my bladder.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you going to the bathroom more often, experiencing excessive thirst, or other problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. My incontinence is a bit better and so is my ankle and foot swelling.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How has your blood sugar been?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: A little better.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you checked your blood pressure recently?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not recently.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any new medications?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm back on Zoloft again because I think I might be depressed. Ever since losing most of my mobility, I haven't been feeling like my usual myself. I'm also sleeping all the time.

reference_section: A 77-year-old white female who is having more problems with joint pain.  It seems to be all over decreasing her mobility, hands and wrists.  No real swelling but maybe just a little more uncomfortable than they have been.  The Daypro generic does not seem to be helping at all.  No fever or chills.  No erythema. She actually is doing better.  Her diarrhea now has settled down and she is having less urinary incontinence, less pedal edema.  Blood sugars seem to be little better as well. The patient also has gotten back on her Zoloft because she thinks she may be depressed, sleeping all the time, just not herself and really is disturbed that she cannot be more mobile in things.  She has had no polyuria, polydipsia, or other problems.  No recent blood pressure checks.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I feel very weak and tired, don't feel like doing anything but resting.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any fever?

turns.text: Yeah, nurse just took my temperature it was one hundred point three.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Did you have these symptoms before?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am twenty eight.

turns.text: Yes, almost one year ago. I lost about two hundred pounds after that.

turns.text: And you felt well after the surgery?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Absolutely! Until yesterday when my nausea and pain started.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: The patient is a 28-year-old, who is status post gastric bypass surgery nearly one year ago.  He has lost about 200 pounds and was otherwise doing well until yesterday evening around 7:00-8:00 when he developed nausea and right upper quadrant pain, which apparently wrapped around toward his right side and back.  He feels like he was on it but has not done so.  He has overall malaise and a low-grade temperature of 100.3.  He denies any prior similar or lesser symptoms.  His last normal bowel movement was yesterday.  He denies any outright chills or blood per rectum.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Okay, so it looks like your blood work shows that your sodium levels are very low. This could explain some of the symptoms you've been having lately.

turns.text: It could be due to a number of-

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good morning, ma'am. Can you tell me more about this low back pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I'm not as young as I used to be, I'm fifty nine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What set this pain off? Is there any injury?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I had a fall in the beginning of two thousand six. I slipped on a freshly waxed floor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What part of your lower back did you fall onto?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I fell onto my tailbone and just general lower back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is this the only fall you've had?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I had another one in March of two thousand six.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What happened when you fell that time?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What made you lose your footing?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.text: What treatments have you had for this?

turns.text: This was in two thousand eight, right?

turns.text: Correct. The P T said I have low back pain and degenerative disc disease.

reference_section: The patient is a 59-year-old female, who was referred to Physical Therapy, secondary to low back pain and degenerative disk disease.  The patient states she has had a cauterization of some sort to the nerves in her low back to help alleviate with painful symptoms.  The patient states that this occurred in October 2008 as well as November 2008.  The patient has a history of low back pain, secondary to a fall that originally occurred in 2006.  The patient states that she slipped on a newly waxed floor and fell on her tailbone and low back region.  The patient then had her second fall in March 2006.  The patient states that she was qualifying on the range with a handgun and lost her footing and states that she fell more due to weakness in her lower extremities rather than loss of balance.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good morning, ma'am. Just to confirm, you're thirty two years old, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, doctor, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, so, have you been able to get a P C P yet?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I haven't gotten one just yet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you in the process of getting one?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, Project Access is trying to find me one.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, um, what seems to be the problem today, then?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I was at Doctor X Y Z's office today, I had an appointment, but they cancelled me because I don't have the Project Access insurance yet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see, what were you going to see Doctor X Y Z for?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm having a lot of pain in my foot.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, have you seen Doctor X Y Z before?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I saw him on May fourteenth two thousand four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: But you still don't have a P C P, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, we've seen you quite a few times in here. You were in here last week and saw Doctor X Y Z for some back pain, how did they treat you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I got some pain medicines and muscle relaxers.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, so, can you tell me more about your foot, please?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I have this pain in my foot, and I had surgery before so there's plates and screws in it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever talked to anyone about removing this hardware?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I was supposed to see Doctor X Y Z about it, but since that appointment was cancelled, I came here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see, how long have you had this foot pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it started hurting a lot yesterday.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there any injury here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, it's just chronically painful, honestly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do any activities bother it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I can't exercise without a lot of pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see, well, we've x rayed this before, and I see the hardware in there, but there's no apparent abnormality or evidence of loosening, at least from what I can see.

reference_section: This 32-year-old female comes in again still having not got a primary care physician.  She said she was at Dr. XYZ office today for her appointment, and they cancelled her appointment because she has not gotten her Project Access insurance into affect.  She says that Project Access is trying to find her a doctor.  She is not currently on Project Access, and so she is here to get something for the pain in her foot.  I did notice that she went in to see Dr. XYZ for a primary care physician on 05/14/2004.  She said she does not have a primary care physician.  She was in here just last week and saw Dr. XYZ for back pain and was put on pain medicines and muscle relaxers.  She has been in here multiple times for different kinds of pain.  This pain she is having is in her foot.  She had surgery on it, and she has plates and screws.  She said she was suppose to see Dr. XYZ about getting some of the hardware out of it.  The appointment was cancelled, and that is why she came here.  It started hurting a lot yesterday, but she had this previous appointment with Dr. XYZ so she thought she would take care of it there, but they would not see her.  She did not injure her foot in any way recently.  It is chronically painful.  Every time she does very much exercise it hurts more.  We have x-rayed it in the past.  She has some hardware there.  It does not appear to be grossly abnormal or causing any loosening or problems on x-ray.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, sir. I see you're being seen for an evaluation for your allergy. Can you please confirm your age?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that's right. Thirty four.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let me take a look at your medical records. I see you were treated at the A B C Medical Center for an allergic reaction, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. I was rushed to the hospital that day. After, they told me to get checked for a follow up.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Who told you to have a follow up?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: One of the E R doctors and the kidney doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Your records indicate you had some swelling around the eye on May third of two thousand and eight. The cause was unknown. I see you were transferred from A B C Medical Center to X Y Z Medical center that day.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that sounds about right. Were there more details about that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yeah, there is. It says here you have a history of renal failure, so you needed dialysis. They believe the allergic reaction was due to this medicine called, Keflex, which was used during your dialysis treatment. Does that name ring a bell?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, it does. I forgot why they gave it to me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Usually, Keflex is used to treat a skin cellulitis dialysis shunt infection.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, I see.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I would like to ask you more about your allergies. What would you say you're allergic to?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've had a lot of problems with grass and sometimes pollen.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. I'll put that down as grass allergies, and environmental and inhalant allergies. Do you have any life-threatening allergic reactions?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope. Never had that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had any swelling under the skin due to something you ate or touched?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope. Never had that either.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's great. I'm taking a look at your medications. I see you aren't taking anything for your allergies, but you are taking Atenolol. Do you have high blood pressure?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I do.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. All that's left from your report are the treatments they gave you before you were discharged from the hospital.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What were the treatments they gave me?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Looks like they monitored you the whole time and gave you some corticosteroid therapy and antihistamine therapy. You didn't have any additional problems as well.

reference_section: A 34-year-old male presents today self-referred at the recommendation of Emergency Room physicians and his nephrologist to pursue further allergy evaluation and treatment.  Please refer to chart for history and physical, as well as the medical records regarding his allergic reaction treatment at ABC Medical Center for further details and studies.  In summary, the patient had an acute event of perioral swelling, etiology uncertain, occurring on 05/03/2008 requiring transfer from ABC Medical Center to XYZ Medical Center due to a history of renal failure requiring dialysis and he was admitted and treated and felt that his allergy reaction was to Keflex, which was being used to treat a skin cellulitis dialysis shunt infection.  In summary, the patient states he has some problems with tolerating grass allergies, environmental and inhalant allergies occasionally, but has never had anaphylactic or angioedema reactions.  He currently is not taking any medication for allergies.  He is taking atenolol for blood pressure control.  No further problems have been noted upon his discharge and treatment, which included corticosteroid therapy and antihistamine therapy and monitoring.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: You must be so proud of your boys.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.text: Go for it.

turns.text: Do you drink or smoke?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Nice. How's the family doing? Are they all well?

turns.text: Yeah, they're doing great. Nobody has been sick for a while.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, you and your husband live together, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. It's a miracle we've lasted this long.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Can't argue that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you able to walk any distance without assistance?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She's most comfortable in her wheelchair, but she usually walks with a walker if she's at home.

turns.text: Yeah, he's right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And how often do you walk with your walker?

turns.text: Great.

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: If I'm nearby, I like to keep any eye on her incase she feels unstable and needs help sitting back down.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's good that you're both looking out for each other. Now moving onto the last few questions. Do you smoke or drink?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No and no.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you smoke or drink in the past?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You do not look so well today. What seems to be the problem?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well‚ I am having a hard time. My whole body aches and I am in pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have a history of drug use?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well yes. I am detoxing.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of drugs have you been using?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Heroin.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. How long have you been using?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't feel well. Maybe a year. I can't sleep or eat.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had a fever, chills, vomiting or diarrhea?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think I have a fever. I feel chilled. I have had some diarrhea.
