turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How would you rate your general health?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've been in reasonably good health at least physically. I try to go on frequent walks and eat a clean diet. However, there was one instance where I was not well mentally. After my husband died in nineteen seventy five, I had what I believe was a nervous breakdown. As a result of this, I was hospitalized for several weeks and treated with E C T.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm so sorry to hear about the loss of your husband. I can't imagine how difficult that must've been. I'm glad that you sought the care that you needed to feel better at that time. Did this happen when you were living in the United States or Korea?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: This all happened when I was living in Korea. I'm grateful that I had my family and friends to support me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Social support is very important, especially when you are processing the loss of a loved one.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I have a few more questions before we move on. Any past medical problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I used to have high blood pressure.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When you say used to, do you mean it's been resolved now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great news. How about surgeries? Have you had any in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: None whatsoever.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any alcohol or tobacco?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I stay away from things like that.

reference_section: The patient has generally been in reasonably good physical health.  She did have a "nervous breakdown" in 1975 after the death of her husband.  She was hospitalized for several weeks and was treated with ECT.  This occurred while she was living in Korea. She does not smoke or drink alcoholic beverages.  She has had no prior surgeries.  There is a past history of hypertension, but this is no longer present.

turns.text: Yes, I had an M R I not too long ago, can you take a look? I have it right here.

turns.text: Thank you, yes, um, this M R I shows that you've torn that rotator cuff again.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh no, can we do another surgery to repair it again?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, we'll have to.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What's the risk of infection of the surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Its less than one percent. We'll use antibiotics to control for infection the entire time.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Will I be asleep again?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, you won't feel a thing.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Great, yes, I'd like to go forward with the surgery. I need to get back to playing tennis.

reference_section: This is a 62-year-old female who previously underwent a repair of rotator cuff.  She continued to have pain within the shoulder.  She had a repeat MRI performed, which confirmed the clinical diagnosis of re-tear of the rotator cuff.  She wished to proceed with a repair.  All risks and benefits of the surgery were discussed with her at length.  She was in agreement with the above treatment plan.

When she awoke, the symptoms had resolved. On 1/13/93 she had an episode of right arm numbness lasting 4-5hours. There was no associated weakness, HA, dysarthria, dysphagia, visual change, vertigo or lightheadedness.

turns.text: Hello, doctor. Let me give you a run down as to what we are dealing with today. This patient was last seen in January two thousand and four. She is coming for a follow up on interstitial disease secondary to lupus pneumonitis. I will let her tell you more about what happened yesterday.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thanks, nurse. How are you feeling today, miss? Welcome back to the Pulmonary Medicine Clinic. What happened yesterday?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I was doing fine since last time. My respiratory issues have been great and I have had no major difficulties breathing.

turns.text: That's good to hear. What happened yesterday that caused you to want to come in so urgently?

turns.text: Are you experiencing any coughing?

turns.text: Have you been producing any mucus the times that you do cough?

turns.text: Do you have any other symptoms currently?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I do notice that I am more tired than usual.

turns.text: During physical activity do you seem out of breath or more tired than usual? I want to see if your pulmonary system is inhibited.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I don't have issues with breathing when I do daily activities.

reference_section: The patient returns to the Pulmonary Medicine Clinic for followup evaluation of interstitial disease secondary to lupus pneumonitis.  She was last seen in the Pulmonary Medicine Clinic in January 2004.  Since that time, her respiratory status has been quite good.  She has had no major respiratory difficulties; however, starting yesterday she began with increasing back and joint pain and as a result a deep breath has caused some back discomfort.  She denies any problems with cough or sputum production.  No fevers or chills.  Recently, she has had a bit more problems with fatigue.  For the most part, she has had no pulmonary limitations to her activity.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Hello sir, it's been a while since your last visit. How have you been?

turns.text: Hello doctor, yes, I have come a long way. I guess last time I was here was in two thousand and two if I am not wrong. Was does your system say?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You are right! It was August second of two thousand and two to be very precise.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Please confirm for the records, you are a white married man and must be forty nine years old now. Am I right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: You got it all right doctor!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you still working in that airplane company?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes sir, still with Alaska Airlines but I have been promoted and work as a plane mechanic.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That is so nice! Good for you man! So, tell me how can I help you today? What brought you to our dermatology department today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm having pain in my stomach on the right side and down here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is it only on the right side or anywhere else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It is on both sides and now I can feel it on the middle part of my left thigh as well.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Tell me more about it. How did it start? When did you first notice it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's been going on and off. It was not there for a while, but now it is like back again mainly on my tummy, down here. It is painful when I touch it. At first, I thought maybe I'm having shingles.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When did you notice it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It all started before the holidays, I think one and a half months before the holidays. It is still going on for the past eight days in my tummy and the hips mainly on the right side.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you get any treatment for this? Any over the counter medicines?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, as I told you I thought it was shingles, but then there was no change in the skin, no rashes, nothing. I was not sure what to take.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, do you bathe every day?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I do but I try to use as little soap as possible.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, here is what I think, all your symptoms are pointing towards hyperesthesia. I would like to run some tests to find the underlying cause and then we will start the treatment. A nurse will come and take you to the lab. Does this sound good to you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

reference_section: This 49-year-old white male, established patient in dermatology, last seen in the office on 08/02/2002, comes in today for initial evaluation of a hyperesthesia on his right abdomen, then on his left abdomen, then on his left medial thigh.  It cleared for awhile.  This has been an intermittent problem.  Now it is back again on his right lower abdomen.  At first, it was thought that he may have early zoster.  This started six weeks before the holidays and is still going on, more so in the past eight days on his abdomen and right hip area.  He has had no treatment on this; there are no skin changes at all.  The patient bathes everyday but tries to use little soap.  The patient is married.  He works as an airplane mechanic.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Did you have surgery after the accident?

turns.text: Yes I did, I had two arthroscopies, and an, um, patellar replacement after those.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, yes, I see.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any imaging of this knee?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, so this M R I from September two thousand six shows some nonspecific edema anterior to the patellar tendon, but thankfully there's no evidence of fracture of ligamentous avulsion or abnormality.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, thank you, that's good.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh certainly, yes, it is. What treatments have you had for this knee, aside from surgery?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, it goes down my, is this the femur?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, that's the femur.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you having any back pain?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does anything make your knee pain worse?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about this, this is the fibular head, which is where you feel the pins and needles. I'm applying pretty heavy pressure here, how would you describe what you're feeling?

turns.text: Um, numbness, tingling, and then that same pins and needles feeling.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is there any instability?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's certainly a possibility. How would you describe your pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'd say its constant, shooting, cramping, aching, throbbing, feels like it's being pulled, sharp, and , um, stabbing. All of those words seem fitting.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, does the pain wake you up at night?

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about at its worst?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Easily, its ten out of ten.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Finally, what about when the pain is at its least?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, when it's not too bad, I'd say it's a three out of ten. I also have this other M R I report from September of O six, here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thanks. I see. They said that there is nonspecific edema anterior to the patellar tendon, but there is no acute fracture or any ligament abnormalities. That's good.

reference_section: Ms. XYZ is an otherwise fairly healthy 44-year-old right-handed aircraft mechanic.  On her date of injury, she reports that she was working on an aircraft when she fell between the airplane and a stand with about an 18-inch gap in between.  She injured her left knee and underwent two arthroscopic procedures followed by patellar replacement and subsequently a left total knee arthroplasty in Month DD, YYYY. The patient is seen with no outside images, but an MRI report of the left knee and office notes from Dr. ABCD. The patient reports that she has undergone a full course of physical therapy and complains primarily of pain in the anterior aspect of the left knee and primarily over the medial and lateral tibial components with pain extending proximally to the distal femur and distally down into the anterior tibial plateau area.  She has intermittent numbness and tingling in the posterolateral thigh and no symptoms at all into her feet.  She has axial low back pain as an ancillary symptom.  Her pain is worse with walking and is associated with swelling, popping and grinding.  She complains of pins and needles sensation over the area of the common peroneal nerve overlying the fibular head.  She has no dysesthetic or allodynic symptoms with light touch over the remainder of the knee and the femoral nerve area.  Heavy pressure and light percussion of the fibular head produce painful numbness, tingling, and pins and needles sensation. The patient underwent a left knee MRI in September of 2006 revealing nonspecific edema anterior to the patellar tendon, but no evidence of an acute fracture or a femoropatellar ligament avulsion or abnormality.  She has continued to complain of persistent instability and pain.  She is not working.  She has a number of allergies to different pain medications and feels that her back has been bothersome mostly due to her gait disturbances relating to her knee.  Her pain is described as constant, shooting, cramping, aching, throbbing, pulling, sharp, and stabbing in nature.  It occasionally awakens her at night.  It is better in recumbency with her leg elevated.   Exacerbating factors include standing, walking, pushing, puling.  VAS pain scale is rated as 6/10 for her average and current pain, 10/10 for worst pain, and 3/10 for her least pain.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm eighty six years old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What gender do you identify with?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long have you had this back and buttock pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Its been a while, now. I know I have a fracture in my lower back.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How have you been managing this?

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: This C T Scan you had recently shows sclerosis, with some healing of a L five compression fracture, but if you look here, the healing is not complete.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What can we do about this? I'm in so much pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I believe you'd be a candidate for a bilateral L five kyphoplasty.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What's that?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's a small procedure on that L five vertebra. Its minimally invasive, and we can actually do it as an outpatient procedure.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, wow, that's good to hear. What are the risks of infection?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Very low, historically, they're less than one percent.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: How is this possible?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We'll use antibiotics in order to control for infection.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's great, will I be under anesthesia?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, you'll be asleep for the whole thing.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Great, yes, I'd like to have this done, I can't keep living in this pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Awesome, I agree. Do you have control over your bladder and bowel movements?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, thankfully, I have complete control over everything like that still.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you wear a brace or corset normally?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I usually wear both.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, last question, can you notice any weakness in your body?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I'm still very strong, even at my age.

reference_section: The patient is to come to the hospital for bilateral L5 kyphoplasty.  The patient is an 86-year-old female with an L5 compression fracture. The patient has a history of back and buttock pain for some time.  She was found to have an L5 compression fracture.  She was treated conservatively over several months, but did not improve.  Unfortunately, she has continued to have significant ongoing back pain and recent CT scan has shown a sclerosis with some healing of her L5 compression fracture, but without complete healing.  The patient has had continued pain and at this time, is felt to be a candidate for kyphoplasty. She denies bowel or bladder incontinence.  She does complain of back pain.  She has been wearing a back brace and corset.  She does not have weakness.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient is an 18-year-old girl brought in by her father today for evaluation of a right knee injury.  She states that approximately 3 days ago while playing tennis she had a non-contact injury in which she injured the right knee.  She had immediate pain and swelling.  At this time, she complains of pain and instability in the knee.  The patient's past medical history is significant for having had an ACL injury to the knee in 2008.  She underwent anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction by Dr. X at that time, subsequently in the same year she developed laxity of the graft due in part to noncompliance and subsequently, she sought attention from Dr. Y who performed a revision ACL reconstruction at the end of 2008.  The patient states she rehabbed the knee well after that and did fine with good stability of the knee until this recent injury.

reference_section: The patient is an 11-month-old with neuroblastoma, which initially presented on the left when he was 6 weeks old and was completely resected.  It was felt to be stage 2.  It was not N-Myc amplified and had favorable Shimada histology.  In followup, he was found to have a second primary in his right adrenal gland, which was biopsied and also consistent with neuroblastoma with favorable Shimada histology.  He is now being treated with chemotherapy per protocol P9641 and not on study.  He last received chemotherapy on 05/21/07, with carboplatin, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin.  He received G-CSF daily after his chemotherapy due to neutropenia that delayed his second cycle.  In the interval since he was last seen, his mother reports that he had a couple of days of nasal congestion, but it is now improving.  He is not acted ill or had any fevers.  He has had somewhat diminished appetite, but it seems to be improving now.  He is peeing and pooping normally and has not had any diarrhea.  He did not have any appreciated nausea or vomiting.  He has been restarted on fluconazole due to having redeveloped thrush recently.

reference_section: The patient is a 32-year-old male seen by Dr. ABC several weeks ago for persistent left hip pain.  He has a long eight to ten year history of pain into the left hip.  He has been worked up by several specialists and evaluated.  He was thought initially to have low back pain with radiculopathy.  He does have a history of antibiotic steroid use as well as heavy drinking.  He reports his symptoms started approximately eight years ago when he was doing some construction at which time he began to have left hip pain.  He has had difficulties on and off ever since then.  On the last visit, radiographs revealed severe degenerative changes of the left hip joint with apparent AVN of the left femoral head.  He was given some pain medication and discussion took place regarding referring him to a specialist for evaluation of possible hip resurfacing versus conventional total hip replacement.  He came for a second opinion in the area and we discussed his problems further.  He continues to have primarily groin pain, which limits his daily activities.  He has used a cane in the past for a short period and he continues to have difficulty with the left hip.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello, miss. Doctor X and I will be going over your medical history with you. Before we begin, could you confirm your age for me?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm twenty five years old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you. Doctor X, could you go over the diagnosis of erythema nodosum? Doctor_2: She was diagnosed in two thousand and four after a biopsy was done that confirmed erythema nodosum, but the detail from the Netherlands is not that specific.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What kind of procedures were done to address it? Doctor_2: She had undergone a colonoscopy to address secondary diseases that may have been present because of the erythema nodosum, correct miss?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Were there any findings, Doctor X? Doctor_2: The findings were uncertain if the terminal ileum had abnormal biopsies. However, the skin biopsy mentioned some fibrosis, basal proliferation, and inflammatory cells in the subcutis.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Her report states something about a tibia and fibula fracture on her right leg before the erythema nodosum. Are these skin lesions due to the fracture? Doctor_2: The skin lesions are not associated with the fracture, correct ma'am?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's correct. The cuts in my skins are on both legs too. Not just the right.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you. Did anything occur before the skin lesions? Doctor_2: She had cosmetic surgery done on her jaw.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ma'am, I see you visited our clinic and the Dermatology several times, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that's correct. I had a rash that I wanted to get checked. Doctor_2: I remember that. I was here when she presented the rash. We suggested the rash in her lower extremities and ankles was erythema nodosum. She also had discomfort, which could have been inflammatory arthritis.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Doctor X, did you confirm with any tests? Doctor_2: Yes. There was an initial S E D above one hundred and ten and her C P R was increased.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great. In the visits after, were there any other problems found? Doctor_2: The reports says that no other abnormalities were found. However, I do see something about her first visit.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Could you explain what it says? Doctor_2: She has some M T P detected, which could have been signs of erythema nodosum. However, the Dermatology did not agree, and they believed it to be venous stasis.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The venous stasis could have been related to the fracture, right? Doctor_2: That is correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Her initial visit reports suspicion of I B D, sarcoid inflammatory arthropathy, and lupus. Why was that? Doctor_2: She had a questionable rheumatoid fracture even though her C C P was negative. Her A N A was positive at one to four zero. There was a persistent speckled pattern. However, the rest of the lupus serologies were negative.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What lupus serologies were used? Doctor_2: Double stranded D N A, R N P, Smith, R O, and L A were used.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did her cardiolipin antibodies panel look? Doctor_2: They were all negative. We made sure I g M, I g G, and I g A were less than ten.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Was there anything else in the report? Doctor_2: She had her beta 2 glycoprotein one or R V V T tested.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That seems important because of the livedo pattern. Doctor_2: Exactly. That's why they concluded it was an onset of lupus and not rheumatoid arthritis because the arthritis couldn't be associated with erythema nodosum.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Why did she undergo a C T scan? Doctor_2: We feared she had lymphoma. The scan of her chest, abdomen, and pelvis were done to rule out sarcoid.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. The results came out normal, right? Doctor_2: That's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you change some of you habits to help your bowels, ma'am?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I tried my best to.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's good. What was found Doctor X? Doctor_2: There was evidence of B twelve deficiency with a high methylmalonic and high homocystine levels along with a low normal B twelve in addition to iron studies consistent with iron deficiency and an initially low M C V.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That gives the possibility of inflammatory bowel disease, right? Doctor_2: Correct. That's stated in the report.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Were there any tests done to confirm this? Doctor_2: She underwent a colonoscopy, which showed nothing. Her endoscopy was also normal. Recently, she underwent a second coloscopy, and no evidence of inflammatory bowel disease was seen after viewing it microscopically.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Nothing was seen microscopically? Doctor_2: Actually, we determined there were aggregates of eosinophils.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That sounds important. That could be due to an allergic reaction or an emergence of Crohn Disease. I will have to discuss with Doctor Y from Gastroenterology to see the significance.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Could I interrupt for a second? I don't think my B twelve and iron deficiency were looked at while I stayed in the United States.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is that correct, Doctor X? Doctor_2: That is. I think these details were from somewhere else.

turns.speaker: doctor

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We did find a heart murmur, so we will conduct an echocardiogram. Doctor X, could you confirm all the details form the workup, please? Doctor_2: Of course. Her A C E levels were normal. Her sed rate was around 30, which was high. Before that, it was around one ten, which is even higher. Her R V V T was normal. The rheumatoid factor was negative. The urinalysis was also normal. She had a C R P level of two point three, which was high. Her C C P came out negative. Her C B C displayed microcytosis and hypochromia with hematocrit levels of thirty seven point seven. Her hematocrit levels improved to forty point three later on, and she did not have any hypochromia, microcytosis, or anemia present.

turns.speaker: patient

reference_section: This is a 25-year-old woman who is attending psychology classes.  She was diagnosed with presumptive erythema nodosum in 2004 based on a biopsy consistent with erythema nodosum, but not entirely specific back in Netherlands.  At that point, she had undergone workup which was extensive for secondary diseases associated with erythema nodosum.  Part of her workup included a colonoscopy.  The findings were equivocal characterizes not clearly abnormal biopsies of the terminal ileum. The skin biopsy, in particular, mentions some fibrosis, basal proliferation, and inflammatory cells in the subcutis. Prior to the onset of her erythema nodosum, she had a tibia-fibula fracture several years before on the right, which was not temporarily associated with the skin lesions, which are present in both legs anyway.  Even, a jaw cosmetic surgery she underwent was long before she started developing her skin lesions.  She was seen in our clinic and by Dermatology on several occasions.  Apart from the first couple of visits when she presented stating a recurrent skin rash with a description suggestive of erythema nodosum in the lower extremities and ankle and there is discomfort pointing towards a possible inflammatory arthritis and an initial high sed rate of above 110 with an increased CRP.  In the following visits, no evident abnormality has been detected.  In the first visit, here some MTP discomfort detected.  It was thought that erythema nodosum may be present.  However, the evaluation of Dermatology did not concur and it was thought that the patient had venous stasis, which could be related to her prior fracture.  When she was initially seen here, a suspicion of IBD, sarcoid inflammatory arthropathy, and lupus was raised.  She had an equivocal rheumatoid fracture, but her CCP was negative.  She had an ANA, which was positive at 1:40 with a speckled pattern persistently, but the rest of the lupus serologies including double-stranded DNA, RNP, Smith, Ro, La were negative.  Her cardiolipin panel antibodies were negative as well.  We followed the IgM, IgG, and IgA being less than 10.  However, she did have a beta-2 glycoprotein 1 or an RVVT tested and this may be important since she has a livedo pattern.  It was thought that the onset of lupus may be the case.  It was thought that rheumatoid arthritis could not be the case since it is not associated with erythema nodosum.  For the fear of possible lymphoma, she underwent CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.  It was done also in order to rule out sarcoid and the result was unremarkable.  Based on some changes in her bowel habits and evidence of B12 deficiency with a high methylmalonic and high homocystine levels along with a low normal B12 in addition to iron studies consistent with iron deficiency and an initially low MCV, the possibility of inflammatory bowel disease was employed.  The patient underwent an initially unrevealing colonoscopy and a capsule endoscopy, which was normal.  A second colonoscopy was done recently and microscopically no evidence of inflammatory bowel disease was seen.  However, eosinophil aggregations were noted in microscopy and this was told to be consistent with an allergic reaction or an emerging Crohn disease and I will need to discuss with Gastroenterology what is the significance of that.  Her possible B12 deficiency and iron deficiency were never addressed during her stay here in the United States. In the initial appointment, she was placed on prednisone 40 mg, which was gradually titrated down this led to an exacerbation of her acne.  We decided to take her off prednisone due to adverse effects and start her on colchicine 0.6 mg daily.  While this kept things under control with the inflammatory markers being positive and no overt episodes of erythema nodosum, the patient still complains for sensitivity with less suspicious skin rash in the lower extremities and occasional ankle swelling and pain.  She was reevaluated by Dermatology for that and no evidence of erythema nodosum was felt to be present.  Out plan was to proceed with a DEXA scan, at some point check a vitamin D level, and order vitamin D and calcium over the counter for bone protection purposes.  However, the later was deferred until we have resolved the situation and find out what is the underlying cause of her disease. Her past medical history apart from the tibia-fibular fracture and the jaw cosmetic surgery is significant for varicella and mononucleosis. Her physical examination had shown consistently diffuse periarticular ankle edema and also venous stasis changes at least until I took over her care last August.  I have not been able to detect any erythema nodosum, however, a livedo pattern has been detected consistently.  She also has evidence of acne, which does not seem to be present at the moment.  She also was found to have a heart murmur present and we are going to proceed with an echocardiogram placed. Her workup during the initial appointment included an ACE level, which was normal.  She also had a rather higher sed rate up to 30, but prior to that, per report, it was even higher, above 110.  Her RVVT was normal, her rheumatoid factor was negative.  Her ANA was 1:40, speckled pattern.  The double-stranded DNA was negative.  Her RNP and Smith were negative as well.  RO and LA were negative and cardiolipin antibodies were negative as well.  A urinalysis at the moment was completely normal.  A CRP was 2.3 in the initial appointment, which was high.  A CCP was negative.  Her CBC had shown microcytosis and hypochromia with a hematocrit of 37.7.  This improved later without any evidence of hypochromia, microcytosis or anemia with a hematocrit of 40.3. The patient returns here today, as I mentioned, complaining of milder bouts of skin rash, which she calls erythema nodosum, which is accompanied by arthralgias, especially in the ankles.  I am mentioning here that photosensitivity rash was mentioned in the past.  She tells me that she had it twice back in Europe after skiing where her whole face was swollen.  Her acne has been very stable after she was taken off prednisone and was started on colchicine 0.6 daily.  Today we discussed about the effect of colchicine on a possible pregnancy.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient is a 79-year-old right-handed man who reports that approximately one and a half years ago, he fell down while walking in the living room from the bedroom.  At that time, he reports both legs gave away on him and he fell.  He reported that he had some lightheadedness just before he fell and was slightly confused, but was aware of what was happening around him.  He was able to get up shortly after falling and according to the patient and his son, subsequently returned back to normal. He was then well until the 3rd of July 2008 when his legs again gave way on him.  This was not preceded by lightheadedness.  He was rushed to the hospital and was found to have pneumonia, and the fall was blamed on the pneumonia.  He started using a walker from that time, prior to that he was able to walk approximately two miles per day.  He again had a fall in August of 2008 after his legs gave way.  Again, there was no lightheadedness associated with this.  He was again found to have pneumonia and again was admitted to hospital after which he went to rehabilitation and was able to use his walker again after this.  He did not, however, return to the pre-July baseline.  In October of 2008, after another fall, he was found to have pneumonia again and shingles.  He is currently in a Chronic Rehabilitation Unit.  He cannot use a walker and uses a wheelchair for everything.  He states that his hands have been numb, involving all the fingers of both hands for the past three weeks.  He is also losing muscle bulk in his hands and has noticed some general weakness of his hands.  He does, however, note that strength in his hands has not been normal since July 2008, but it is clearly getting worse.  He has been aware of some fasciculations in his legs starting in August 2008, these are present both in the lower legs and the thighs.  He does not report any cramps, problems with swallowing or problems with breathing.  He reports that he has had constipation alternating with diarrhea, although there has been no loss of control of either his bowel or bladder.  He has had some problems with blood pressure drops, and does feel presyncopal when he stands.  He also reports that he has no feeling in his feet, and that his feet feel like sponges.  This has been present for about nine months.  He has also lost joint position sense in his feet for approximately nine months.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

reference_section: The patient relates the persistence of pain since the motor vehicle accident. Symptoms began immediately following the MVA. Because of persistent symptoms, the patient subsequently sought chiropractic treatment. Neck pain is described as severe. Neck pain remains localized and is non-radiating. There are no associated paresthesias. Back pain originates in the lumbar region and radiates down both lower extremities. Back pain is characterized as worse than the neck pain. There are no associated paresthesias.   Stiffness is provoked by attempts at strenuous activity. The patient also reports difficulty sleeping, unable to find a comfortable position. The patient denies any previous back problems. During the day, the pain is exacerbated by strenuous activities. Pain may be eased by resting or recumbency and sitting. The patient's activity level has been significantly restricted. Some improvement has been noted with chiropractic treatment. Since the onset of the problem, the pain has continued at more less the same level. The patient reports that, prior to the present problem described above, there had been no episodes of neck or lower back pain.

reference_section: This 17-year-old male was fighting with some other kids in Juvenile Hall when he felt some pain in his left elbow, causing sudden pain.  He also has pain in his left ankle, but he is able to walk normally.  He has had previous pain in his left knee.  He denies any passing out, any neck pain at this time even though he did get hit in the head.  He has no chest or abdominal pain.  Apparently, no knives or guns were involved.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hello. Before we begin your visit, I noticed some information missing. Could I verify the information with you?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay I am looking at you for multiple issues today. One of the biggest being swelling on your left leg. Can you tell me more about that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes sure. I got this swelling for almost three years now, and it has been worse for the past two to three months. Sometimes it gets better in the morning when I get up, but then throughout the day it begins to swell again.  Lately it is staying bigger, and it feel uncomfortable with it being so large.  The right leg also swells, but not nearly like the left leg.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How old are you, miss?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I am forty four. My biggest problem is this pain in my left shoulder. I feel as if this low back pain is due to a poor mattress.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you hurt your shoulder?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I don't remember hurting shoulder, but gradually I am losing some mobility.  It is hard for me to get my hands behind my back or behind my head.  I am losing strength in the left shoulder gradually for the last year.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ok let's look at your labs.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: So far white counts are high. In April two thousand five Doctor X Y Z was asked to look at my high white count, but she thought it wasn't a problem and asked me to come for follow up.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any other complaints?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have a lot of frequency with urination, and I get up to pee at night at least two to three times.   Also, I have gained weight, I think about twelve pounds since March.  Right now, I am two eighty four pounds.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. So, I can see that your blood pressure is staying stable.  You do take Atenolol twelve point five M G per day and Lasix as needed.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's correct. It makes me pee so much. I do not take it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How about chest pain or shortness of breath?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No chest pain, but I am gradually feeling short of breath.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What work you do?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I work for the city of Wichita as bus dispatcher. My work demands sitting a lot, and just really does not move around much.  But towards the end of the day my leg swells up.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay that's okay.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I need cholesterol check right?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, you do, but all the other labs are normal.

reference_section: The patient is a 44-year-old white female who is here today with multiple problems.  The biggest concern she has today is her that left leg has been swollen.  It is swollen for three years to some extent, but worse for the past two to three months.  It gets better in the morning when she is up, but then through the day it begins to swell again.  Lately it is staying bigger and she somewhat uncomfortable with it being so large.  The right leg also swells, but not nearly like the left leg.  The other problem she had was she has had pain in her shoulder and back.  These occurred about a year ago, but the pain in her left shoulder is of most concern to her.  She feels like the low back pain is just a result of a poor mattress.  She does not remember hurting her shoulder, but she said gradually she has lost some mobility.  It is hard time to get her hands behind her back or behind her head.  She has lost strength in the left shoulder.  As far as the blood count goes, she had an elevated white count.  In April of 2005, Dr. XYZ had asked Dr. XYZ to see her because of the persistent leukocytosis; however, Dr. XYZ felt that this was not a problem for the patient and asked her to just return here for follow up.  She also complains of a lot of frequency with urination and nocturia times two to three.  She has gained weight; she thinks about 12 pounds since March.  She now weighs 284.  Fortunately, her blood pressure is staying stable.  She takes atenolol 12.5 mg per day and takes Lasix on a p.r.n. basis, but does not like to take it because it causes her to urinate so much.  She denies chest pain, but she does feel like she is becoming gradually more short of breath.  She works for the city of Wichita as bus dispatcher, so she does sit a lot, and just really does not move around much.  Towards the end of the day her leg was really swollen.  I reviewed her lab work.  Other than the blood count her lab work has been pretty normal, but she does need to have a cholesterol check.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi there! What brings you back to see me so soon?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi! I have had these sores in my mouth.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long have you had the sores?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They started about ten to twelve days ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We have been currently treating your rheumatoid arthritis with methotrexate. How much have you been taking?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, we have tried lots of different treatments and methotrexate has been working well.  I have been on it for ten years now. I have been taking about twenty or twenty five M G of per week.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did we recently increase your dosage? I see in your chart that we have changed your dosage a few times.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: About a year ago we lowered the dosage for twenty five M G to twenty but my arthritis flared up so we went to twenty two point five.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had any side effects from the methotrexate in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. I don't think so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you taking any other medications?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had a sinus infection and the doctor put me on an antibiotic. That was about two weeks ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you know what the antibiotic the doctor gave you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't remember the name of the antibiotic, but I know that I have taken antibiotics before and I didn't have a problem.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long was your antibiotic course?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It was three or four days long. I had to take it three times a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had any allergic reactions to medications?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any history of mouth sores?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you taking anything to help with the pain of the mouth sores?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I took Aspirin a month ago. I started taking it again because my mouth was sore.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any other problems with your skin? Any new rashes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Sorry to side track, but where is your accent from? My family is Cuban and my mom and you speak the same.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What a surprise! I am Cuban. A proud fifty seven year old Cuban.

reference_section: The patient is a very pleasant 57-year old white female, a native of Cuba, being seen for evaluation and treatment of sores in her mouth that she has had for the last 10-12 days.  The patient has a long history of severe and debilitating rheumatoid arthritis for which she has had numerous treatments, but over the past ten years she has been treated with methotrexate quite successfully.  Her dosage has varied somewhere between 20 and 25 mg per week.  About the beginning of this year, her dosage was decreased from 25 mg to 20 mg, but because of the flare of the rheumatoid arthritis, it was increased to 22.5 mg per week.  She has had no problems with methotrexate as far as she knows.  She also took an NSAID about a month ago that was recently continued because of the ulcerations in her mouth.  About two weeks ago, just about the time the stomatitis began she was placed on an antibiotic for suspected upper respiratory infection.  She does not remember the name of the antibiotic.  Although she claims she remembers taking this type of medication in the past without any problems.  She was on that medication three pills a day for three to four days.  She notes no other problems with her skin.  She remembers no allergic reactions to medication.  She has no previous history of fever blisters.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: Hello, miss. How are you feeling today?

turns.text: Do you have a history of allergies?

turns.text: Yeah, I do. I had them all the time when I lived in Seattle, but they got a lot worse when I moved here. I am a strong German woman and I hate how something as little as allergies gets the best of me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Your notes say you took Allegra after, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Correct. I tried out Allegra last summer, but I don't know if it was doing its job. I tried it again two weeks ago because my allergies were getting bad, but it still didn't work.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Your notes state you've tried some nasal sprays, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I did. I wanted to see if they would work.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Were you prescribed these nasal sprays?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope. I bought them at my local pharmacy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Sounds good. I'm looking at your medical history, and it sates here you have asthma too, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I've had it for a long time, but it hasn't gotten worse.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Do you think you need any medication to help alleviated your asthma?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. It doesn't bother me as much as my allergies.

reference_section: This 23-year-old white female presents with complaint of allergies.  She used to have allergies when she lived in Seattle but she thinks they are worse here.  In the past, she has tried Claritin, and Zyrtec.  Both worked for short time but then seemed to lose effectiveness.  She has used Allegra also.  She used that last summer and she began using it again two weeks ago.  It does not appear to be working very well.  She has used over-the-counter sprays but no prescription nasal sprays.  She does have asthma but doest not require daily medication for this and does not think it is flaring up.

turns.text: Good afternoon, sir. Did you see the nurse already?

turns.text: Yes, I just saw her.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great, you're seventy eight years old, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I'm not as young as I used to be.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Who is? What seems to be the problem today, sir?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have right hand pain, and it's been there for a while now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you having numbness sir?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, and I can't move it very well, either.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Which fingers are you having these symptoms in?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I told you it's all in the right hand, but it's in the index and middle fingers.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are your fingers catching?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What does that mean, doctor?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you having any problems extending your fingers?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, they seem to lock up when I try to extend my fingers.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you seen another doctor for this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I had an E M G and it showed, um, carpal tunnel on both hands.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's in both hands, but the right is worse than the left, correct?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, that's correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What treatments have you had for this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I only had an injection so far.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did this help at all?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, some, but it was really only temporary relief. Is there surgery for this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I think you'd be a good candidate for surgery.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What are the risks of infection from the surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's less than one percent. We use prophylactic antibiotics to control for infection the entire time.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Even though it's on my hand, will I be asleep for this procedure?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, you won't feel a thing.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, yes. I'd like to do the surgery.

reference_section: This is a 78-year-old male who is complaining of right hand pain and numbness with decreased range of the middle index finger and right middle finger complaining of catching and locking.  The patient was diagnosed with carpal tunnel syndrome on bilateral hands the right being worse than the left.  He had positive EMG findings as well as clinical findings.  The patient did undergo an injection, which only provided him with temporary relief and is for this reason, he has consented to undergo the above-named procedure. All risks as well as complications were discussed with the patient and consent was obtained.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.text: No, I've never smoked. I have tried a beer once, but I never liked it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, never did that.

reference_section: Married. One son deceased. Salesperson. Denied tobacco/ETOH/illicit drug use.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you going to visit rehab?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, what choice do I have?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, please do visit Mercy Manor for P T and Rehab.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I will.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That will help your right side hip pain.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think so too.

reference_section: Right hip pain, the patient to undergo physical therapy and rehabilitation at Mercy Manor.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you tell me about your Immunizations?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I had them all.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good, looks like you are up to date.

reference_section: Up-to-date.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Welcome back to the clinic. How are you feeling today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you. I am doing better.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It looks like we are following up on your severe osteoarthritis in both knees. And you also have been experiencing some flexion contracture limitations.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um hum.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How is your physical therapy going?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It is going really well. She kicks my butt but it seems to be helping. Doing my exercises at home is really helping.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Were you not doing them in the beginning?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I wasn't. She got on me to start doing them and I have definitely seen the difference.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you experienced any worsening of pain since you were last seen?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, the right knee is worse than the left? It mostly hurts after physical therapy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you describe what the pain feels like?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It feels achy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Is it a continuous pain, or?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. It is not all the time. Every once and a while. It feels stiff all the time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any weakness or instability?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any burning sensations associated with the pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long have you been dealing with this?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Several months.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had any trouble sleeping?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. When I sit down or lie down at night there's no pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, the pain is when you are weight bearing, right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. And it hurts when I move around. It makes it difficult to do things.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you noticed any pain with the cold weather change?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I have not noticed anything.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I am just going to take a look here.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I don't see any swelling or redness. And I don't feel any warmth coming from the area. Have you noticed any of these symptoms?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any radiating pain through the knees here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any pain any where else in the body?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, just the knees.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, no pain in the hips or back?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

reference_section: The patient presents today for follow up of osteoarthritis Grade IV of the bilateral knees and flexion contracture, doing great.  Physical therapy is helping. The subjective pain is on the bilateral knees right worse than left. Pain:  Localized to the bilateral knees right worse than left. Quality:  There is no swelling, no redness, or warmth.  The pain is described as aching occasionally.  There is no burning.  Duration:  Months. Associated symptoms:  Includes stiffness and weakness.  There is no sleep loss and no instability.   Hip Pain:  None.  Back pain: None.  Radicular type pain:  None.  Modifying factors: Includes weight bearing pain and pain with ambulation.  There is no sitting, and no night pain.  There is no pain with weather change.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi, what is going on?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She was doing well until this morning, but now she can barely move her right arm and is having speech issues. She can't seem to comprehend words. I think it is a stroke.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: We see this a lot at A B C Medical Center. I am glad you came. You just saw Doctor H, right?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yes. We did a C T head scan and labs.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay. Where is she living? With you?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No. She is at the Life Care Center.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ma'am, do you have headache or chest pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What? What? Huh?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She has not complained of anything like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ma'am. Do you have vision issues?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What? I can see. Of course I can see.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any shortness of breath?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She is breathing fine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have your symptoms improved at all? Or have they worsened since this morning?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: No. They have stayed constant.

reference_section: The patient was doing well until this morning when she was noted to have right-sided arm weakness with speech difficulties. She was subsequently sent to ABC Medical Center for evaluation and treatment. At ABC, the patient was seen by Dr. H including labs and a head CT which is currently pending. The patient has continued to have right-sided arm and hand weakness, and has difficulty expressing herself. She does seem to comprehend words. The daughter states the patient is in the Life Care Center, and she believes this started this morning. The patient denies headache, visual changes, chest pain and shortness of breath. These changes have been constant since onset this morning, have not improved or worsened, and the patient notes no modifying factors.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I think you have a muscular strain.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So right side shoulder strain and maybe a little bit of nerve compression.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh really!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Maybe. I will do further evaluation and treatment.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: Right shoulder pain, most likely secondary to muscular strain.  He does have a very mild evidence of impingement.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Can you tell me more about your daughter, ma'am?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Sure, well she's fourteen now, um, she's right handed, and she just started high school.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Has she ever had surgery?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Yeah, she had an, um, lipomyomeningocele repair when she was about three days old, and then again when she was three and a half years old.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When was her last surgery?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: Um, it was in March of nineteen ninety five.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did she do following the second surgery?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She did well, honestly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, what brings you in for a visit today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I've been having some leg pain on the side of my legs.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long have you had this pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's been several months at this point.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: When is your pain the worst?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it's the worst at night, I have to take medicine for the pain.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What do you take?

turns.speaker: guest_family
turns.text: She takes Advil, Motrin, and Tylenol P M.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Wow, that's a lot. Looks like you have some patch sensory loss in the L four to S one region. Are you going to the bathroom regularly?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, there's no problems there. I do have some loss of feeling in my big toe and calf though.

reference_section: Briefly, she is a 14-year-old right handed female who is in 9th grade, who underwent a lipomyomeningocele repair at 3 days of age and then again at 3-1/2 years of age.  The last surgery was in 03/95.  She did well; however, in the past several months has had some leg pain in both legs out laterally, worsening at night and requiring Advil, Motrin as well as Tylenol PM. Denies any new bowel or bladder dysfunction or increased sensory loss.  She had some patchy sensory loss from L4 to S1.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: How is the patient's condition now?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, he has improved clinically but would require acute care.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Oh, I see.

reference_section: Clinically improved, however, requiring acute care.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good morning, ma'am. Can you confirm your age for me, please?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good morning, I'm sixty five years old, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you recovering from your operation?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm doing okay. Can you remind me what operation I had?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Um, we did a left upper lobectomy for your stage I A non small cell lung cancer.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Absolutely, do you have the results of your pelvic C T?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I have the report right here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Thank you, so this shows an enlarging simple cyst of the left kidney.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What can we do about this?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Well, that's why we did the barium swallow, which showed a small hiatal hernia with minimal reflux.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, yeah, I remember that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, I have your x rays from November twenty third two thousand nine here, we did an A P and lateral view, and they're normal.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, well that's good too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you having any pain with swallowing food?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I get some chest pain, but I'd say it's pretty mild. Look at my calf, doctor, it's much bigger than the right one.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Chest pain is probably due to tertiary contractions with some delayed emptying. Is it tender?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, there's no real tenderness.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How long has this calf been enlarged?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, it's been several months at this point.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had D V T?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, um, in nineteen seventy five, and in nineteen eighty five.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you having any abnormal weight loss?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, everything is normal there, and I'm eating normally.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about any cold or flu symptoms? Any fever or chills?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, that's all fine too.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any new aches or pains?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, all my muscles feel pretty good.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you had a cough, or coughed up any blood.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's a negative, doctor.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What about shortness of breath while at rest or difficulty breathing with exercise?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, that's normal too. I'm breathing just fine.

reference_section: The patient is a 65-year-old female who underwent left upper lobectomy for stage IA non-small cell lung cancer.  She returns for a routine surveillance visit. She has undergone since her last visit an abdominopelvic CT, which shows an enlarging simple cyst of the left kidney.  She underwent barium swallow, which demonstrates a small sliding hiatal hernia with minimal reflux.  She has a minimal delayed emptying secondary tertiary contractions.  PA and lateral chest x-ray from the 11/23/09 was also reviewed, which demonstrates no lesions or infiltrates.  Review of systems, the patient continues to have periodic odynophagia and mid thoracic dysphagia.  This most likely is secondary to tertiary contractions with some delayed emptying.  She has also had increased size of the left calf without tenderness, which has not resolved over the past several months.  She has had a previous DVT in 1975 and 1985.  She denies weight loss, anorexia, fevers, chills, headaches, new aches or pains, cough, hemoptysis, shortness of breath at rest, or dyspnea on exertion.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's talk about your family's medical history.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hm, well both my father and my brother had colon cancer. My daughter was detected with breast cancer.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you remember what her age was?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, she was forty.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I see. Anything else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Well, I have a heart condition and high blood pressure. I also had a stroke.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay.

reference_section: Positive for heart disease, hypertension and cerebrovascular accidents.  Family history is positive for colon cancer affecting her father and a brother.  The patient has a daughter who was diagnosed with breast cancer at age 40.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any fever?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No nausea and vomiting or black stool? Did you notice any blood in your stools?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope, nothing like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you notice any blood in urine or painful urination?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, any chest pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, no.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any shortness of breath, cough or cold like symptoms?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: No diabetes or thyroid problem, right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Absolutely not!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Looks like you have no history of C V A or stroke.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Correct.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Everything else looks fine.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Cool.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Your eyes, nose, and throat look good.

reference_section: CONSTITUTIONAL:  No fever. ENT:  Not remarkable. RESPIRATORY:  No cough or shortness of breath. CARDIOVASCULAR:  The patient denies chest pain. GASTROINTESTINAL:  No nausea.  No vomiting.  No history of GI bleed. GENITOURINARY:  No dysuria.  No hematuria. ENDOCRINE:  Negative for diabetes or thyroid problems. NEUROLOGIC:  No history of CVA or TIA. Rest of review of systems is not remarkable.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you doing miss? How are your sugar numbers coming along?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm doing good. Thank you. Sugar has consistently been one hundred and thirty five or under it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you checking it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have a glucose monitor at home I'm using that only.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Nice. Did you eat anything in the morning today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I'm fasting for my test.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, let's see. We have an Accu Chek here in our office. I will do a quick sugar test for you, and this will be a fasting sugar test. It will be just a quick prick on your finger.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Don't worry doctor. I'm used to poking my finger all the time.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let's see what we got here. Your reading says one hundred and twenty. I will write it down for my record. Are you being active?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I'm exercising as a rule three times every week. I don't miss it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you feel any tingling or numbness or any kind of cramps?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any kind of blurry vision?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any weight loss?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not that I notice.

reference_section: Overall, she has been doing well.  Her blood sugars have usually been less than or equal to 135 by home glucose monitoring.  Her fasting blood sugar today is 120 by our Accu-Chek.  She is exercising three times per week.  Review of systems is otherwise unremarkable.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How did your last visit go with the cardiologist?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It looks like they diagnosed you with sick sinus syndrome. Do you have any questions about this new diagnosis?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, she explained everything to me. I'm planning to follow-up with her in the next two weeks.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great. So it looks like your past medical history is the same? Nothing new other than the sick sinus syndrome.

reference_section: Sick sinus syndrome.  The rest of her past medical history remained the same.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So Mister J, where do you stay?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh, I stay at a care facilit. It's very near to your clinic. Have you heard about this place called South Valley Care Center?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh yes, I have heard of it.

citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How are you Mister James?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have been better!

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh, tell me what's going on with you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have this leg pain on my left side.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hm, left leg pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah.

reference_section: Left leg pain.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had an allergic reaction to drugs you've taken in the past?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: More than once. I've reacted poorly to sulfa drugs, penicillin, and some mycins. I also think I'm allergic to contrast medium.

citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hey, do you smoke cigarettes?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes I do smoke. Do you?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Nope. Are you planning on quitting?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I just smoke one pack per day, it's not bad.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Oh my God. No. It is bad. You should think about quitting.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay I will think about it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Where do you work?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I work at local christmas tree farm.

reference_section: The patient works at a local Christmas tree farm.  He smokes cigarettes approximately one pack per day.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you still working?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Retired some time ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What was your profession?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I used to work at a car repair shop called Champion Automotive Company.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Nice. How did you enjoy the work?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I liked it a lot, but there came a time where I knew it was the end of the road for me. I'm really enjoying retirement.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I bet. I have cousin who owns a car repair shop. He's almost always busy.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, it can be a lot sometimes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any smoking, drinking, or hard drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I can confidently say no to each one.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Great to hear.

reference_section: Retired employee of Champion Automotive Co. Denies use of TOB/ETOH/Illicit drugs.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Do you have his full medical history?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I confirmed with his wife. He had a CABG done in ninety one. He has a history of radical prostate cancer for which he underwent a radical prostatectomy and nephrectomy.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: Any additional surgeries?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes. He had lumbar surgery twice before. He suffered from lumbar stenosis many years ago in the sixties and seventies. He's actually due for another lumbar surgery with Doctor Y. He takes Percocet daily for his back pain.  He also has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia.

turns.speaker: guest_clinician
turns.text: I think I got it all down.

reference_section: Includes coronary artery disease, status post CABG in 1991, radical prostate cancer, status post radical prostatectomy, nephrectomy for the same cancer, hypertension, lumbar surgery done twice previously, lumbar stenosis many years ago in the 1960s and 1970s, now followed by Dr. Y with another lumbar surgery scheduled to be done shortly after this evaluation, and hyperlipidemia.  Note that due to back pain, he had been taking Percocet daily prior to his hospitalization.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you have any history of major surgeries?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Nothing major.

reference_section: Nothing significant.
citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good morning, sir.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good morning, doctor.

turns.text: Before we begin, have you ever had surgery?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I had a vasectomy some time ago.

citation: Ben Abacha et al. 2023, EACL, aclanthology.org/2023.eacl-main.168

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Okay, so let's go over your medications. I'd like you to take these to help your muscle spasms.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sounds good.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I've prescribed eight hundred milligrams of Ibuprofen to be taken every eight hours as needed along with Tylenol number three every six hours as needed.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What does the number three stand for?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Tylenol number three is combined with Codeine.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, I see.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And finally, I'm prescribing Methocarbamol seven fifty milligrams which needs to be taken four times a day for maximum relief. Do you have any questions for me?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I think you answered them all.
